# Credo

> Credo is an open source TypeScript framework for verifiable credentials. It is used to build issuers, verifiers, wallets and mediators that exchange SD-JWT VC, mdoc, W3C and AnonCreds credentials over OpenID4VC and DIDComm, on Node.js and React Native.

Credo 0.7 (stable).

# Credo documentation

> Build issuers, verifiers, wallets and mediators for verifiable credentials with Credo, an open source TypeScript framework.

Credo is an open source TypeScript framework for verifiable credentials. You use it to build issuers, verifiers, wallets and mediators that exchange SD-JWT VC, mdoc, W3C and AnonCreds credentials over OpenID4VC and DIDComm, on Node.js and React Native.

## Start here

[Choose your setup](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started.md#choose-your-setup) recommends a platform, protocol, credential format and storage to start with.

- [Installation](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/installation.md): Set up a Node.js or React Native project and install Credo.
- [Your first agent](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/first-agent.md): Configure storage and keys, initialize an agent and create a DID.
- [Verifiable credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/verifiable-credentials.md): Issuers, holders and verifiers, and how protocols and formats fit together.
- [Example setups](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/example-setups.md): Complete agent configurations for a mobile wallet, an issuer and verifier service, a multi-tenant service, a mediator and tests.

## Build by role

- [Issue credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/issuer.md): Run an OpenID4VCI issuer and offer credentials to any compliant wallet.
- [Build a wallet](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/receive.md): Receive, store and present credentials from a mobile or cloud wallet.
- [Verify credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/verifier.md): Request claims with DCQL and verify presentations with OpenID4VP.
- [Run a mediator](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/mediation.md): Relay DIDComm messages for mobile wallets that can't receive them directly.

## Explore the docs

- [Agent setup](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup.md): Storage, key management, caching, multi-tenancy and logging.
- [Protocols](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols.md): OpenID4VC and DIDComm, role by role, and how to use each credential format with them.
- [Credential formats](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats.md): SD-JWT VC, mdoc, W3C Verifiable Credentials, AnonCreds and status lists.
- [DIDs and trust](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust.md): DID methods, X.509 certificates and deciding which issuers to trust.

## Use with AI coding agents

Point your coding agent at [llms.txt](https://credo.js.org/llms.txt), an index of these docs as Markdown. Every page is also available as Markdown by adding `.md` to its URL. See [AI coding agents](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/ai-agents.md).

Ask questions in the [#credo channel on Discord](https://discord.com/channels/1022962884864643214/1179453305856991263), open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/openwallet-foundation/credo-ts/issues), or join the [working group calls](https://github.com/openwallet-foundation/credo-ts/wiki/Meeting-Information).

# Getting started

> What you need to build with Credo, and the order to read the getting started pages in.

Credo is a TypeScript framework for issuing, holding and verifying verifiable credentials. It supports OpenID4VC and DIDComm, and formats such as SD-JWT VC, mdoc, W3C Verifiable Credentials and AnonCreds. This section takes you from an empty project to a running agent.

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 20.19 or later (Credo is tested on Node.js 22 and 24), or React Native. These pages use Expo for React Native.
- A TypeScript project that uses ES modules. Credo is published as ES modules only.

Browsers aren't supported, and Bun and Deno aren't tested. See [Platforms](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/platform-and-environment.md).

## Choose your setup

Four choices come up before you write any code. If you're not sure, start with the default. You can add a protocol or format later, and an agent can use several at once.

| Choice | Default | Pick the other option when | Details |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Platform | Node.js, for issuers, verifiers, mediators and cloud wallets | You build a mobile wallet: use React Native with Expo | [Platforms](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/platform-and-environment.md) |
| Protocol | OpenID4VC | Use DIDComm if you need a lasting connection with messaging between agents, or AnonCreds, or your ecosystem is built on Aries. A wallet can support both | [Protocols](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols.md) |
| Credential format | SD-JWT VC | Your ecosystem asks for another one: mdoc for mobile driving licences, W3C VCs for Open Badges or EBSI, AnonCreds (DIDComm only) for predicates and unlinkable presentations. The EUDI Wallet uses SD-JWT VC and mdoc | [Credential formats](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats.md) |
| Storage | On a server, Drizzle on PostgreSQL for the records, as SQL tables that scale to many tenants and instances, and Askar for the keys. In a mobile wallet, Askar for both | Use SQLite instead of PostgreSQL for a single server instance or local development. A mobile wallet can also use Drizzle on `expo-sqlite` | [Storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage.md) |

The getting started pages use Drizzle on SQLite with Askar for the keys on Node.js, and Askar on React Native. They work for any protocol and format.

## Read in this order

- [1. Installation](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/installation.md): Set up a Node.js or Expo project and install Credo and its storage.
- [2. Your first agent](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/first-agent.md): Create an agent, initialize it, create a DID and shut it down.
- [3. Example setups](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/example-setups.md): Complete configurations for wallets, issuers, verifiers, mediators and tests.

## Where to go next

Once your agent runs, pick the guide for what you're building:

- [Issue credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/issuer.md): Run an OpenID4VCI issuer that wallets receive credentials from.
- [Verify credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/verifier.md): Request and verify presentations with OpenID4VP.
- [Build a wallet](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/receive.md): Receive, store and present credentials in a mobile or server wallet.
- [Use DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm.md): Connect to other agents and exchange messages and credentials over DIDComm.

If you're new to verifiable credentials, start with [Concepts](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts.md). If you use an AI coding assistant, see [AI coding agents](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/ai-agents.md).

# Installation

> Set up a Node.js or React Native (Expo) project and install Credo with its storage and key management packages.

This page sets up a project and installs Credo, its platform package, and the packages for storage and keys. Every agent needs a storage module. On Node.js the next pages store records with [Drizzle](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md) in SQLite and keys with [Askar](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/askar.md). On React Native, Askar stores both. Use Node.js for a server and React Native for a mobile wallet. [Choose your setup](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started.md#choose-your-setup) covers the other choices to make first.

## Set up the project

**Node.js**

Credo needs Node.js 20.19 or later. It's published as ES modules only, so create a project with `"type": "module"`:

```bash
mkdir my-agent
cd my-agent
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
```

Add TypeScript and [tsx](https://tsx.is) to run TypeScript files:

```bash
npm install --save-dev typescript tsx
```

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "module": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  }
}
```

- `"module": "nodenext"` resolves the `exports` of the Credo packages, including subpaths such as `@credo-ts/core/kms`. `"moduleResolution": "bundler"` works too. The older `"node"` resolution doesn't find subpaths.
- `skipLibCheck` is needed because some of Credo's dependencies ship type definitions that don't type-check.

**React Native**

Create an Expo app, or use an existing one:

```bash
npx create-expo-app@latest my-wallet
```

Credo uses native modules, so it doesn't run in Expo Go. Build the app with [Continuous Native Generation](https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/continuous-native-generation/), for example with `npx expo run:android` and `npx expo run:ios` or with EAS Build. Expo's TypeScript and Metro defaults work with Credo's ES modules, so you don't need to change them.

## Install Credo

Keep all `@credo-ts/*` packages on the same version. They depend on each other with exact versions.

**Node.js**

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 @libsql/client @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1
```

`@libsql/client` is the SQLite driver for Drizzle. Keep `drizzle-orm` on the version range shown, which `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage` requires.

**React Native**

Install the peer dependencies of `@credo-ts/react-native` with `npx expo install`, so you get the versions that match your Expo SDK:

```bash
npx expo install expo-crypto react-native-get-random-values @dr.pogodin/react-native-fs
```

| Package | Why Credo needs it |
| --- | --- |
| `react-native-get-random-values` | Secure random numbers. `@credo-ts/react-native` imports it for you, so you don't need a polyfill in your entry file. |
| `expo-crypto` | Hashing in the JSON-LD libraries Credo uses. |
| `@dr.pogodin/react-native-fs` | File system access. `react-native-fs` works too. Importing `@credo-ts/react-native` throws if neither is installed. |

`@credo-ts/react-native` declares `expo-crypto@^15` as its peer range, which only matches Expo SDK 54. With a newer SDK, npm refuses to install Credo with an `ERESOLVE` error. Add an override to your `package.json` first:

```json
{
  "overrides": {
    "@credo-ts/react-native": {
      "expo-crypto": "$expo-crypto"
    }
  }
}
```

pnpm and Yarn print a peer dependency warning instead.

Then install Credo:

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/react-native@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1
```

`@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native` is linked automatically and doesn't need a config plugin. Rebuild the native app after you install it.

The Askar platform package depends on `@openwallet-foundation/askar-shared` with its exact version, and `@credo-ts/askar` needs the same copy. Install a single Askar version: with two versions of `askar-shared` in your project, `agent.initialize()` fails with `Native askar has not been registered yet`.

:::note[pnpm and Bun]

The Askar packages download their native library in an install script. pnpm and Bun don't run install scripts of dependencies unless you allow them. With pnpm, run `pnpm approve-builds`. With Bun, add the package to `trustedDependencies` in your `package.json`.

:::

## Next steps

- [Your first agent](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/first-agent.md) configures the agent and runs it.
- [Storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage.md) compares Drizzle with Askar.

# Your first agent

> Create, initialize and shut down a minimal Credo agent that stores records with Drizzle in SQLite and keys in Askar, and creates a did:key.

This page builds the smallest complete agent: it stores records in an SQLite file with Drizzle and keys in Askar, creates a `did:key`, resolves it and shuts down. On React Native, Askar stores both. You need the packages from [Installation](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/installation.md).

## Create the agent

**Node.js**

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent, ConsoleLogger, type KeyDidCreateOptions, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql'

const agent = new Agent({
  config: {
    logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info),
  },
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    // Records go in the tables of an SQLite file
    storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({
      database: drizzle('file:agent.db'),
      bundles: [],
    }),
    // Drizzle doesn't store keys, so Askar keeps them
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      enableStorage: false,
      store: {
        id: 'my-first-agent',
        // Use a secret from your environment or a secure store in a real application
        key: 'my-first-agent-key',
      },
    }),
  },
})
```

**React Native**

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent, ConsoleLogger, type KeyDidCreateOptions, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native'

const agent = new Agent({
  config: {
    logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info),
  },
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      store: {
        id: 'my-first-agent',
        // Use a key from the device's secure storage in a real app
        key: 'my-first-agent-key',
      },
    }),
  },
})
```

The `Agent` constructor takes three options:

- `dependencies` are the platform implementations of the file system, `fetch`, WebSocket and events. Import `agentDependencies` from `@credo-ts/node` or `@credo-ts/react-native`.
- `modules` adds features to the agent. On Node.js, the `DrizzleStorageModule` stores the records, and the `AskarModule` with `enableStorage: false` is the [key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md) backend. On React Native, the `AskarModule` does both. An agent needs a storage module: without one, `new Agent()` throws `Missing required dependency: 'StorageService'`.
- `config` holds agent-wide settings, such as the logger. See [Agent configuration](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup.md).

`drizzle('file:agent.db')` opens `agent.db` in the current directory. For PostgreSQL and the record bundles of other modules, see [Drizzle](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md). `store.id` names the Askar database and `store.key` encrypts it. On Node.js the Askar database is created at `~/.afj/data/wallet/<id>/sqlite.db`. See [Askar](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/askar.md) for the options and how to choose the key.

## Modules and their APIs

The key you register a module under is the name of its API: `agent.modules.askar` for the module above. `didcomm` and `openid4vc` are also available as `agent.didcomm` and `agent.openid4vc` when you register them under those keys. Default modules, such as DIDs, key management and SD-JWT VC, are always registered and have their APIs at the top level, for example `agent.dids` and `agent.kms`.

TypeScript infers these APIs from the `modules` you pass, so using a module you didn't register is a type error. [Agent configuration](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup.md) lists the default modules and shows how to type an agent you pass around.

## Initialize

```ts
await agent.initialize()
```

`initialize()` opens the storage and the Askar store, creates the store on the first run, and checks that the storage is up to date for this version of Credo. Call it once, before you use the agent.

## Create and resolve a DID

```ts
const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({
  method: 'key',
  options: {
    createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } },
  },
})

if (didState.state !== 'finished') {
  throw new Error(`Creating the DID failed: ${didState.state === 'failed' ? didState.reason : didState.state}`)
}

const didDocument = await agent.dids.resolveDidDocument(didState.did)
console.log(JSON.stringify(didDocument.toJSON(), null, 2))
```

`agent.dids.create()` creates an Ed25519 key in Askar, stores a DID record that links the DID to the key, and returns the `did:key`. `resolveDidDocument()` resolves the DID to its DID document, and throws if that fails. See [DIDs](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust.md) for other DID methods.

## Shut down

```ts
await agent.shutdown()
```

`shutdown()` stops the modules and closes the storage. Call it before your process exits or your app is closed.

## Run it

**Node.js**

Drizzle doesn't create tables, so apply the migrations of the core bundle first, and again after every Credo upgrade. Without them, `initialize()` fails with `no such table: StorageVersion`.

```bash
npx drizzle-storage --bundle core migrate --dialect sqlite --database-url file:agent.db
```

Then run the agent:

```bash
npx tsx src/index.ts
```

The agent logs its startup at the info level and prints the DID document:

```text
INFO: Creating agent with config { ... }
INFO: Agent storage is up to date.
{
  "@context": [
    "https://www.w3.org/ns/did/v1",
    ...
  ],
  "id": "did:key:z6Mkg...",
  "verificationMethod": [ ... ],
  ...
}
```

Run it again and the agent adds a second DID to the same database.

**React Native**

Metro doesn't support top-level `await`, so the React Native version wraps the steps in `runFirstAgent()`. Call it from your app, for example in a `useEffect` of your root component, and check the Metro logs for the DID document.

## Next steps

- [Example setups](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/example-setups.md) shows complete configurations for wallets, issuers, verifiers and mediators.
- [Agent configuration](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup.md) describes all agent options.

# Example setups

> Complete Credo agent configurations for a mobile wallet, an issuer and verifier service, a multi-tenant service, a DIDComm mediator and tests.

Each recipe on this page is a complete, type-checked agent configuration for a common deployment. Start from the one closest to what you build. The linked pages explain the options.

## Mobile wallet

Start here if you build a wallet app for phones. This React Native app [receives](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/receive.md) and [presents](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/present.md) credentials with OpenID4VC, and connects to other agents over [DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm.md) through a mediator. Askar stores the data and keys, and keys that must stay in the device's secure hardware use the secure environment backend.

Install the packages from [Installation](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/installation.md), and:

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 @animo-id/expo-secure-environment@^0.1.5
```

```ts
import { AskarKeyManagementService, AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent, ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import {
  DidCommHttpOutboundTransport,
  DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy,
  DidCommModule,
  DidCommWsOutboundTransport,
} from '@credo-ts/didcomm'
import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc'
import { agentDependencies, SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/react-native'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native'

interface WalletAgentOptions {
  // A raw key from Store.generateRawKey(), kept in the device keychain
  walletKey: string
  // Invitation URL of the mediator that receives DIDComm messages for this wallet
  mediatorInvitationUrl: string
}

export function createWalletAgent({ walletKey, mediatorInvitationUrl }: WalletAgentOptions) {
  return new Agent({
    config: {
      logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Warn),
    },
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      askar: new AskarModule({
        askar: NativeAskar,
        store: { id: 'wallet', key: walletKey, keyDerivationMethod: 'raw' },
        // The Askar backend is registered in the kms module below, so it can be the default
        enableKms: false,
      }),
      kms: new KeyManagementModule({
        backends: [new AskarKeyManagementService(), new SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService()],
        defaultBackend: 'askar',
      }),
      openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(),
      didcomm: new DidCommModule({
        // No inbound transports: messages for the wallet go through the mediator
        transports: {
          outbound: [new DidCommWsOutboundTransport(), new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()],
        },
        mediationRecipient: {
          mediatorInvitationUrl,
          mediatorPickupStrategy: DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.PickUpV2LiveMode,
        },
        mediator: false,
      }),
    },
  })
}

export type WalletAgent = ReturnType<typeof createWalletAgent>
```

Askar is the default [key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md) backend. A key goes to the secure environment only when you create it with `backend: 'secureEnvironment'`, which supports P-256 keys and ES256 signatures. `walletKey` is a raw key that you generate once and keep in the device keychain, see [Askar](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/askar.md).

If the wallet only uses OpenID4VC, leave out the `didcomm` module and package. [Mediation](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/mediation.md) explains the pickup strategies.

## Issuer and verifier service

Start here if your organization issues or verifies credentials from its own backend. This Node.js service issues credentials with [OpenID4VCI](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/issuer.md) and verifies presentations with [OpenID4VP](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/verifier.md). It stores its records in PostgreSQL with [Drizzle](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md), its keys in Askar and its cache in Redis, so you can run several instances of it.

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 pg express@^5 ioredis
```
```bash
npm install --save-dev @types/express@^5
```

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent, CacheModule, ClaimFormat, ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import {
  OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile,
  type OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapper,
  OpenId4VcModule,
} from '@credo-ts/openid4vc'
import { RedisCache } from '@credo-ts/redis-cache'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres'
import express from 'express'
import { Redis } from 'ioredis'

function env(name: string) {
  const value = process.env[name]
  if (!value) throw new Error(`Environment variable ${name} is not set`)
  return value
}

// The URL wallets use to reach this service, for example https://issuer.example.com
const publicUrl = env('PUBLIC_URL')

// Issues an SD-JWT VC with the claims you set as issuanceMetadata when creating the offer
const credentialRequestToCredentialMapper: OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapper = ({
  credentialConfiguration,
  holderBinding,
  issuanceSession,
}) => {
  if (credentialConfiguration.format !== OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.SdJwtDc) {
    throw new Error(`Unsupported credential format '${credentialConfiguration.format}'`)
  }

  return {
    type: 'credentials',
    format: ClaimFormat.SdJwtDc,
    credentials: holderBinding.keys.map((holder) => ({
      payload: { vct: credentialConfiguration.vct, ...issuanceSession.issuanceMetadata },
      holder,
      issuer: { method: 'did', didUrl: env('ISSUER_DID_URL') },
    })),
  }
}

const app = express()
const redis = new Redis(env('REDIS_URL'))

const agent = new Agent({
  config: {
    logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info),
  },
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    // Records go in PostgreSQL tables. Run the migrations of the core and openid4vc bundles first.
    storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({
      database: drizzle(env('DATABASE_URL')),
      bundles: [openid4vcBundle],
    }),
    // Drizzle doesn't store keys, so Askar keeps them, in a PostgreSQL database of its own
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      enableStorage: false,
      store: {
        // Also the name of the PostgreSQL database
        id: 'issuer-verifier-keys',
        key: env('STORE_KEY'),
        database: {
          type: 'postgres',
          config: { host: env('POSTGRES_HOST') },
          credentials: { account: env('POSTGRES_USER'), password: env('POSTGRES_PASSWORD') },
        },
      },
    }),
    // Shared by all instances of the service
    cache: new CacheModule({ cache: new RedisCache(redis) }),
    openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({
      app,
      issuer: { baseUrl: `${publicUrl}/oid4vci`, credentialRequestToCredentialMapper },
      verifier: { baseUrl: `${publicUrl}/oid4vp` },
    }),
  },
})

// Mounts the OpenID4VC routes on the Express app
await agent.initialize()
const server = app.listen(4000)

process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
  server.close()
  await agent.shutdown()
  // The agent doesn't close the Redis connection
  await redis.quit()
})
```

`credentialRequestToCredentialMapper` decides which credential the issuer signs for a request. This one signs SD-JWT VCs with a DID that the agent created before, set in `ISSUER_DID_URL`. Before you can offer credentials, create an issuer record. [Issuing credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/issuer.md) covers the mapper, issuer records and offers.

`agent.initialize()` adds the OpenID4VC routes to the Express app, so start the server after it.

Drizzle doesn't create tables. Run the migrations before every deploy:

```bash
npx drizzle-storage --bundle core --bundle openid4vc migrate --dialect postgres --database-url "$DATABASE_URL"
```

## Multi-tenant service

Start here if you host issuers or verifiers for many organizations in one deployment. Each organization is a tenant with its own DIDs, keys and records. See [Multi-tenancy](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md).

Install the packages of the issuer and verifier service, and:

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/tenants@^0.7.2
```

```ts
import { AskarModule, AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent, CacheModule, ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc'
import { tenantsBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/tenants'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc'
import { RedisCache } from '@credo-ts/redis-cache'
import { TenantsModule } from '@credo-ts/tenants'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres'
import express from 'express'
import { Redis } from 'ioredis'

function env(name: string) {
  const value = process.env[name]
  if (!value) throw new Error(`Environment variable ${name} is not set`)
  return value
}

const app = express()
const redis = new Redis(env('REDIS_URL'))

const modules = {
  // The records of all tenants in one PostgreSQL database. Run the migrations of the core,
  // openid4vc and tenants bundles first.
  storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({
    database: drizzle(env('DATABASE_URL')),
    bundles: [openid4vcBundle, tenantsBundle],
  }),
  // Drizzle doesn't store keys, so Askar keeps them: one database, with a profile per tenant
  askar: new AskarModule({
    askar: NativeAskar,
    enableStorage: false,
    multiWalletDatabaseScheme: AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme.ProfilePerWallet,
    store: {
      id: 'multi-tenant-keys',
      key: env('STORE_KEY'),
      database: {
        type: 'postgres',
        config: { host: env('POSTGRES_HOST') },
        credentials: { account: env('POSTGRES_USER'), password: env('POSTGRES_PASSWORD') },
      },
    },
  }),
  // Required: the default cache throws as soon as a second agent context (a tenant) uses it
  cache: new CacheModule({ cache: new RedisCache(redis) }),
  openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({
    app,
    verifier: { baseUrl: `${env('PUBLIC_URL')}/oid4vp` },
  }),
}

const agent = new Agent({
  config: {
    logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info),
  },
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...modules,
    // Tenant agents share the modules of the root agent. The type argument types their API.
    tenants: new TenantsModule<typeof modules>({ sessionLimit: 500 }),
  },
})

await agent.initialize()
app.listen(4000)
```

Replace the default cache: it works with one agent context only, and throws as soon as a tenant uses it. Use `InMemoryLruCache` for a single instance or `RedisCache` for several, see [Caching](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/caching.md). Drizzle keeps the records of all tenants in one database. `ProfilePerWallet` does the same for the keys, with an Askar profile per tenant.

Run the migrations with the tenants bundle:

```bash
npx drizzle-storage --bundle core --bundle openid4vc --bundle tenants migrate --dialect postgres --database-url "$DATABASE_URL"
```

Tenant agents use the modules of the root agent, and the OpenID4VC endpoints route each request to the tenant that owns the issuer or verifier. Create a tenant and set it up through a tenant agent:

```ts
export async function createVerifierTenant(label: string) {
  const tenant = await agent.modules.tenants.createTenant({ config: { label } })

  const verifier = await agent.modules.tenants.withTenantAgent({ tenantId: tenant.id }, (tenantAgent) =>
    tenantAgent.openid4vc.verifier.createVerifier({ clientMetadata: { client_name: label } })
  )

  return { tenantId: tenant.id, verifierId: verifier.verifierId }
}
```

## DIDComm mediator

Start here if the mobile wallets in your DIDComm ecosystem need a mediator. This public Node.js service receives DIDComm messages for wallets without an endpoint of their own, and holds them until the wallet picks them up. It stores records in PostgreSQL with Drizzle, keeps keys in Askar and caches in Redis. See [Mediation](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/mediation.md).

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/core@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/node@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/didcomm@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1 drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 pg ioredis
```

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent, CacheModule, ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { DidCommHttpOutboundTransport, DidCommModule, DidCommWsOutboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/didcomm'
import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
import { didcommBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/didcomm'
import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport, DidCommWsInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { RedisCache } from '@credo-ts/redis-cache'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres'
import { Redis } from 'ioredis'

function env(name: string) {
  const value = process.env[name]
  if (!value) throw new Error(`Environment variable ${name} is not set`)
  return value
}

const redis = new Redis(env('REDIS_URL'))

const agent = new Agent({
  config: {
    logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info),
    autoUpdateStorageOnStartup: true,
  },
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    // Run the Drizzle migrations for the core and didcomm bundles before you start the agent
    storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({
      database: drizzle(env('DATABASE_URL')),
      bundles: [didcommBundle],
    }),
    // Drizzle doesn't store keys, so Askar provides the KMS
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      enableStorage: false,
      store: {
        id: 'mediator-keys',
        key: env('STORE_KEY'),
        database: {
          type: 'postgres',
          config: { host: env('POSTGRES_HOST') },
          credentials: { account: env('POSTGRES_USER'), password: env('POSTGRES_PASSWORD') },
        },
      },
    }),
    cache: new CacheModule({ cache: new RedisCache(redis) }),
    didcomm: new DidCommModule({
      // The public URLs of the HTTP and WebSocket transports, for example behind a reverse proxy
      endpoints: [env('HTTP_ENDPOINT'), env('WS_ENDPOINT')],
      transports: {
        inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port: 4000 }), new DidCommWsInboundTransport({ port: 4001 })],
        outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport(), new DidCommWsOutboundTransport()],
      },
      connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true },
      mediator: { autoAcceptMediationRequests: true },
      // Message pickup is enabled by default. A mediator doesn't need the other protocols.
      mediationRecipient: false,
      credentials: false,
      proofs: false,
      basicMessages: false,
    }),
  },
})

await agent.initialize()

process.on('SIGTERM', async () => {
  await agent.shutdown()
  await redis.quit()
})
```

Run the migrations before you start it:

```bash
npx drizzle-storage --bundle core --bundle didcomm migrate --dialect postgres --database-url "$DATABASE_URL"
```

Queued messages are kept in memory by default, so they're lost on restart and not shared between instances. For production, pass a persistent `queueTransportRepository` to the `DidCommModule`. [DIDComm Mediator Credo](https://github.com/openwallet-foundation/didcomm-mediator-credo) is a complete mediator that can keep the queue in PostgreSQL or DynamoDB.

`autoUpdateStorageOnStartup` migrates the storage when you upgrade Credo. Back up the database first, see [Updating](https://credo.js.org/guides/updating.md).

## Tests

Start here for unit and integration tests of your own code. Each agent gets its own in-memory SQLite database and keeps its keys in memory, so tests don't share state and nothing is written to disk.

```ts
import { after, before, test } from 'node:test'
import { Agent, type KeyDidCreateOptions } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
import { coreBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/core'
import { agentDependencies, NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage, NodeKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { createClient } from '@libsql/client'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql'
import { migrate } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql/migrator'

export async function createTestAgent() {
  // A new in-memory database for every agent keeps parallel tests apart
  const database = drizzle(createClient({ url: ':memory:' }))
  await migrate(database, {
    migrationsFolder: coreBundle.migrations.sqlite.migrationsPath,
    // Give every bundle you add its own migrations table
    migrationsTable: 'credo_migrations__core',
  })

  return new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database, bundles: [] }),
      // Keeps the keys in memory
      kms: new KeyManagementModule({
        backends: [new NodeKeyManagementService(new NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage())],
      }),
    },
  })
}
```

The Node.js [key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md) backend is lighter than Askar and needs no store. DIDComm needs XSalsa20-Poly1305, which only Askar has, so tests that use DIDComm keep the keys in Askar with an in-memory store. A test with Node.js's test runner:

```ts
const agent = await createTestAgent()

before(() => agent.initialize())
after(() => agent.shutdown())

test('creates a did:key', async () => {
  const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({
    method: 'key',
    options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } },
  })

  if (didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the DID failed')
})
```

# Concepts

> Background on verifiable credentials, Credo agents and modules, DIDs and DIDComm, and the platforms Credo runs on.

These pages explain the ideas behind Credo: how verifiable credentials work, what an agent is, and where DIDs and DIDComm fit in. Read them if you're new to verifiable credentials or to Credo. If you want to get an agent running first, start with [Getting started](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started.md).

- [Verifiable credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/verifiable-credentials.md): Issuers, holders and verifiers, credentials and presentations, and how exchange protocols, credential formats, key binding, selective disclosure, status and trust fit together in Credo.
- [Agents and modules](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/agents.md): What a Credo agent is, how modules add functionality to it, and how agent contexts and tenants keep data apart.
- [DIDs and DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/did-and-didcomm.md): What decentralized identifiers and DID documents are, and how DIDComm uses them for messaging between agents.
- [Platforms](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/platform-and-environment.md): The platforms Credo supports, Node.js and React Native, how its packages are published, and which runtimes aren't supported.

# Verifiable credentials

> Issuers, holders and verifiers, credentials and presentations, and how exchange protocols, credential formats, key binding, selective disclosure, status and trust fit together in Credo.

A verifiable credential is a set of claims about a subject, such as a name or a date of birth, signed by the party that makes the claims. Anyone who receives it can check that the claims came from that party and weren't changed. This page explains the model and the terms the rest of the docs use, and links to the section that covers each part.

## Issuer, holder and verifier

Three roles take part:

- The issuer signs a credential and gives it to the holder. A government issuing an ID or a university issuing a diploma are issuers.
- The holder receives the credential, stores it and decides when to share it.
- The verifier asks the holder for credentials and checks them.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Issuer -- issues credential --> Holder
  Holder -- presents credential --> Verifier
  Verifier -. checks signature and trust .-> Issuer
```

The issuer doesn't take part when the holder presents a credential. The verifier only needs the issuer's public key, which it gets from a DID or an X.509 certificate (see [Trust](#trust)).

These docs use *holder* for the role, as the Credo APIs do (`agent.openid4vc.holder`), and *wallet* for the application that takes the holder role for a person, such as a mobile wallet app.

A Credo agent can take any of these roles, and one agent can take more than one. Issuers and verifiers usually run on a server with Node.js. A holder usually runs in a mobile wallet built with React Native, but it can also be a cloud wallet on a server.

## Credentials and presentations

The issuer creates a credential. When the holder shares it, they create a presentation: the credential, or the parts of it the verifier asked for, plus proof that the holder is the one it was issued to. A presentation is bound to the verifier's request, usually through a nonce, so it can't be replayed to another verifier.

## Exchange protocols and credential formats

Credo separates two things:

- An exchange protocol defines how the parties talk: how an issuer offers a credential, how the holder requests it, how a verifier asks for a presentation. Credo supports [OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc.md) (OpenID4VCI for issuance, OpenID4VP for presentation), [DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm.md) (Issue Credential and Present Proof) and the [ISO mdoc](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/mdoc.md) presentation protocols (in person over BLE or NFC, and online through the Digital Credentials API).
- A credential format defines what a credential looks like and how it's signed: [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/sd-jwt-vc.md), [mdoc](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/mdoc.md), [W3C Verifiable Credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/w3c-vc.md) and [AnonCreds](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/anoncreds.md).

Several formats work over more than one protocol, and you can sign, store and verify a credential without any protocol. That's why the docs are split the same way: [Protocols](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols.md) covers the flows, [Credential formats](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats.md) covers what you can do with a format on its own, and pages such as [SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/sd-jwt-vc.md) combine the two.

| Format | OpenID4VC | DIDComm | ISO mdoc |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SD-JWT VC | Yes | No | No |
| mdoc | Yes | No | Yes |
| W3C VC | Yes | Yes | No |
| AnonCreds | No | Yes | No |

Not every W3C data model and signature type works over both OpenID4VC and DIDComm. See [Supported standards](https://credo.js.org/guides/supported-standards.md) for the full matrix. [Getting started](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started.md#choose-your-setup) recommends a protocol and format to start with.

## Key binding

Most credentials are bound to a key that the holder controls. The issuer puts the holder's public key (or a DID that resolves to it) in the credential, and the holder signs each presentation with the private key. Someone who copies the credential can't present it without that key. AnonCreds binds credentials to a link secret instead of a key.

In Credo the holder's keys live in a key management service (KMS). See [Key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md).

## Selective disclosure

Selective disclosure lets the holder share some claims of a credential and keep the rest private:

- SD-JWT VC and mdoc: the issuer signs a salted hash of each claim, and the holder reveals only the claims the verifier asks for.
- AnonCreds: the holder creates a zero-knowledge proof, which can also prove a predicate, such as being over 18, without revealing the date of birth.
- W3C VCs: those secured with SD-JWT (data model 2.0) work like SD-JWT VC. Those signed as a plain JWT or with a Linked Data proof are always shared as a whole.

## Revocation and status

An issuer may need to revoke a credential, or suspend it for a while. With a status list, the issuer publishes a list with one entry per credential, and each credential points to its entry. The verifier fetches the list and checks the entry. Credo supports [Token Status Lists](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/status-lists.md) for SD-JWT VC and mdoc. AnonCreds uses its own revocation registries, and the holder proves the credential isn't revoked as part of the presentation (see [AnonCreds](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/anoncreds.md)).

## Trust

A valid signature only proves who signed a credential. The verifier still has to decide whether it trusts that issuer. Credo identifies issuers in two ways:

- [DIDs](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust.md): the issuer's key is published in a DID document, on a ledger, a web server, or in the DID itself. See [DIDs and DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/did-and-didcomm.md).
- [X.509 certificates](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/x509.md): the issuer signs with a certificate that chains up to a root certificate the verifier trusts. mdoc always works this way, and SD-JWT VC often does.

You tell Credo which issuers to trust per verification, or with a callback on the agent. See [Trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md).

# Agents and modules

> What a Credo agent is, how modules add functionality to it, and how agent contexts and tenants keep data apart.

Everything you do with Credo goes through an agent. This page explains what an agent holds, how modules extend it, and what agent contexts and tenants are.

## The agent

An agent is an instance of `Agent` from `@credo-ts/core`. It holds the configuration, the storage, the keys and the modules for one party, such as an issuer, a verifier, a wallet or a mediator. These roles all use the same `Agent` class. What an agent can do depends on the modules you register.

You pass three things to the constructor:

- `dependencies`: platform-specific dependencies, such as file system access and `fetch`. Import `agentDependencies` from `@credo-ts/node` or `@credo-ts/react-native`. See [Platforms](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/platform-and-environment.md).
- `modules`: the modules to register, by key. A storage module is required.
- `config`: optional agent-wide settings, such as the logger.

```ts
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(),
  },
})

await agent.initialize()
```

`storage` holds the storage and key management modules, such as Drizzle for the records and Askar for the keys on a server. [Storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage.md) helps you choose, and [Your first agent](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/first-agent.md) walks through a complete setup step by step.

## Modules

A module adds functionality to the agent: an API, services, storage records, and sometimes HTTP endpoints or message handlers. Credo is split into packages that each provide one or more modules, so you install only what you use.

- Default modules are always registered: among others DIDs, W3C credentials, SD-JWT VC, mdoc, X.509 and key management. You use them through properties such as `agent.dids`, `agent.sdJwtVc` and `agent.kms`. Register a module under the same key to configure it, for example `dids: new DidsModule({ ... })`.
- Other modules you register yourself, such as `DrizzleStorageModule` or `AskarModule` for storage, `DidCommModule`, `OpenId4VcModule`, `AnonCredsModule` and `TenantsModule`. Their APIs are available under `agent.modules.<key>`.
- `DidCommModule` and `OpenId4VcModule` are also available as `agent.didcomm` and `agent.openid4vc`, but only when you register them under the keys `didcomm` and `openid4vc`.

The agent's type follows from the modules you pass, so TypeScript knows which APIs exist. [Agent configuration](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup.md) covers storage, key management, caching and logging.

## Agent context

Credo keeps the data of one agent or tenant apart from others through an agent context. The context links storage, keys and configuration to an identifier, the `contextCorrelationId`. An agent has one root context. Credo passes the context along for you, so you only see it in callbacks, such as `getTrustedIssuersForVerification(agentContext, ...)`, and when you write your own modules.

## Tenants

With `@credo-ts/tenants`, one agent can host many tenants. Each tenant gets its own agent context, so its own storage and keys, while all tenants share the modules, configuration and transports of the root agent. This uses fewer resources than running an agent per tenant, which matters for hosted issuers, verifiers and cloud wallets. See [Multi-tenancy](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md).

# DIDs and DIDComm

> What decentralized identifiers and DID documents are, and how DIDComm uses them for messaging between agents.

Credo uses DIDs to identify issuers, holders and the keys they sign with, and DIDComm to exchange messages between agents. This page explains the basics of both.

## DIDs

A [decentralized identifier](https://www.w3.org/TR/did-1.0/) (DID) is an identifier such as `did:web:issuer.example.com` that you can resolve to a DID document. You create DIDs yourself: no central party issues them.

The part after `did:` is the DID method. It defines where the document lives and how you create and update it:

- `did:key` and `did:jwk` encode a single public key in the DID itself. Nothing is published.
- `did:peer` is shared only with the other party of a DIDComm connection.
- `did:web` and `did:webvh` are published on a web server under your domain.
- `did:cheqd`, `did:indy` and `did:hedera` are anchored on a ledger.

[DIDs](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust.md) lists the methods Credo supports and shows how to create and resolve DIDs.

## DID documents

A DID document lists:

- Verification methods: the public keys of the DID.
- Verification relationships, which say what each key may be used for, for example `assertionMethod` to sign credentials, `authentication` to prove control of the DID, and `keyAgreement` to encrypt messages.
- Services, such as the endpoint where the DID controller receives DIDComm messages.

A verifier resolves the issuer's DID to get the key that signed a credential. Another agent resolves a DID to find out where and how to send it a message.

## DIDComm

[DIDComm](https://identity.foundation/didcomm-messaging/spec/) is a way for agents identified by DIDs to send each other messages. A message is encrypted for the recipient's `keyAgreement` key and sent to its service endpoint, over any transport, such as HTTP or WebSockets. Credo implements DIDComm Messaging v1, the version the Aries protocols use.

On top of this messaging layer, protocols define specific exchanges: setting up a connection with Out of Band and DID Exchange, issuing credentials, requesting proofs, mediation and basic messages. Credo also still includes the v1 versions of the Connection, Issue Credential and Present Proof protocols. They're deprecated and removed in 0.8, so use DID Exchange and the v2 protocols. A mobile wallet has no public endpoint, so it uses a mediator: an agent that receives and stores messages until the wallet picks them up.

You don't need DIDComm to use DIDs. OpenID4VC uses DIDs or X.509 certificates for keys, and HTTPS and OAuth 2.0 for transport. See [Verifiable credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/verifiable-credentials.md) for how the protocols compare, and [DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm.md) to set it up.

# Platforms

> The platforms Credo supports, Node.js and React Native, how its packages are published, and which runtimes aren't supported.

Credo runs on Node.js and React Native. This page describes what each platform is used for, what you need to know about how Credo is packaged, and which runtimes don't work. [Installation](https://credo.js.org/guides/getting-started/installation.md) has the setup steps.

## Node.js

Use `@credo-ts/node` for agents that run on a server, such as issuers, verifiers and mediators. Credo requires Node.js 20.19 or later. It's tested on Node.js 22 and 24, so use one of those.

Some parts of Credo only run on Node.js: the DIDComm inbound transports from `@credo-ts/node`, and the OpenID4VC issuer and verifier, which serve their endpoints with Express.

## React Native

Use `@credo-ts/react-native` for mobile wallets. It needs `react-native-get-random-values`, `expo-crypto`, and a file system package (`@dr.pogodin/react-native-fs` or `react-native-fs`).

Askar, AnonCreds and Indy VDR are native modules. With Expo, that means you need a development build: Expo Go can't load them.

## ESM only

All `@credo-ts/*` packages are published as ES modules only. Use `import` in your code. A CommonJS project can still load them with `require()` on Node.js versions that support `require(esm)`, but ESM is recommended.

In TypeScript, set `moduleResolution` to `nodenext`, `node16` or `bundler`. Other settings don't read the `exports` field of `package.json`, so subpath imports such as `@credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm` don't resolve.

## Package versions

All `@credo-ts/*` packages are released together and depend on exact versions of each other. Install the same version of every Credo package you use.

## Other runtimes

- Browsers aren't supported. Credo has no storage, key management or platform dependencies for the browser, and the OpenID4VC issuer and verifier depend on Express.
- Bun, Deno and Electron aren't tested. Credo's CI only runs on Node.js. They may work through their Node.js compatibility, but there's no guarantee.

# Agent configuration

> The options of the Credo Agent class, the modules every agent has, and how to start, stop and update an agent.

This page describes what you pass to `new Agent()`, the modules every agent has, and how to start and stop an agent. The other pages in this section cover the choices you make when you set up an agent.

## Choices to make

| Choice | Mobile wallet | Server | Details |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Storage | Askar on SQLite | Drizzle on PostgreSQL, or on SQLite for a single instance or development | [Storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage.md) |
| Key management | Askar, plus the secure environment for keys that must stay in hardware | Askar, with its storage turned off | [Key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md) |
| Cache | The default | The default for one agent, `InMemoryLruCache` with tenants, Redis with several instances | [Caching](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/caching.md) |
| Multi-tenancy | Not needed | Only when one service hosts many isolated issuers, verifiers or wallets | [Multi-tenancy](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md) |

For tests, use Drizzle on an in-memory SQLite database and keep the keys in memory with the Node.js backend.

## Agent options

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `dependencies` | Required. The platform implementations of the file system, `fetch`, WebSocket and events: `agentDependencies` from `@credo-ts/node` or `@credo-ts/react-native`. |
| `modules` | The modules of the agent, keyed by the name of their API. Include a storage module, [Drizzle](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md) or [Askar](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/askar.md): without one, `new Agent()` throws `Missing required dependency: 'StorageService'`. |
| `config` | Agent-wide settings, described below. |

## Config

| Field | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `logger` | `ConsoleLogger` at `LogLevel.Off` | The logger of the agent and its modules. See [Logging](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/logging.md). |
| `autoUpdateStorageOnStartup` | `false` | Update the storage during `initialize()` when it was written by an older version of Credo. See [Storage updates](#storage-updates). |
| `allowInsecureHttpUrls` | `false` | Accept `http://` URLs where HTTPS is otherwise required, such as OpenID4VC endpoints. For local development only. The OpenID4VC module applies it to the whole process, so it also affects other agents in it. |
| `validitySkewSeconds` | `30` | The clock skew, in seconds, allowed when checking the validity period of credentials, status lists and other signed objects. Phones often run a little behind. |
| `getTrustedIssuersForVerification` | none | A callback that returns the DIDs and X.509 certificates to trust for a verification. See [Trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md). |

## Default modules

Credo registers these modules on every agent:

| Key | Module | API |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dids` | `DidsModule` | `agent.dids` |
| `kms` | `KeyManagementModule` | `agent.kms` |
| `sdJwtVc` | `SdJwtVcModule` | `agent.sdJwtVc` |
| `mdoc` | `MdocModule` | `agent.mdoc` |
| `w3cCredentials` | `W3cCredentialsModule` | `agent.w3cCredentials` |
| `w3cV2Credentials` | `W3cV2CredentialsModule` | `agent.w3cV2Credentials` |
| `w3cDataIntegrity` | `W3cDataIntegrityModule` | `agent.w3cDataIntegrity` |
| `x509` | `X509Module` | `agent.x509` |
| `tokenStatusList` | `TokenStatusListModule` | `agent.tokenStatusList` |
| `genericRecords` | `GenericRecordsModule` | `agent.genericRecords` |
| `cache` | `CacheModule` with a `SingleContextStorageLruCache` of 500 entries | none |
| `dcql` | `DcqlModule` | none |
| `pex` | `DifPresentationExchangeModule` | none |

The `kms` module starts without a backend. `AskarModule` adds one, also when Drizzle stores the records. Without Askar, configure a backend yourself (see [Key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md)). The default cache doesn't work with [multi-tenancy](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md), so replace it when you use tenants (see [Caching](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/caching.md)).

## Replace a default module

To configure a default module, pass your own instance under the same key:

```ts
import {
  Agent,
  ConsoleLogger,
  DidsModule,
  JwkDidRegistrar,
  JwkDidResolver,
  KeyDidRegistrar,
  KeyDidResolver,
  LogLevel,
  WebDidResolver,
} from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'

function getAgentModules() {
  return {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    // Same key as the default module, so it replaces it
    dids: new DidsModule({
      registrars: [new KeyDidRegistrar(), new JwkDidRegistrar()],
      resolvers: [new KeyDidResolver(), new JwkDidResolver(), new WebDidResolver()],
    }),
  }
}

const agent = new Agent({
  config: {
    logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Warn),
  },
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: getAgentModules(),
})
```

The API stays where it was, at `agent.dids`. When you pass `resolvers` or `registrars` to the `DidsModule`, your list replaces the defaults, except for `did:key` and `did:peer`, which are always added.

## Module APIs and types

Default modules are at the top level, for example `agent.dids`, also when you replace them. Other modules are under `agent.modules`, for example `agent.modules.askar` or `agent.modules.tenants`. The exceptions are `didcomm` and `openid4vc`: registered under exactly those keys, they're also at `agent.didcomm` and `agent.openid4vc`. Modules without an API, such as `cache`, have no property on the agent.

The `Agent` class infers these types from the `modules` you pass to the constructor. To type an agent you pass to other functions, derive the type from a function that returns the modules:

```ts
export type MyAgent = Agent<ReturnType<typeof getAgentModules>>

export async function createDid(agent: MyAgent) {
  const { didState } = await agent.dids.create({
    method: 'jwk',
    options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } } },
  })
  return didState.did
}
```

`Agent` without a type argument accepts any agent, but loses the types of `agent.modules`.

## Start and stop the agent

```ts
await agent.initialize()
console.log(`Created ${await createDid(agent)}`)

await agent.shutdown()
console.log(`Agent initialized: ${agent.isInitialized}`)
```

`initialize()` initializes the modules: it opens the storage (Askar creates the store on the first run), starts DIDComm transports and adds OpenID4VC routes to the Express app. Then it checks the storage version. Calling `initialize()` on an agent that is already initialized throws.

`shutdown()` stops the modules and their transports and closes the storage. Afterwards `agent.isInitialized` is `false`, and you can initialize the agent again.

## Storage updates

Credo stores the version of its storage format. When you start a newer version of Credo on storage that needs an update, `initialize()` throws `Current agent storage is not up to date`. Set `autoUpdateStorageOnStartup: true` to run the update during `initialize()`, or run it yourself. Credo doesn't back up the storage first, so make a backup before you upgrade. See [Updating](https://credo.js.org/guides/updating.md).

With Drizzle, the database schema has its own SQL migrations, which you run separately. See [Drizzle](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md#run-migrations).

## In this section

- [Storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage.md): Compare Askar and Drizzle, the two storage modules for a Credo agent, and pick the one that fits your platform and deployment.
- [Key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md): Choose and configure the key management backends of a Credo agent (Askar, Node.js, hardware-backed keys on React Native, or your own), and use agent.kms to create keys and sign.
- [Caching](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/caching.md): Choose and configure the cache a Credo agent uses for resolved DID documents, ledger objects and certificate revocation lists.
- [Multi-tenancy](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md): Run many isolated tenants in one Credo agent with the tenants module, choose how their data is stored, and manage tenant sessions.
- [Logging](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/logging.md): Log what a Credo agent does with the built-in ConsoleLogger or your own logger, and choose the log level.

# Storage

> Compare Askar and Drizzle, the two storage modules for a Credo agent, and pick the one that fits your platform and deployment.

Every Credo agent needs a storage module to keep its state between restarts: DIDs, credentials, OpenID4VC issuers and sessions, DIDComm connections, tenants and generic records. Credo ships two, Drizzle and Askar, and one of them stores the records. Without one, `new Agent()` throws `Missing required dependency: 'StorageService'`.

## Which should I use?

| You're building | Records | Keys |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A server | Drizzle on PostgreSQL | Askar, with storage turned off |
| A server with one instance, or local development | Drizzle on SQLite | Askar, with storage turned off |
| A mobile wallet | Askar on SQLite | Askar |
| Tests | Drizzle on [in-memory SQLite](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md#in-memory-database-for-tests) | Node.js backend, in memory. Askar in memory for DIDComm, which needs algorithms only Askar has |

Drizzle scales better on servers: records are SQL tables with indexes that the database can query, and many tenants and instances share one database.

On phones, Askar encrypts the wallet with a key you keep in the device keychain, includes key management, and has no schema migrations to ship with app updates. Drizzle on `expo-sqlite` is an option there too.

Drizzle doesn't encrypt records, so rely on encryption of the database or disk. It also adds SQL migrations, also in non-breaking Credo releases, and Credo doesn't work until you apply them. If you can't run migrations on every deploy, use Askar on PostgreSQL for the records as well: it has no schema and encrypts everything with the store key. For many tenants on Askar, use a [profile per tenant](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md#where-tenant-data-is-stored).

## Askar and Drizzle compared

|  | Askar | Drizzle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Package | `@credo-ts/askar` | `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage` |
| Encryption at rest | Record values and tags are encrypted with the store key | None. Use encryption of the database or disk |
| Key management included | Yes | No, add a backend such as Askar |
| Databases | SQLite, PostgreSQL | PostgreSQL (`pg` driver), SQLite (`libsql` or `expo-sqlite` driver) |
| Platforms | Node.js, React Native | Node.js, React Native (with `expo-sqlite`) |
| Schema and migrations | No schema, nothing to migrate | SQL tables. Run migrations on every Credo upgrade |
| Multi-tenancy | A database or a profile per tenant | One database, rows scoped per tenant |
| Read records outside Credo | No, the data is encrypted | Yes, a table per record type |
| Cursor pagination in queries | No, only `limit` and `offset` | Yes |

Keys aren't records: the [key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md) backend stores them. With Drizzle, Askar usually keeps the keys in a store of its own.

## Move from Askar to Drizzle

A server that already stores its records in Askar can copy them to Drizzle. The keys stay in Askar. See [Migrate from Askar](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md#migrate-from-askar).

To use a storage backend Credo doesn't ship, implement the `StorageService` interface from `@credo-ts/core`.

- [Askar](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/askar.md): Configure Askar for encrypted storage and key management in a Credo agent, on SQLite or PostgreSQL, in Node.js and React Native.
- [Drizzle](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md): Store Credo records in PostgreSQL or SQLite tables with Drizzle ORM, run the migrations, and move an existing Askar agent to Drizzle.

# Askar

> Configure Askar for encrypted storage and key management in a Credo agent, on SQLite or PostgreSQL, in Node.js and React Native.

[Askar](https://github.com/openwallet-foundation/askar) is an encrypted store for records and keys. `AskarModule` registers it as the agent's storage and as a [key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md) backend. It runs on SQLite or PostgreSQL, in Node.js and React Native.

Askar is the default for mobile wallets: it encrypts the wallet, includes key management, and has no migrations to ship with app updates. On a server, [Drizzle](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md) stores the records and Askar keeps the keys, with [storage turned off](#storage-and-key-management). Use SQLite, the default, on phones and for a server with one instance, and PostgreSQL when several instances share the keys. To choose between Askar and Drizzle, see [Storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage.md).

## Install

**Node.js**

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1
```

**React Native**

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1
```

Askar is a native module, so it doesn't run in Expo Go. Use a [development build](https://docs.expo.dev/develop/development-builds/introduction/).

The platform package pins `@openwallet-foundation/askar-shared` to its own version, so use a single Askar version across your project. With mixed versions, npm installs a second copy of `askar-shared` for `@credo-ts/askar`, and `initialize()` fails with `Native askar has not been registered yet`. The Askar to Drizzle migration package needs exactly `0.6.0`; see [Migrate from Askar](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md#migrate-from-askar).

## Configure

**Node.js**

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      store: {
        id: 'my-agent',
        // Load the key from a secret store in production
        key: 'my-agent-store-key',
      },
    }),
  },
})

// Creates the store on the first run, opens it on later runs
await agent.initialize()
```

**React Native**

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native'

// walletKey: created once with Store.generateRawKey() and kept in the device keychain
export async function initializeAgent(walletKey: string) {
  const agent = new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      askar: new AskarModule({
        askar: NativeAskar,
        store: {
          id: 'wallet',
          key: walletKey,
          keyDerivationMethod: 'raw',
        },
      }),
    },
  })

  // Creates the store on the first run, opens it on later runs
  await agent.initialize()
  return agent
}
```

Pass the `NativeAskar` class as `askar`. The `askar` instance export of the platform package is deprecated: it's only set once the platform package has run, which depends on import order.

`store.id` names the store. It's also the root agent's profile, the SQLite directory and the PostgreSQL database name. `agent.initialize()` opens the store, and creates it if it doesn't exist yet. `agent.shutdown()` closes it.

With the wrong key, `initialize()` throws a `CredoError` caused by `AskarStoreInvalidKeyError`. A different `id` or SQLite `path` doesn't fail: it creates a new, empty store. To open an existing wallet, check that the database exists before you initialize.

## Store key

Askar encrypts the store with `store.key`. `keyDerivationMethod` decides how it turns the key into the encryption key:

| `keyDerivationMethod` | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `raw` | Random keys that you keep somewhere safe, such as the device keychain or a secret manager. Skips key derivation, so opening the store is fast. |
| `kdf:argon2i:mod` (default) | Passwords and PINs. Argon2i makes guessing the key slow. |
| `kdf:argon2i:int` | The same, faster and less secure. |

Use `raw` when you can keep a random key in a keychain or secret manager, and Argon2i when the key is something a person types. Generate a `raw` key once with `Store.generateRawKey()` from the platform package: any other string fails when Askar creates the store.

To change the key of an existing store, call `agent.modules.askar.rotateStoreKey({ newKey, newKeyDerivationMethod })` and then update the key in your configuration.

## Databases

### SQLite

The store is a file at `<data path>/wallet/<store id>/sqlite.db`. The data path is `~/.afj/data` on Node.js, and `.afj` in the app's document directory on React Native. To use another file, set the full path of the database file:

```ts
database: { type: 'sqlite', config: { path: '/var/lib/my-agent/agent.db' } }
```

### In-memory SQLite

For tests that need Askar, such as DIDComm tests, keep the store in memory. The data is gone when the agent shuts down. Other tests can use the lighter [Drizzle and Node.js setup](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md#in-memory-database-for-tests).

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAskar, Store } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      store: {
        id: 'test-agent',
        // A random raw key skips the slow key derivation, which keeps tests fast
        key: Store.generateRawKey(),
        keyDerivationMethod: 'raw',
        database: { type: 'sqlite', config: { inMemory: true } },
      },
    }),
  },
})
```

### PostgreSQL

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      store: {
        // Also the name of the Postgres database
        id: 'my-agent',
        key: 'my-agent-store-key',
        database: {
          type: 'postgres',
          config: {
            host: 'localhost:5432',
            maxConnections: 10,
            connectionParameters: { sslmode: 'require' },
          },
          credentials: {
            account: 'credo',
            password: 'credo-password',
          },
        },
      },
    }),
  },
})

await agent.initialize()
```

The store `id` is the database name. On the first `initialize()` Askar creates that database, so the account needs permission to create databases, or you pass a separate `adminAccount` and `adminPassword` in `credentials` for that.

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `config.host` | Host and port, for example `localhost:5432`. |
| `config.maxConnections`, `config.minConnections` | Size of the connection pool. Also available for SQLite. |
| `config.connectTimeout`, `config.idleTimeout` | Timeouts. |
| `config.connectionParameters` | Extra connection string parameters, such as `sslmode`, `sslrootcert` and `application_name`. Parameters that Credo sets itself, such as `host`, `user` and `dbname`, throw. |
| `credentials.account`, `credentials.password` | The account to connect with. |
| `credentials.adminAccount`, `credentials.adminPassword` | Optional account for creating and deleting databases. |

## Storage and key management

`AskarModule` registers storage and a key management backend named `askar`. Turn either off:

| `enableStorage` | `enableKms` | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `true` | `true` | Askar stores records and keys. The default. |
| `false` | `true` | Another module stores records, such as [Drizzle](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md). Askar still creates its store, for the keys. |
| `true` | `false` | You register `AskarKeyManagementService` yourself in the `KeyManagementModule`, for example to make Askar the default next to another backend. See [Key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md#multiple-backends). |

If you add `AskarKeyManagementService` to the `KeyManagementModule` backends and keep `enableKms` on, registering the module throws.

## Multi-tenancy

With the [tenants module](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md), `multiWalletDatabaseScheme` decides where tenant data goes: `AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme.ProfilePerWallet` keeps all tenants in the root store with a profile each, `DatabasePerWallet` (the default) gives each tenant its own store. This also applies when Askar only keeps the keys. Use `ProfilePerWallet`. See [Where tenant data is stored](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md#where-tenant-data-is-stored) for the trade-offs, and for why you shouldn't set a SQLite `path` with `DatabasePerWallet`.

## Manage the store

`agent.modules.askar` (the module's key in `modules`) has methods for store-level tasks:

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `rotateStoreKey({ newKey, newKeyDerivationMethod? })` | Changes the store key. Update your configuration afterwards. |
| `exportStore({ exportToStore })` | Copies the open store to a new store, for example a backup with its own id, key and path. On SQLite, the target file must not exist yet. |
| `importStore({ importFromStore })` | Copies another store, such as a backup, to the configured store location. Call `closeStore()` first. On SQLite, the configured file must not exist yet. |
| `deleteStore()` | Deletes the store and all its data. |
| `closeStore()`, `openStore()`, `provisionStore()`, `isStoreOpen` | Manual control. `initialize()` and `shutdown()` already do this. |

With `ProfilePerWallet` these methods act on the whole store, including all tenants, so they throw when you call them from a tenant agent.

# Drizzle

> Store Credo records in PostgreSQL or SQLite tables with Drizzle ORM, run the migrations, and move an existing Askar agent to Drizzle.

`@credo-ts/drizzle-storage` stores the agent's records in regular SQL tables in PostgreSQL or SQLite, through [Drizzle ORM](https://orm.drizzle.team). You create the database connection, choose the record bundles and run migrations. Drizzle doesn't store keys, so you also need a [key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md) backend, usually Askar.

Drizzle is the storage for servers: records are SQL tables with indexes that the database can query, and many tenants and instances share one database. It doesn't encrypt records, and you run its migrations on every Credo upgrade. To compare it with Askar, see [Storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage.md).

## Install

**PostgreSQL**

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 pg @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1
```

**SQLite**

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 @libsql/client @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.1
```

`@credo-ts/drizzle-storage` requires `drizzle-orm` 0.44 (`^0.44.6`). Version 0.45 doesn't satisfy the peer dependency. It includes `drizzle-kit` for the migration CLI, so you don't install that yourself. The Askar packages provide the key management backend.

Use PostgreSQL with the `pg` driver on servers, and always when several instances share the data. SQLite works for a single instance or local development, with `libsql` on Node.js or `expo-sqlite` on React Native. For another driver, open an issue in the Credo repository: Credo has to map the driver's error codes.

## Configure

**PostgreSQL**

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/node-postgres'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({
      database: drizzle('postgresql://credo:credo-password@localhost:5432/credo'),
      // The core bundle is always included. Add one bundle per module that stores records.
      bundles: [openid4vcBundle],
    }),
    // Drizzle doesn't store keys: Askar provides the KMS, in its own Postgres database
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      enableStorage: false,
      store: {
        id: 'credo-keys',
        key: 'my-agent-store-key',
        database: {
          type: 'postgres',
          config: { host: 'localhost:5432' },
          credentials: { account: 'credo', password: 'credo-password' },
        },
      },
    }),
    openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(),
  },
})

// Run the migrations first: the module doesn't create tables
await agent.initialize()
```

**SQLite**

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({
      database: drizzle('file:agent.db'),
      bundles: [],
    }),
    // Drizzle doesn't store keys: Askar provides the KMS
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      enableStorage: false,
      store: { id: 'credo-keys', key: 'my-agent-store-key' },
    }),
  },
})

// Run the migrations first: the module doesn't create tables
await agent.initialize()
```
