`database` takes any Drizzle PostgreSQL or SQLite database. `drizzle()` accepts a connection string, or a client or pool you created yourself.

The module doesn't create tables. Run the [migrations](#run-migrations) before the first `initialize()`.

## Bundles

A bundle holds the tables for the records of one Credo module. Pass a bundle for every module you use that stores records. Without it, saving or reading such a record throws `Could not find a registered drizzle adapter for record type`.

| Bundle | Import | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `coreBundle` | `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/core` | `@credo-ts/core`. Always included by the module. |
| `didcommBundle` | `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/didcomm` | `@credo-ts/didcomm` |
| `actionMenuBundle` | `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/action-menu` | `@credo-ts/action-menu` |
| `anoncredsBundle` | `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/anoncreds` | `@credo-ts/anoncreds` |
| `openid4vcBundle` | `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc` | `@credo-ts/openid4vc` |
| `drpcBundle` | `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/drpc` | `@credo-ts/drpc` |
| `tenantsBundle` | `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/tenants` | `@credo-ts/tenants` |
| `questionAnswerBundle` | `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/question-answer` | `@credo-ts/question-answer` |

Order the bundles as in this table, so a bundle comes after the bundles it depends on (`actionMenuBundle` uses the connection table from `didcommBundle`). Put your own bundles last.

## Key management

Without a key management backend the agent still initializes, but every key operation throws. The examples above keep the keys in Askar with `enableStorage: false`, so Askar creates a store for the keys only. Back that store up together with the Drizzle database: records such as DIDs refer to keys in it. The Node.js backend from `@credo-ts/node` keeps keys in memory only, so it's for [tests](#in-memory-database-for-tests). See [Key management](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md).

## Run migrations

Credo ships the SQL migrations for each bundle. Run them before you start the agent for the first time, and again after every Credo upgrade: Drizzle storage adds migrations in non-breaking releases, and Credo doesn't work until you apply them. Running the migrations when there's nothing new does nothing.

### With the CLI

The package has a `drizzle-storage` command:

```sh
# PostgreSQL
npx drizzle-storage --bundle core --bundle openid4vc migrate --dialect postgres --database-url "postgresql://credo:credo-password@localhost:5432/credo"

# SQLite
npx drizzle-storage --bundle core migrate --dialect sqlite --database-url "file:agent.db"
```

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `--bundle`, `-b` | A bundle to migrate. Repeat it for every bundle. Required, and the CLI adds no bundles itself, so always pass `--bundle core`. Takes the bundle names from the table above, or a path or package name for your own bundles. |
| `migrate --dialect` | `postgres` or `sqlite`. |
| `migrate --database-url` | The database to migrate. You can set `DRIZZLE_DATABASE_URL` instead. |

Run the CLI with the same Credo version as your agent. The CLI keeps track of applied migrations in a table per bundle, such as `credo_migrations__core`. `drizzle-storage studio --dialect <dialect> --database-url <url>` opens [Drizzle Studio](https://orm.drizzle.team/drizzle-studio/overview) on the database.

### In code

**Node.js**

Each bundle has the absolute path of its migration folders in `bundle.migrations`. Apply them with the Drizzle migrator for your driver, before you initialize the agent:

```ts
import { coreBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/core'
import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql'
import { migrate } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql/migrator'

const database = drizzle('file:agent.db')

// The core bundle first, then the bundles you pass to the DrizzleStorageModule
for (const bundle of [coreBundle, openid4vcBundle]) {
  await migrate(database, {
    migrationsFolder: bundle.migrations.sqlite.migrationsPath,
    // The table names the drizzle-storage CLI uses, so you can switch between the CLI and this code
    migrationsTable: `credo_migrations__${bundle.name.replace('-', '_')}`,
  })
}
```

For PostgreSQL, import `migrate` from `drizzle-orm/node-postgres/migrator` and use `bundle.migrations.postgres.migrationsPath`.

**React Native**

On React Native, use `expo-sqlite` as the driver and the React Native Askar package for the keys:

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/drizzle-storage@^0.7.2 drizzle-orm@^0.44.6 expo-sqlite @credo-ts/askar@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native@0.6.1
```

A phone has its own database, so the app applies the migrations itself. Import the SQLite migrations of each bundle from `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/<bundle>/migrations/sqlite` and apply them with `applyReactNativeMigrations`:

```ts
import { applyReactNativeMigrations, DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
import coreMigrations from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/core/migrations/sqlite'
import { openid4vcBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc'
import openid4vcMigrations from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc/migrations/sqlite'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/expo-sqlite'
import { migrate } from 'drizzle-orm/expo-sqlite/migrator'
import { openDatabaseSync } from 'expo-sqlite'

const database = drizzle(openDatabaseSync('credo.db'))

// Run on every app start, before agent.initialize()
await applyReactNativeMigrations({
  db: database,
  migrate,
  migrations: [coreMigrations, openid4vcMigrations],
})

export const storage = new DrizzleStorageModule({ database, bundles: [openid4vcBundle] })
```

The migrations import `.sql` files, so the bundler has to inline them. Install `babel-plugin-inline-import` as a dev dependency, add the `inline-import` plugin to your Babel config with `extensions: ['.sql']`, and add `sql` to `resolver.sourceExts` in your Metro config.

## In-memory database for tests

For tests, use an in-memory SQLite database and keep the keys in memory with the Node.js backend, so there's nothing to set up or clean up. A new in-memory database is empty, so apply the migrations each time you create an agent:

```ts
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
import { coreBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/core'
import { agentDependencies, NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage, NodeKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql'
import { migrate } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql/migrator'

export async function createTestAgent() {
  // Every in-memory database starts empty, so apply the migrations each time
  const database = drizzle(':memory:')
  for (const bundle of [coreBundle]) {
    await migrate(database, {
      migrationsFolder: bundle.migrations.sqlite.migrationsPath,
      // A migrations table per bundle, as the drizzle-storage CLI uses
      migrationsTable: `credo_migrations__${bundle.name.replace('-', '_')}`,
    })
  }

  return new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database, bundles: [] }),
      // Keys in memory as well, with node:crypto
      kms: new KeyManagementModule({
        backends: [new NodeKeyManagementService(new NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage())],
      }),
    },
  })
}
```

The Node.js backend can't encrypt DIDComm messages, which need XSalsa20-Poly1305. For DIDComm tests, keep the keys in Askar on [in-memory SQLite](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/askar.md#in-memory-sqlite), with `enableStorage: false`.

## Migrate from Askar

`@credo-ts/askar-to-drizzle-storage-migration` copies all records from an Askar store to an empty Drizzle database. Use it when a server that runs on Askar should move to Drizzle, for example to get SQL access to its records. It doesn't move keys: after the migration, Askar stays your key management backend with storage turned off.

In 0.7 the migration package requires exactly version `0.6.0` of Askar, so install `0.6.0` of both the Askar platform package and `askar-shared` for the migration:

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/askar-to-drizzle-storage-migration@^0.7.2 @openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs@0.6.0 @openwallet-foundation/askar-shared@0.6.0
```

1. Stop the agent and back up the Askar store. The migrator doesn't make a backup.
2. Create the Drizzle database and [run the migrations](#run-migrations) for every bundle you'll use. The database must be empty.
3. Run the migration with your current Askar configuration and your new Drizzle configuration:

   ```ts
   import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
   import { AskarToDrizzleStorageMigrator } from '@credo-ts/askar-to-drizzle-storage-migration'
   import { ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core'
   import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
   import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
   import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'
   import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql'
   
   // The Askar config your agent uses today, with storage still enabled
   const askarModule = new AskarModule({
     askar: NativeAskar,
     store: { id: 'my-agent', key: 'my-agent-store-key' },
   })
   
   // The Drizzle config your agent will use: an empty, migrated database and a bundle for
   // every module that stored records in Askar
   const drizzleModule = new DrizzleStorageModule({
     database: drizzle('file:agent.db'),
     bundles: [],
   })
   
   const migrator = await AskarToDrizzleStorageMigrator.initialize({
     askarModule,
     drizzleModule,
     agentDependencies,
     logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info),
   })
   
   // Copies all records from Askar to Drizzle. The keys stay in Askar.
   await migrator.migrate()
   ```

4. Start the agent with the `DrizzleStorageModule` and the same Askar store configuration, with `enableStorage: false`, so Credo still finds the keys.
5. When everything works, you can remove the copied records from the Askar store:

   ```ts
   // Removes the copied records from the Askar store, keeping the keys
   await migrator.deleteStorageRecords()
   ```

   From then on, only open the store with `enableStorage: false`. With storage on, `initialize()` fails because the storage version record is gone.

If a record in Askar has no bundle in the Drizzle module, the migration throws. `skipMigrationForMissingAdapter: true` skips such records instead, and they're lost. For a multi-tenant agent, pass `tenantsModule` and include `tenantsBundle` to migrate every tenant as well. Tenants that had their own Askar database all end up in the one Drizzle database.

# Key management

> Choose and configure the key management backends of a Credo agent (Askar, Node.js, hardware-backed keys on React Native, or your own), and use agent.kms to create keys and sign.

The key management service (KMS) creates and stores keys and does the cryptography with them: signing, verifying, encrypting and key agreement. Credo modules use it for DIDs, credentials, DIDComm and OpenID4VC, and you can call it directly through `agent.kms`. The KMS hands the work to one or more backends.

## Which backend should I use?

| You're building | Use | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A server | Askar | Keys are stored encrypted and survive restarts. With [Drizzle](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md) storing the records, Askar keeps only the keys. |
| A mobile wallet | Askar, plus the secure environment for keys that must stay in hardware | Askar handles everything the secure environment can't, such as verifying, encryption and Ed25519. |
| Tests and other short-lived agents | Node.js, with in-memory key storage | Lighter than Askar: it only uses `node:crypto`, and the keys are gone when the process stops. |
| Keys in a cloud KMS or an HSM | Your own backend | Credo doesn't ship one, but a backend is a single interface. See [Build your own backend](#build-your-own-backend). |

Add the Node.js backend next to Askar to [verify RSA signatures](#verify-rsa-signatures) and other algorithms Askar lacks, for example of an X.509 certificate authority. Verifying with a public key stores nothing. Don't make the Node.js backend a server's only backend for keys it creates: it keeps them in memory, unless you give it a key storage of your own.

### Hardware-bound keys in a wallet

Keys in the [secure environment](#secure-environment-react-native) are created in the phone's secure hardware and never leave it, so a copy of the wallet's data can't sign with them. Use it for the keys that credentials are bound to when issuers ask for it. Under HAIP, an issuer can require a [key attestation](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/authorization.md#wallet-and-key-attestations) that says how the keys are protected, and the EUDI Wallet requires hardware-protected keys for credentials such as the PID. When no issuer asks for it, keep the keys in Askar, because hardware keys come with trade-offs:

- Every signature shows a biometric prompt, so a presentation or a batch issuance asks the user to authenticate for each key it signs with.
- Only P-256 keys and ES256 signatures. DIDs and credentials that need Ed25519 stay in Askar.
- The keys can't be backed up or moved, so on a new phone the user needs new credentials. Changing the enrolled biometrics also invalidates the keys.

## Backends

`KeyManagementModule` is a default module under the key `kms`, registered without backends. `AskarModule` adds the `askar` backend, unless you set `enableKms: false`. For other backends, register `new KeyManagementModule({ backends, defaultBackend })` yourself under the key `kms`, as in the examples below. Import `KeyManagementModule` and the other KMS classes from `@credo-ts/core/kms`.

Credo doesn't check for a backend at startup. Without one, the agent initializes, and every key operation throws `No key management service backend found that supports ...`.

### Askar

`AskarKeyManagementService` (backend `askar`) keeps keys in the Askar store, encrypted with the store key, on Node.js and React Native. See [Askar](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/askar.md).

### Node.js

`NodeKeyManagementService` from `@credo-ts/node` (backend `node`) uses `node:crypto`, so it needs no native library. It supports more algorithms than Askar, such as RSA, P-521 and HMAC. It has two common uses: the only backend of a test or other short-lived agent, and a second backend that verifies what Askar can't (see [Verify RSA signatures](#verify-rsa-signatures)).

It needs a key storage. For a test agent, keep the keys in memory:

```ts
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import { agentDependencies, NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage, NodeKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/node'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    kms: new KeyManagementModule({
      // Keys only live in memory: they are lost when the process stops
      backends: [new NodeKeyManagementService(new NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage())],
    }),
    storage, // Storage, see Agent setup
  },
})
```

:::warning[Keys are kept in memory]
`NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage` is the only key storage that Credo ships. Keys are lost when the process stops, while DIDs and credentials in storage still refer to them. To keep keys, implement the `NodeKeyManagementStorage` interface (`get`, `has`, `set`, `delete`). It receives private keys as JWKs, so encrypt them at rest.
:::

### Secure environment (React Native)

`SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService` from `@credo-ts/react-native` (backend `secureEnvironment`) creates keys in the Secure Enclave on iOS and the Android Keystore, protected with biometrics. It needs `@animo-id/expo-secure-environment` 0.1 (version 0.2 doesn't match the peer dependency range). The package's README lists its platform requirements, such as Android API 30 or higher.

```bash
npm install @animo-id/expo-secure-environment@^0.1.5
```

It only creates P-256 keys, signs with ES256 and deletes keys. It can't verify, encrypt, import keys or generate random bytes, so you always use it next to Askar. See [Askar and the secure environment](#askar-and-the-secure-environment-on-react-native).

### Capabilities

| | Askar | Node.js | Secure environment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Platforms | Node.js, React Native | Node.js | React Native |
| Keys are stored | In the Askar store | In memory, or your own storage | In secure hardware |
| EC curves | P-256, P-384, secp256k1 | P-256, P-384, P-521, secp256k1 | P-256 |
| OKP curves | Ed25519, X25519 | Ed25519, X25519 | No |
| RSA | No | Yes | No |
| Symmetric keys | AES-128, AES-256, ChaCha20-Poly1305 | AES, HMAC | No |
| Sign and verify | EdDSA, ES256, ES384, ES256K | EdDSA, ES256, ES384, ES512, ES256K, RS\*, PS\*, HS\* | ES256, sign only |
| Encrypt and decrypt | AES-GCM, AES-CBC-HMAC, (X)ChaCha20, XSalsa20, AES key wrap, ECDH-ES, HPKE | AES-GCM, AES-CBC, AES-CBC-HMAC, ChaCha20, ECDH-ES, HPKE | No |
| Import keys | EC and OKP keys | EC, OKP, RSA and symmetric keys | No |

## Multiple backends

Every backend has a name (`askar`, `node`, `secureEnvironment`). Credo decides which one handles an operation like this:

1. If you pass `backend`, that backend handles it, or the call throws if it can't.
2. `sign` and `getPublicKey` use the backend that holds the key, which they look up by its key id.
3. Otherwise, the default backend handles it if it supports the operation, and else the first other backend that does. This applies to `createKey`, `importKey`, `randomBytes`, `deleteKey`, `verify`, `encrypt` and `decrypt`.

So pass `backend` to `verify`, `encrypt`, `decrypt` and `deleteKey` when the key isn't in the default backend.

The default backend is `defaultBackend`, or else the first backend in the list. The list starts with the backends you pass to `KeyManagementModule`, and `AskarModule` adds `askar` after them. `defaultBackend` must name a backend in your own `backends` list. So to make Askar the default, add `AskarKeyManagementService` to `backends` yourself and set `enableKms: false` on `AskarModule`:

```ts
import { AskarKeyManagementService, AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent, TypedArrayEncoder } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import { agentDependencies, NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage, NodeKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    storage, // Storage, see Agent setup
    kms: new KeyManagementModule({
      backends: [new AskarKeyManagementService(), new NodeKeyManagementService(new NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage())],
      defaultBackend: 'askar',
    }),
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      // Askar only keeps the keys, and its backend is already in the backends list above
      enableStorage: false,
      enableKms: false,
      store: { id: 'kms-backends-example', key: 'kms-backends-example-store-key' },
    }),
  },
})
```

Then each key goes to a backend that supports it:

```ts
// Askar supports Ed25519, so the default backend creates this key
const ed25519Key = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } })

// Askar doesn't support P-521, so this falls back to the node backend
const p521Key = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-521' } })

// Pass a backend to choose it explicitly
const rsaKey = await agent.kms.createKey({ backend: 'node', type: { kty: 'RSA', modulusLength: 2048 } })

// sign finds the backend that holds the key
const data = TypedArrayEncoder.fromUtf8String('Hello, Credo')
await agent.kms.sign({ keyId: p521Key.keyId, algorithm: 'ES512', data })
```

### Askar and the secure environment on React Native

On a phone, make Askar the default and use the secure environment only for the keys that need hardware protection:

```ts
import { AskarKeyManagementService, AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent, TypedArrayEncoder } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import { agentDependencies, SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/react-native'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native'

export async function initializeAgent(walletKey: string) {
  const agent = new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      kms: new KeyManagementModule({
        backends: [new AskarKeyManagementService(), new SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService()],
        defaultBackend: 'askar',
      }),
      askar: new AskarModule({
        askar: NativeAskar,
        // The Askar backend is already in the backends list above
        enableKms: false,
        store: { id: 'wallet', key: walletKey, keyDerivationMethod: 'raw' },
      }),
    },
  })

  await agent.initialize()
  return agent
}
```

Don't only list the secure environment in `backends` and let `AskarModule` add its backend: the secure environment then comes first and becomes the default, and every P-256 key Credo creates ends up in hardware behind biometrics.

Create a hardware key by passing `backend`. Signing finds the key by its key id:

```ts
export async function signWithHardwareKey(agent: Agent, message: string) {
  // Only P-256 keys and ES256 signatures are supported in the secure environment
  const { keyId, publicJwk } = await agent.kms.createKey({
    backend: 'secureEnvironment',
    type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' },
  })

  const { signature } = await agent.kms.sign({
    keyId,
    algorithm: 'ES256',
    data: TypedArrayEncoder.fromUtf8String(message),
  })

  return { publicJwk, signature }
}
```

To verify a signature from a hardware key, pass the `publicJwk` instead of the key id, so the default backend does it.

### Verify RSA signatures

Neither Askar nor the secure environment supports RSA. You still meet RSA signatures from others, for example X.509 certificate authorities that sign with RSA, or JWTs signed by an external RSA key. Credo can't check those without a backend that verifies RSA, and the error doesn't always say so: an mdoc issued under an RSA certificate authority fails with an error about the certificate chain.

On Node.js, add the Node.js backend next to Askar. A verification with a public key needs no stored key, so the in-memory key storage is enough:

```ts
import { AskarKeyManagementService, AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import { agentDependencies, NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage, NodeKeyManagementService } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    storage, // Storage, see Agent setup
    kms: new KeyManagementModule({
      backends: [
        new AskarKeyManagementService(),
        // Only verifies with public keys passed in the call, so nothing is stored in it
        new NodeKeyManagementService(new NodeInMemoryKeyManagementStorage()),
      ],
      defaultBackend: 'askar',
    }),
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      enableStorage: false,
      enableKms: false,
      store: { id: 'kms-node-verify-example', key: 'kms-node-verify-example-store-key' },
    }),
  },
})
```

Credo then sends RSA verifications to it:

```ts
// Askar can't verify RS256, so Credo falls back to the node backend
const { verified } = await agent.kms.verify({
  key: { publicJwk: { kty: 'RSA', n, e } },
  algorithm: 'RS256',
  data,
  signature,
})
```

On React Native, the Node.js backend isn't available. Add your own backend that only verifies RSA signatures, as described in [Build your own backend](#build-your-own-backend). Paradym Wallet has one, built on `react-native-quick-crypto`: [`RsaVerificationKeyManagementService`](https://github.com/animo/paradym-wallet/blob/226083df04e183b06e7a379b2b4938bbafe84f3c/packages/sdk/src/kms/RsaVerificationKeyManagementService.ts). Register it next to the other backends:

```ts
new KeyManagementModule({
  backends: [
    new AskarKeyManagementService(),
    new SecureEnvironmentKeyManagementService(),
    new RsaVerificationKeyManagementService(),
  ],
  defaultBackend: 'askar',
})
```

## Build your own backend

A backend is a class that implements `KeyManagementService` from `@credo-ts/core/kms`. Write one to keep keys in a cloud KMS such as Google Cloud KMS or AWS KMS, in an HSM, or on a platform Credo has no backend for. Implement only what your key store can do, and leave the rest to Askar or the Node.js backend in the same agent.

Credo uses these parts of the interface to route operations:

| Member | What Credo expects |
| --- | --- |
| `backend` | A unique name. Users pass it as `backend` to choose this backend. |
| `isOperationSupported(agentContext, operation)` | `true` for each operation and algorithm the backend handles, such as `createKey` for P-256 keys or `sign` with ES256. Credo never sends this backend an operation it returns `false` for. A call that names this backend for such an operation throws. |
| `getPublicKey(agentContext, keyId)` | The public JWK, with `kid`, or `null` when the backend doesn't hold the key. For `sign` and `getPublicKey`, Credo asks each backend in turn to find the one that holds a key. |
| `createKey`, `importKey`, `deleteKey` | Manage keys. Return the key id that Credo stores in DIDs and credential records, so keep it stable. Respect `options.keyId` when it's set. |
| `sign`, `verify`, `encrypt`, `decrypt`, `randomBytes` | The cryptography. Throw `KeyManagementAlgorithmNotSupportedError` or `KeyManagementError` for what you don't support. |

This backend creates P-256 keys in a cloud KMS and signs with them. The `CloudKmsClient` interface stands in for your KMS SDK:

```ts
import { createHash, createPublicKey } from 'node:crypto'
import { type AgentContext, utils } from '@credo-ts/core'
import {
  derEcSignatureToRaw,
  KeyManagementAlgorithmNotSupportedError,
  KeyManagementError,
  type KeyManagementService,
  type KmsCreateKeyOptions,
  type KmsCreateKeyReturn,
  type KmsCreateKeyType,
  type KmsJwkPublic,
  type KmsOperation,
  type KmsSignOptions,
  type KmsSignReturn,
  PublicJwk,
} from '@credo-ts/core/kms'

// The calls the backend needs from your cloud KMS SDK. With Google Cloud KMS these are
// `createCryptoKey`, `getPublicKey` and `asymmetricSign` of its `KeyManagementServiceClient`.
export interface CloudKmsClient {
  createP256SigningKey(keyId: string): Promise<void>
  // PEM encoded public key, or null when the key doesn't exist
  getPublicKeyPem(keyId: string): Promise<string | null>
  // Signs a SHA-256 digest and returns a DER encoded ECDSA signature
  signDigest(keyId: string, digest: Uint8Array): Promise<Uint8Array>
}

export class CloudKeyManagementService implements KeyManagementService {
  public readonly backend = 'cloud'

  public constructor(private client: CloudKmsClient) {}

  // Credo only routes the operations this returns true for to this backend
  public isOperationSupported(_agentContext: AgentContext, operation: KmsOperation): boolean {
    if (operation.operation === 'createKey') {
      return operation.type.kty === 'EC' && operation.type.crv === 'P-256'
    }
    return operation.operation === 'sign' && operation.algorithm === 'ES256'
  }

  // Credo asks each backend for a key id, so return null for keys this backend doesn't hold
  public async getPublicKey(_agentContext: AgentContext, keyId: string): Promise<KmsJwkPublic | null> {
    const pem = await this.client.getPublicKeyPem(keyId)
    if (!pem) return null

    const publicJwk = PublicJwk.fromUnknown(createPublicKey(pem).export({ format: 'jwk' }))
    publicJwk.keyId = keyId
    return publicJwk.toJson()
  }

  public async createKey<Type extends KmsCreateKeyType>(
    agentContext: AgentContext,
    options: KmsCreateKeyOptions<Type>
  ): Promise<KmsCreateKeyReturn<Type>> {
    if (options.type.kty !== 'EC' || options.type.crv !== 'P-256') {
      throw new KeyManagementAlgorithmNotSupportedError(`kty '${options.type.kty}'`, this.backend)
    }

    // Credo stores the key id in DIDs and credential records, so keep it stable
    const keyId = options.keyId ?? utils.uuid()
    await this.client.createP256SigningKey(keyId)

    const publicJwk = await this.getPublicKey(agentContext, keyId)
    if (!publicJwk) throw new KeyManagementError(`Key '${keyId}' was not found after creating it`)

    // The generic return type follows from the requested key type, which is checked above
    return { keyId, publicJwk } as KmsCreateKeyReturn<Type>
  }

  public async sign(_agentContext: AgentContext, options: KmsSignOptions): Promise<KmsSignReturn> {
    if (options.algorithm !== 'ES256') {
      throw new KeyManagementAlgorithmNotSupportedError(`algorithm '${options.algorithm}'`, this.backend)
    }

    const digest = createHash('sha256').update(options.data).digest()
    const derSignature = await this.client.signDigest(options.keyId, digest)

    // JWA signatures are the raw r || s values, cloud KMSs return them DER encoded
    return { signature: derEcSignatureToRaw(derSignature, 'P-256') }
  }

  // isOperationSupported returns false for these, so Credo uses another backend for them
  public async verify(): Promise<never> {
    throw new KeyManagementError(`Verifying is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`)
  }

  public async importKey(): Promise<never> {
    throw new KeyManagementError(`Importing keys is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`)
  }

  public async deleteKey(): Promise<never> {
    throw new KeyManagementError(`Deleting keys is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`)
  }

  public async encrypt(): Promise<never> {
    throw new KeyManagementError(`Encrypting is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`)
  }

  public async decrypt(): Promise<never> {
    throw new KeyManagementError(`Decrypting is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`)
  }

  public randomBytes(): never {
    throw new KeyManagementError(`Generating random bytes is not supported by backend '${this.backend}'`)
  }
}
```

Signing has two traps with most cloud KMSs. They sign a digest, so hash the data yourself with the hash of the JWA algorithm (SHA-256 for ES256). And they return ECDSA signatures DER encoded, while JWA uses the raw `r || s` form: convert them with `derEcSignatureToRaw`.

Register the backend in `KeyManagementModule`. Here it's the default, so Credo creates P-256 keys in the cloud KMS, and Askar creates the other keys, verifies and encrypts:

```ts
import { AskarKeyManagementService, AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { KeyManagementModule } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'

export function createAgent(cloudKmsClient: CloudKmsClient) {
  return new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      storage, // Storage, see Agent setup
      kms: new KeyManagementModule({
        backends: [new CloudKeyManagementService(cloudKmsClient), new AskarKeyManagementService()],
        // P-256 keys are created in the cloud KMS. Askar creates the other keys, such as Ed25519,
        // and verifies and encrypts.
        defaultBackend: 'cloud',
      }),
      askar: new AskarModule({
        askar: NativeAskar,
        enableStorage: false,
        enableKms: false,
        store: { id: 'cloud-kms-example', key: 'cloud-kms-example-store-key' },
      }),
    },
  })
}
```

Import from `@credo-ts/core` before `@credo-ts/core/kms` in the file your app loads first, as the `kms` entry point doesn't load the `reflect-metadata` polyfill that Credo needs.

## Use `agent.kms`

```ts
const { keyId, publicJwk } = await agent.kms.createKey({
  type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' },
})

const data = TypedArrayEncoder.fromUtf8String('Hello, Credo')
const { signature } = await agent.kms.sign({ keyId, algorithm: 'EdDSA', data })

const result = await agent.kms.verify({
  key: { publicJwk },
  algorithm: 'EdDSA',
  data,
  signature,
})
console.log(result.verified) // true
```

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `createKey({ type, keyId?, backend? })` | Creates a key and returns `{ keyId, publicJwk }`. `type` is for example `{ kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' }` or `{ kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' }`. |
| `createKeyForSignatureAlgorithm({ algorithm })` | Creates a key that fits a JWA signature algorithm, such as `ES256`. |
| `importKey({ privateJwk })` | Imports a private JWK. Set `privateJwk.kid` to choose the key id. |
| `getPublicKey({ keyId })` | Returns the public JWK of a key. |
| `sign({ keyId, algorithm, data })` | Signs `data` (a `Uint8Array`). |
| `verify({ key, algorithm, data, signature })` | Verifies with `key: { keyId }` or `key: { publicJwk }`. Returns `{ verified }`. |
| `encrypt(...)`, `decrypt(...)` | Encrypts and decrypts with a key, a JWK or key agreement. |
| `deleteKey({ keyId })` | Deletes a key. |
| `randomBytes({ length })` | Returns random bytes. |
| `supportedBackendsForOperation(operation)` | The backends that support an operation. |

To use a key in a DID, pass its `keyId` when you create the DID. See [DIDs](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust.md).

# Caching

> Choose and configure the cache a Credo agent uses for resolved DID documents, ledger objects and certificate revocation lists.

Credo caches data that is slow to fetch: resolved DID documents, AnonCreds objects from ledgers and revocation lists of X.509 certificates. A cache is always registered, and you only replace it in two cases: when you use [multi-tenancy](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md), and when several instances of the agent run side by side.

## Which should I use?

Keep the default for a single agent without tenants, such as a mobile wallet: nothing to configure, and entries survive a restart. Use `InMemoryLruCache` when the agent has tenants, because the default throws as soon as a tenant uses it. Use `RedisCache` when several instances of the agent run behind a load balancer, so they share one cache. With the default, instances overwrite each other's cache record in the shared storage, and with `InMemoryLruCache` each instance fetches and caches everything on its own.

| Cache | Package | Tenants | Several processes share it | Survives a restart |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `SingleContextStorageLruCache` (default) | `@credo-ts/core` | No | No | Yes |
| `InMemoryLruCache` | `@credo-ts/core` | Yes | No | No |
| `RedisCache` | `@credo-ts/redis-cache` | Yes | Yes | Yes |

The default keeps up to 500 entries in memory and saves them as a record in the agent's storage. When a tenant uses it, it throws `SingleContextStorageLruCache can not be used with multiple agent context instances`.

## Configure the cache

Register a `CacheModule` under the key `cache` to replace the default:

```ts
import { Agent, CacheModule, InMemoryLruCache } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    cache: new CacheModule({
      cache: new InMemoryLruCache({ limit: 500 }),
    }),
  },
})
```

`InMemoryLruCache` removes the least recently used entries when it reaches `limit`. The limit applies to all agent contexts together.

| `CacheModule` option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `cache` | The cache to use. Required. |
| `defaultExpiryInSeconds` | Expiry for entries set without one. `RedisCache` uses it. Default `60`. |
| `useCachedStorageService` | Also caches DIDComm connection, mediation and mediator routing records, to save storage reads on busy DIDComm agents such as mediators. Default `false`. With several instances, only turn it on with a cache they share, such as Redis. |

## Redis

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/redis-cache@^0.7.2 ioredis
```

```ts
import { Agent, CacheModule } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { RedisCache } from '@credo-ts/redis-cache'
import { Redis } from 'ioredis'

const redis = new Redis('redis://localhost:6379')

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    cache: new CacheModule({
      // Also accepts ioredis options, e.g. new RedisCache({ host: 'localhost', port: 6379 })
      cache: new RedisCache(redis),
      defaultExpiryInSeconds: 300,
    }),
  },
})
```

`RedisCache` takes an `ioredis` client or `ioredis` options. Keys are prefixed with the agent context, or with `global:` for shared entries, so tenants and instances can share one Redis database. When you create the client yourself, close it after the agent shuts down:

```ts
await agent.shutdown()
// The agent doesn't close the Redis connection for you
await redis.quit()
```

`cache.destroy(agentContext)` removes all entries of one agent context, for example after you delete a tenant.

## What is cached

| Data | Cached for | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resolved DID documents, for methods whose resolver allows caching (`did:web`, `did:webvh`, `did:cheqd`, `did:indy`, `did:sov`, `did:hedera`). `did:key`, `did:jwk` and `did:peer` aren't cached. | 5 minutes, change it with `cacheDurationInSeconds` when resolving | Global for methods in `DidsModule({ publicDidMethods })`, otherwise per agent context |
| AnonCreds schemas, credential definitions, revocation registry definitions and status lists | 5 minutes | Global |
| Summaries of X.509 certificate revocation lists | Until the list's next update | Global |
| Indy VDR: which ledger a DID is on | Until evicted | Global |
| DIDComm connection, mediation and mediator routing records, with `useCachedStorageService: true` | Until evicted | Per agent context |

Global entries are public data that all tenants share. `publicDidMethods` defaults to `web`, `indy`, `sov`, `cheqd`, `hedera` and `webvh`.

## Custom cache

Implement the `Cache` interface: `get`, `set` and `remove`. Each method receives the agent context and an optional `scope`. Keep entries of different agent contexts apart, and only share entries when `scope` is `'global'`:

```ts
import type { AgentContext, Cache, CacheOptions } from '@credo-ts/core'

export class MapCache implements Cache {
  private entries = new Map<string, { value: unknown; expiresAt?: number }>()

  // Isolate entries per agent context unless the caller asks for the global scope
  private key(agentContext: AgentContext, key: string, options?: CacheOptions) {
    return options?.scope === 'global' ? `global:${key}` : `${agentContext.contextCorrelationId}:${key}`
  }

  public async get<CacheValue>(agentContext: AgentContext, key: string, options?: CacheOptions) {
    const namespacedKey = this.key(agentContext, key, options)
    const entry = this.entries.get(namespacedKey)
    if (!entry) return null

    if (entry.expiresAt && entry.expiresAt < Date.now()) {
      this.entries.delete(namespacedKey)
      return null
    }

    return entry.value as CacheValue
  }

  public async set<CacheValue>(
    agentContext: AgentContext,
    key: string,
    value: CacheValue,
    expiresInSeconds?: number,
    options?: CacheOptions
  ) {
    this.entries.set(this.key(agentContext, key, options), {
      value,
      expiresAt: expiresInSeconds ? Date.now() + expiresInSeconds * 1000 : undefined,
    })
  }

  public async remove(agentContext: AgentContext, key: string, options?: CacheOptions) {
    this.entries.delete(this.key(agentContext, key, options))
  }
}
```

# Multi-tenancy

> Run many isolated tenants in one Credo agent with the tenants module, choose how their data is stored, and manage tenant sessions.

With `@credo-ts/tenants`, one agent hosts many tenants. Each tenant has its own storage, keys, DIDs and credentials, while all tenants share the agent's modules, configuration and endpoints.

## When to use tenants

Use tenants for a service that issues, verifies or holds credentials on behalf of many organizations or users, such as an issuance platform or a cloud wallet. The alternative, an agent per customer, needs a process, a database and endpoints for each of them.

You don't need tenants for a mobile wallet, which has one user. You don't need them either to run several issuers or verifiers for one organization: one agent can host many [OpenID4VC issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/issuer.md) and verifiers. Use tenants when each of them needs keys, DIDs and data of its own.

## Install

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/tenants@^0.7.2
```

## Configure

```ts
import { AskarModule, AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent, CacheModule, InMemoryLruCache } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { DrizzleStorageModule } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage'
import { tenantsBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/tenants'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { TenantsModule } from '@credo-ts/tenants'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-nodejs'
import { drizzle } from 'drizzle-orm/libsql'

// Run the migrations of the core and tenants bundles first
const database = drizzle('file:agent.db')

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    // The records of all tenants in one database
    storage: new DrizzleStorageModule({ database, bundles: [tenantsBundle] }),
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      enableStorage: false,
      store: { id: 'credo-keys', key: 'my-agent-store-key' },
      // The keys of all tenants in one Askar store, with a profile per tenant
      multiWalletDatabaseScheme: AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme.ProfilePerWallet,
    }),
    tenants: new TenantsModule({ sessionLimit: 100, sessionAcquireTimeout: 5000 }),
    // The default cache throws as soon as a second agent context (a tenant) uses it
    cache: new CacheModule({ cache: new InMemoryLruCache({ limit: 5000 }) }),
  },
})
```

The example stores the records of all tenants in one [Drizzle](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md) database and their keys in one Askar store. Add `tenantsBundle` to `bundles`, pass `--bundle tenants` when you run the migrations, and use PostgreSQL in production.

Replace the default cache: it throws as soon as a tenant uses it. Use `InMemoryLruCache`, or `RedisCache` when several instances run the agent. See [Caching](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/caching.md).

| `TenantsModule` option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `sessionLimit` | Maximum number of tenant sessions open at the same time. Default `100`, which is low on purpose: set it based on your hardware and load. `Infinity` removes the limit. |
| `sessionAcquireTimeout` | How long, in milliseconds, opening a session waits for a free slot when the limit is reached, before it throws `Failed to acquire an agent context session`. Default `1000`. |

Tenant agents get the modules you register on the root agent. To type them, pass the modules to the generic, for example `new TenantsModule<{ openid4vc: OpenId4VcModule }>()`.

## Where tenant data is stored

With Drizzle, all tenants share the one database, and each row is tagged with its tenant. Tenant keys are in Askar, where `multiWalletDatabaseScheme` decides where they go. Set it to `AskarMultiWalletDatabaseScheme.ProfilePerWallet`, as in the example: all tenants in one Askar store, with a profile each.

### With Askar storage

When Askar also stores the records, `multiWalletDatabaseScheme` decides where all tenant data goes:

| `multiWalletDatabaseScheme` | Tenant records and keys |
| --- | --- |
| `ProfilePerWallet` | A profile per tenant in the root store |
| `DatabasePerWallet` (default) | A store per tenant, a SQLite file or a PostgreSQL database each, with a generated key that Credo saves in the tenant record |

Use `ProfilePerWallet`. It keeps all tenants in one database, performs better with many tenants, and doesn't create a PostgreSQL database per tenant. Store-level tasks, such as rotating the store key or exporting the store, then cover all tenants at once. `DatabasePerWallet` is the default for backwards compatibility: use it only to back up or delete tenants one by one.

:::warning[No SQLite `path` with `DatabasePerWallet`]
Tenant stores reuse the root store's `database` config. With an explicit SQLite `path`, all tenants resolve to the root store's file, and `createTenant` fails. Leave `path` unset so each tenant gets its own file in the data directory.
:::

## Create a tenant

```ts
const tenantRecord = await agent.modules.tenants.createTenant({
  config: { label: 'Tenant 1' },
})
```

`createTenant` saves a `TenantRecord` in the root agent's storage and creates the tenant's storage. The label is for your own use. Use the tenant record's `id` to open the tenant later.

## Use a tenant

Work in a tenant through a tenant agent, which has the same API as the root agent, scoped to the tenant. `withTenantAgent` opens a session, runs your callback and ends the session, also when the callback throws:

```ts
// Opens a session, runs the callback and always ends the session
const did = await agent.modules.tenants.withTenantAgent({ tenantId: tenantRecord.id }, async (tenantAgent) => {
  const { didState } = await tenantAgent.dids.create({
    method: 'key',
    options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } },
  })
  return didState.did
})
```

`getTenantAgent` returns the tenant agent without a callback. End the session yourself with `endSession()`:

```ts
const tenantAgent = await agent.modules.tenants.getTenantAgent({ tenantId: tenantRecord.id })
try {
  const createdDids = await tenantAgent.dids.getCreatedDids()
  console.log(`Tenant has ${createdDids.length} DID(s)`)
} finally {
  // Every session counts against the session limit until you end it
  await tenantAgent.endSession()
}
```

Each open session takes a slot of `sessionLimit` until it ends, so a missing `endSession()` eventually blocks new sessions. Inbound DIDComm messages and OpenID4VC requests for a tenant open their own session.

## Manage tenants

`agent.modules.tenants` has methods to look up and change tenants:

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `getTenantById(tenantId)`, `findTenantsByLabel(label)`, `findTenantsByQuery(query)`, `getAllTenants()` | Find tenant records. |
| `updateTenant(tenantRecord)` | Saves changes to a tenant record. |
| `deleteTenantById(tenantId)` | Deletes the tenant record and the tenant's storage. |
| `getTenantsWithOutdatedStorage()`, `updateTenantStorage({ tenantId })` | Update tenant storage after a Credo upgrade. With `autoUpdateStorageOnStartup`, Credo updates a tenant when it opens a session. |

```ts
await agent.modules.tenants.deleteTenantById(tenantRecord.id)
```

## Route messages and requests to tenants

Tenants share the root agent's endpoints, and Credo finds the tenant for each incoming message or request:

- DIDComm: when a tenant creates routing keys, for example for a connection, Credo saves which tenant they belong to, and it routes each encrypted message by its recipient key. See [DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm.md).
- OpenID4VC: create issuers and verifiers with a tenant agent. Credo routes requests to their URLs to that tenant. See [Issuing credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/issuer.md) and [Verifying credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/verifier.md).

# Logging

> Log what a Credo agent does with the built-in ConsoleLogger or your own logger, and choose the log level.

A Credo agent logs nothing until you give it a logger. The agent and all its modules, including tenant agents, use that one logger.

## Console logger

Pass a logger as `config.logger`:

```ts
import { Agent, ConsoleLogger, LogLevel } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'

const agent = new Agent({
  config: {
    // Logs Info, Warn, Error and Fatal messages
    logger: new ConsoleLogger(LogLevel.Info),
  },
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
  },
})
```

`ConsoleLogger` prints each message with its level as a prefix, such as `INFO: Creating agent with config`, using the console method that matches the level. Data passed with a message is printed as JSON. Errors in the data keep their message and stack.

## Log levels

A logger prints messages at its own level and above:

| Level | What Credo logs at this level |
| --- | --- |
| `LogLevel.Test` | Nothing. Set it to print every message. |
| `LogLevel.Trace` | The most detailed steps, such as key imports, and requests to ledgers and their results. |
| `LogLevel.Debug` | Processing steps of protocols, including the content of DIDComm messages the agent sends. |
| `LogLevel.Info` | Lifecycle events, such as the agent's config when it's created, storage updates, received DIDComm messages and created tenants. |
| `LogLevel.Warn` | Problems the agent recovers from, such as a credential that breaks a recommendation of its specification. |
| `LogLevel.Error` | Failed operations, such as a DIDComm message that can't be delivered. |
| `LogLevel.Fatal` | A storage update that failed. |
| `LogLevel.Off` | Nothing. The default. |

Use `Info` or higher in production. At `Debug` and `Trace`, logs can contain message contents, credential data and other personal data.

## Your own logger

To send logs to your own logging library, implement the `Logger` interface from `@credo-ts/core`: a `logLevel` property and the methods `test`, `trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` and `fatal`, each taking a `message` and optional `data`. Extending `BaseLogger` saves some work: it stores the level and has `isEnabled(level)`. This logger writes one JSON object per line:

```ts
import { BaseLogger, LogLevel, replaceError } from '@credo-ts/core'

type LogData = Record<string, unknown>

export class JsonLogger extends BaseLogger {
  private log(level: LogLevel, message: string, data?: LogData) {
    if (!this.isEnabled(level)) return

    // replaceError keeps the message and stack of errors, which JSON.stringify would drop
    console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: LogLevel[level], time: new Date().toISOString(), message, data }, replaceError))
  }

  public test(message: string, data?: LogData) {
    this.log(LogLevel.Test, message, data)
  }

  public trace(message: string, data?: LogData) {
    this.log(LogLevel.Trace, message, data)
  }

  public debug(message: string, data?: LogData) {
    this.log(LogLevel.Debug, message, data)
  }

  public info(message: string, data?: LogData) {
    this.log(LogLevel.Info, message, data)
  }

  public warn(message: string, data?: LogData) {
    this.log(LogLevel.Warn, message, data)
  }

  public error(message: string, data?: LogData) {
    this.log(LogLevel.Error, message, data)
  }

  public fatal(message: string, data?: LogData) {
    this.log(LogLevel.Fatal, message, data)
  }
}
```

Pass it as `config.logger`, for example `new JsonLogger(LogLevel.Info)`.

# Protocols

> How OpenID4VC, DIDComm and the ISO mdoc protocols differ, which credential formats each one carries, and which one to use.

An exchange protocol defines how issuers, holders and verifiers talk to each other. Credo supports OpenID4VC, DIDComm and the ISO mdoc protocols.

## Which protocol should I use?

| Use | When |
| --- | --- |
| [OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc.md) | By default, for new issuers, wallets and verifiers. It only needs HTTPS, carries SD-JWT VC and mdoc, and is what the EU Digital Identity Wallet and the HAIP profile use. |
| [ISO mdoc](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/mdoc.md) | A wallet presents mdocs, such as a mobile driving licence, in person to a reader over BLE or NFC. A wallet usually receives those mdocs with OpenID4VCI. |
| [DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm.md) | You join an ecosystem built on DIDComm and AnonCreds, or the parties need a lasting connection to exchange messages beyond a single issuance or presentation. |

## OpenID4VC

[OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc.md) builds on OAuth 2.0 and plain HTTPS. OpenID4VCI covers issuance and OpenID4VP covers presentation. An issuer or verifier starts each exchange with a QR code or link, and the wallet completes it with a few HTTPS requests. Nothing persists between exchanges. This is the protocol family of the EU Digital Identity Wallet and its HAIP profile, and of mobile driving licences (mDL) presented online.

## DIDComm

[DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm.md) is a messaging protocol between agents that identify each other with DIDs. Two agents first set up a connection, usually from an out-of-band invitation. Over that connection either side can then offer credentials, request proofs or send other messages, for as long as the connection lasts. Mobile wallets can't accept incoming connections, so they receive messages through a mediator. DIDComm is used in ecosystems built on Hyperledger Aries and AnonCreds.

## ISO mdoc

[ISO mdoc](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/mdoc.md) covers the presentation protocols of ISO/IEC 18013-5 and 18013-7, which carry only mdocs, such as the mobile driving licence. A wallet presents in person to a reader over BLE or NFC (proximity), or to a website through the browser (ISO 18013-7 Annex C). Like OpenID4VC, each presentation stands alone. These protocols don't cover issuance.

## Digital Credentials API

The W3C [Digital Credentials API](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/dc-api.md) lets a website request credentials through the browser, which passes the request to a wallet. It's a channel for other protocols: Credo supports it with OpenID4VP and with ISO 18013-7 Annex C.

## Comparison

| | OpenID4VC | DIDComm | ISO mdoc |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Transport | HTTPS requests from the wallet to the issuer or verifier | Encrypted messages over HTTP or WebSocket, through a mediator for mobile wallets | BLE or NFC in person, or the browser with the Digital Credentials API |
| Relationship | None: each exchange stands alone | A connection that both agents keep | None: each presentation stands alone |
| Starts with | A credential offer or authorization request | An out-of-band invitation | A QR code or NFC tap, or a website calling the Digital Credentials API |
| Issuer and verifier | Node.js | Node.js | No issuer. Verifier on Node.js |
| Holder | Node.js and React Native | Node.js and React Native | Node.js and React Native |
| Typical ecosystems | EU Digital Identity Wallet, HAIP, mDL | Aries and AnonCreds ecosystems | mDL and EU PID, in person and online |

## Credential formats

| Format | OpenID4VC | DIDComm | ISO mdoc |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SD-JWT VC | Yes | No | No |
| mdoc | Yes | No | Yes |
| W3C VC | Yes | Yes | No |
| AnonCreds | No | Yes | No |

Which W3C data models and proof types work depends on the protocol and on whether you issue or present. [Supported standards](https://credo.js.org/guides/supported-standards.md) has the full matrix.

## How these pages are organised

- Protocol pages cover each role. For OpenID4VC these are [Issuing credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/issuer.md), [Receiving credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/receive.md), [Presenting credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/present.md) and [Verifying credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/verifier.md). For DIDComm they're [Connections](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/connections.md), [Issuing credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/issue-credential.md) and [Requesting proofs](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/present-proof.md). The ISO mdoc pages cover [proximity presentation (ISO 18013-5)](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/mdoc/proximity.md).
- Pages named "… with OpenID4VC" or "… with DIDComm", such as [SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/sd-jwt-vc.md) and [AnonCreds with DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/anoncreds.md), cover what's specific to one format on one protocol.
- What you can do with a format on its own, such as signing, storing and verifying credentials or checking their status, is under [Credential formats](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats.md).

- [OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc.md): Issue, receive and verify credentials over HTTPS with OpenID4VCI and OpenID4VP, using the @credo-ts/openid4vc module.
- [ISO mdoc](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/mdoc.md): How the ISO/IEC 18013-5 and 18013-7 presentation protocols for mdocs work, how they differ from OpenID4VP, and what Credo does for proximity and the Digital Credentials API.
- [Digital Credentials API](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/dc-api.md): How the W3C Digital Credentials API passes credential requests from a website to a wallet, the two protocols Credo supports over it (OpenID4VP and ISO 18013-7 Annex C), platform support, and which protocols and options to choose.
- [DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm.md): Set up DIDComm messaging in Credo with the DidCommModule, choose protocols and transports, and listen for state changes.

# OpenID4VC

> Issue, receive and verify credentials over HTTPS with OpenID4VCI and OpenID4VP, using the @credo-ts/openid4vc module.

OpenID for Verifiable Credentials (OpenID4VC) is a family of protocols, built on OAuth 2.0, for issuing and presenting credentials over HTTPS. This page explains the protocols and roles, and how to set up the `@credo-ts/openid4vc` module. The pages below it cover each role.

## Protocols

| Specification | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| OpenID4VCI | Issuance. A holder gets credentials from an issuer. The issuer authorizes it with a pre-authorized code in the offer, or with the OAuth authorization code flow. |
| OpenID4VP | Presentation. A verifier sends an authorization request with a DCQL query, and the holder responds with presentations of matching credentials. |
| HAIP | The High Assurance Interoperability Profile of both protocols, used by ecosystems such as the EU Digital Identity Wallet. It requires SD-JWT VC or mdoc. For issuance: the authorization code flow with PKCE, DPoP, and wallet authentication, usually with wallet attestations. For presentation: DCQL, requests signed with an X.509 certificate (`x509_hash`) and encrypted responses. [Authorization and wallet security](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/authorization.md) explains the issuance part, [Verifying credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/verifier.md) the presentation part. |

There is no connection between the parties. Each exchange is a separate session, started by a credential offer or an authorization request that the holder receives as a QR code or link.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Issuer
  participant Holder
  participant Verifier
  Issuer->>Holder: credential offer (QR code or link)
  Holder->>Issuer: OpenID4VCI token and credential requests
  Issuer-->>Holder: credentials
  Verifier->>Holder: authorization request (QR code or link)
  Holder->>Verifier: OpenID4VP authorization response with presentations
```

[Supported standards](https://credo.js.org/guides/supported-standards.md) lists the versions and drafts Credo supports, and which credential formats work with each protocol.

## Roles

| Role | API | Platform | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Issuer | `agent.openid4vc.issuer` | Node.js | [Issuing credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/issuer.md) |
| Holder | `agent.openid4vc.holder` | Node.js and React Native | [Receiving](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/receive.md) and [presenting](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/present.md) credentials |
| Verifier | `agent.openid4vc.verifier` | Node.js | [Verifying credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/verifier.md) |

Issuers and verifiers serve HTTP endpoints with Express, so they run on Node.js. On React Native only the holder is available.

## Install

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/openid4vc@^0.7.2
```

For an issuer or verifier, also install Express 5:

```bash
npm install express@^5
```
```bash
npm install --save-dev @types/express@^5
```

## Configure the module

An agent that issues and verifies credentials:

```ts
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc'
import express from 'express'

const app = express()

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    // The key must be `openid4vc` for the module to be available as agent.openid4vc
    openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({
      app,
      issuer: {
        baseUrl: 'https://example.com/oid4vci',
        credentialRequestToCredentialMapper,
      },
      verifier: {
        baseUrl: 'https://example.com/oid4vp',
      },
    }),
  },
})

await agent.initialize()

// Credo adds its routes to the app, you start the server. Make https://example.com
// reach this server, for example through a reverse proxy.
const server = app.listen(4022)
```

Register the module under the key `openid4vc`, so it's available as `agent.openid4vc`. `issuer` and `verifier` are optional and turn on that role. The holder is always available, so a wallet registers the module without options:

```ts
openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(),
```

The module stores issuers, verifiers and sessions as records. With [Drizzle storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md), add `openid4vcBundle` from `@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/openid4vc` to the bundles.

`baseUrl` is the public URL of the endpoints, and Credo serves them under its path (`/oid4vci` and `/oid4vp` here). OpenID4VCI also requires the issuer metadata at the root of the host (`/.well-known/openid-credential-issuer/oid4vci/<issuerId>`), so your server must pass requests for the whole host to the Express app.

`app` is your Express app. Without it, Credo creates one, available as `agent.openid4vc.config.app`. Either way, you start the server. Credo adds its routes during `agent.initialize()`, so register your own middleware and routes after that.

The issuer and verifier support [multi-tenancy](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md): Credo finds the tenant from the issuer or verifier id in the URL.

For local development over `http://localhost`, set `allowInsecureHttpUrls: true` in the agent config of all parties. Never enable it in production.

## The example flow

The pages for each role build one example: an issuer that issues an employee badge as an SD-JWT VC with the pre-authorized code flow, a holder that receives and presents it, and a verifier that requests two of its claims. This runs them in one process:

```ts
import { holder, presentCredential, receiveCredential } from './openid4vc-holder.js'
import { createEmployeeBadgeOffer, issuer, issuerServer } from './openid4vc-issuer.js'
import { createEmployeeBadgeRequest, getEmployeeBadgeClaims, verifier, verifierServer } from './openid4vc-verifier.js'

// Issuer: create an offer for a known user
const { credentialOffer, txCode } = await createEmployeeBadgeOffer('employee-123')

// Holder: resolve the offer, enter the code, store the credential
await receiveCredential(credentialOffer, txCode)

// Verifier: request given_name and department
const { authorizationRequest, verificationSessionId } = await createEmployeeBadgeRequest()

// Holder: resolve the request and share the credential
await presentCredential(authorizationRequest)

// Verifier: read the verified claims
console.log(await getEmployeeBadgeClaims(verificationSessionId))
```

# Issuing credentials

> Run an OpenID4VCI issuer with Credo, define credential configurations, create credentials for incoming requests and create credential offers.

This page covers issuing credentials with OpenID4VCI from a Node.js agent: the issuer metadata, the callback that creates each credential, and credential offers with the pre-authorized code flow. The examples issue an SD-JWT VC.

## How issuance works

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant App as Your app
  participant Issuer as Credo issuer
  participant Holder
  App->>Issuer: createCredentialOffer()
  Issuer-->>App: offer URI and tx code
  App->>Holder: QR code or link (tx code by email)
  Holder->>Issuer: fetch offer and issuer metadata
  Holder->>Issuer: token request with pre-authorized code and tx code
  Holder->>Issuer: credential request with proof of possession
  Issuer->>App: credentialRequestToCredentialMapper()
  Issuer-->>Holder: signed credential
```

Your application decides who gets which credential and creates the offer. Credo hosts the OpenID4VCI endpoints, checks the holder's requests and signs the credentials your callback returns.

## Choose a credential format

| Format | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/sd-jwt-vc.md) | By default. JSON claims with selective disclosure, required by HAIP and used for the EU PID. |
| [mdoc](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/mdoc.md) | The credential follows an ISO document type, such as the mobile driving licence, or holders must also present it in person over BLE or NFC. |
| [W3C VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/w3c.md) | Your ecosystem requires the W3C data model. Use `jwt_vc_json` or VCDM 2.0 with SD-JWT. |

You can offer the same credential in several formats, each as its own credential configuration. The format pages cover the configuration and signing for each.

## Set up the issuer

Register `OpenId4VcModule` with an `issuer` configuration. [OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc.md) explains the module options.

```ts
import { Agent, ClaimFormat, Kms, type SdJwtVcSignOptions } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import {
  OpenId4VcIssuanceSessionState,
  type OpenId4VcIssuanceSessionStateChangedEvent,
  OpenId4VcIssuerEvents,
  OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile,
  type OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapperOptions,
  type OpenId4VciSignSdJwtCredentials,
  OpenId4VcModule,
} from '@credo-ts/openid4vc'
import express from 'express'

const issuerPort = 4020
const app = express()

export const issuer = new Agent({
  config: {
    // Allows the http://localhost URLs of this example. Never enable this in production.
    allowInsecureHttpUrls: true,
  },
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule({
      app,
      issuer: {
        baseUrl: `http://localhost:${issuerPort}/oid4vci`,
        credentialRequestToCredentialMapper,
      },
    }),
  },
})

await issuer.initialize()
export const issuerServer = app.listen(issuerPort)
```

`baseUrl` is the public URL of the issuer endpoints. Each issuer you create gets the credential issuer identifier `<baseUrl>/<issuerId>`. `credentialRequestToCredentialMapper` creates the credentials when a holder requests them, see [Create the credentials](#create-the-credentials).

## Create a signing key and certificate

The issuer signs credentials with a key from the agent's KMS. For SD-JWT VC and mdoc it includes an X.509 certificate for that key, so holders and verifiers can check who signed.

```ts
const issuerKey = await issuer.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })

// Self-signed for this example. In production, a CA issues the certificate for your key.
export const issuerCertificate = await issuer.x509.createCertificate({
  authorityKey: Kms.PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(issuerKey.publicJwk),
  issuer: { commonName: 'Example Corp', countryName: 'NL' },
})
```

The example uses a self-signed certificate. In production a certificate authority issues it, and holders and verifiers trust that CA. See [X.509 certificates](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/x509.md). If you load a certificate instead of creating it, set `certificate.keyId` to the KMS key id of its key so Credo can sign with it. To sign with a DID instead, use `issuer: { method: 'did', didUrl }` in the callback.

## Create the issuer

An issuer record holds the metadata that holders fetch from `/.well-known/openid-credential-issuer`: the issuer's display name and the credentials it offers. One agent can host several issuers.

```ts
const issuerRecord = await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createIssuer({
  display: [{ name: 'Example Corp', locale: 'en' }],
  credentialConfigurationsSupported: {
    'employee-badge': {
      format: OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.SdJwtDc,
      vct: 'urn:example:employee-badge:1',
      cryptographic_binding_methods_supported: ['jwk'],
      credential_signing_alg_values_supported: [Kms.KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256],
      proof_types_supported: {
        jwt: { proof_signing_alg_values_supported: [Kms.KnownJwaSignatureAlgorithms.ES256] },
      },
      credential_metadata: {
        display: [{ name: 'Employee badge', locale: 'en', background_color: '#12107c', text_color: '#ffffff' }],
        claims: [
          { path: ['given_name'], display: [{ name: 'Given name', locale: 'en' }] },
          { path: ['family_name'], display: [{ name: 'Family name', locale: 'en' }] },
          { path: ['department'], display: [{ name: 'Department', locale: 'en' }] },
        ],
      },
    },
  },
})
```

Each key of `credentialConfigurationsSupported` is a credential configuration id. You use these ids when you create offers. For each configuration:

- Set `proof_types_supported`. Credo only issues credentials bound to a holder key, so it always asks for a proof of possession, and a Credo holder rejects configurations without this field.
- Put display information under `credential_metadata`, as OpenID4VCI 1.0 defines. Wallets that implement draft 15 read `display` and `claims` at the top level of the configuration, so add them there as well if you need to support those wallets.

Create the issuer once, for example when you deploy, and keep its `issuerId`. Credo generates a UUID unless you pass one. Change the metadata later with `updateIssuerMetadata`.

For batch issuance, set `batchCredentialIssuance: { batchSize }` on the issuer. A holder can then request up to that many instances of a credential in one request, each bound to a different key, so verifiers can't link its presentations to each other.

## Create the credentials

Credo checks each credential request (the access token and the holder's proof of possession of its keys) and then calls your `credentialRequestToCredentialMapper` with, among others:

- `issuanceSession`: the session created with the offer, including the `issuanceMetadata` you passed.
- `credentialConfigurationId` and `credentialConfiguration`: the configuration the holder requests.
- `holderBinding`: the verified keys or DIDs to bind the credentials to.

```ts
// Stands in for your own user database
const employees = new Map([['employee-123', { given_name: 'Jane', family_name: 'Doe', department: 'Engineering' }]])

async function credentialRequestToCredentialMapper({
  credentialConfiguration,
  holderBinding,
  issuanceSession,
}: OpenId4VciCredentialRequestToCredentialMapperOptions): Promise<OpenId4VciSignSdJwtCredentials> {
  if (credentialConfiguration.format !== OpenId4VciCredentialFormatProfile.SdJwtDc) {
    throw new Error(`Unsupported credential format '${credentialConfiguration.format}'`)
  }

  // Set as issuanceMetadata when creating the offer
  const employeeId = issuanceSession.issuanceMetadata?.employeeId
  const employee = typeof employeeId === 'string' ? employees.get(employeeId) : undefined
  if (!employee) throw new Error('Unknown employee')

  return {
    type: 'credentials',
    format: ClaimFormat.SdJwtDc,
    // One credential per key the wallet wants the credential bound to
    credentials: holderBinding.keys.map(
      (holder): SdJwtVcSignOptions => ({
        payload: { vct: credentialConfiguration.vct, ...employee },
        holder,
        issuer: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate] },
        disclosureFrame: { _sd: ['given_name', 'family_name', 'department'] },
      })
    ),
  }
}
```

Return exactly one credential for each entry in `holderBinding.keys`. With batch issuance there are several entries, and Credo rejects the result if the counts differ. The `format` you return decides how Credo signs: `ClaimFormat.SdJwtDc` for SD-JWT VC, `ClaimFormat.MsoMdoc` for mdoc, or one of the W3C formats. To issue the credential later, return a deferral instead (see [Deferred issuance](#deferred-issuance)).

## Create a credential offer

An offer tells the holder which credentials it can get and how to get authorization. Pick the flow:

- **Pre-authorized code** (this page): your application has already identified the user, for example after a login on your website, and the offer itself carries the authorization. Use it by default.
- **Authorization code**: the holder sends the user to an authorization server to log in, or presents a credential such as a PID first. Use it when the user isn't known yet, or when your ecosystem follows HAIP. See [Authorization and wallet security](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/authorization.md).

```ts
export async function createEmployeeBadgeOffer(employeeId: string) {
  const { credentialOffer, issuanceSession } = await issuer.openid4vc.issuer.createCredentialOffer({
    issuerId: issuerRecord.issuerId,
    credentialConfigurationIds: ['employee-badge'],
    preAuthorizedCodeFlowConfig: {
      txCode: { input_mode: 'numeric', length: 6, description: 'Enter the code from the email we sent you' },
    },
    issuanceMetadata: { employeeId },
  })

  // Show credentialOffer as a QR code or link. Send the code (userPin) to the user over another channel.
  return { credentialOffer, txCode: issuanceSession.userPin }
}
```

`credentialOffer` is a URI such as `openid-credential-offer://?credential_offer_uri=...`. Show it as a QR code when the wallet runs on another device, or as a link on the same device. `baseUri` changes the `openid-credential-offer://` prefix, for example to a custom scheme or an HTTPS link.

`txCode` makes the wallet ask the user for a transaction code. Credo generates the code and stores it as `issuanceSession.userPin` (4 digits unless you set `length`). Send it over a different channel than the offer, such as email or SMS, so that someone who intercepts the offer can't redeem it.

The holder must finish the whole issuance before the offer expires: 3 minutes by default. Change it per offer with `expirationInSeconds`, or for all offers with `statefulCredentialOfferExpirationInSeconds` in the issuer configuration.

## Track issuance sessions

Each offer creates an issuance session. Listen for state changes to update your application:

```ts
issuer.events.on<OpenId4VcIssuanceSessionStateChangedEvent>(
  OpenId4VcIssuerEvents.IssuanceSessionStateChanged,
  ({ payload: { issuanceSession } }) => {
    if (issuanceSession.state === OpenId4VcIssuanceSessionState.Completed) {
      console.log(`Issuance session ${issuanceSession.id} completed`)
    } else if (issuanceSession.state === OpenId4VcIssuanceSessionState.Error) {
      console.error(`Issuance session ${issuanceSession.id} failed: ${issuanceSession.errorMessage}`)
    }
  }
)
```

In the pre-authorized code flow a session goes through `OfferCreated`, `OfferUriRetrieved`, `AccessTokenRequested`, `AccessTokenCreated`, `CredentialRequestReceived` and `Completed`. Other states:

| State | When |
| --- | --- |
| `AuthorizationInitiated`, `AuthorizationGranted` | Authorization code flow with Credo as the authorization server. |
| `CredentialsPartiallyIssued` | The offer has several credential configurations and the holder hasn't requested all of them yet. |
| `Error` | The session failed or expired. `errorMessage` says why. |

To read a session at any time, call `agent.openid4vc.issuer.getIssuanceSessionById(id)`.

## Deferred issuance

If a credential isn't ready when the holder asks for it, for example because it needs manual approval, return `{ type: 'deferral', transactionId, interval }` from the mapper. The holder retries at the deferred credential endpoint after `interval` seconds. Credo then calls `deferredCredentialRequestToCredentialMapper` from the issuer configuration, which returns the credentials or another deferral. The session stays valid for `interval` plus `deferralIntervalGracePeriodInSeconds` (7 days by default).

## Next steps

- [Receiving credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/receive.md): the holder side of this flow.
- [SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/sd-jwt-vc.md): claims, selective disclosure and type metadata.
- [Authorization and wallet security](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/authorization.md): the authorization code flow, PKCE, DPoP and wallet attestations.

# Receiving credentials

> Receive credentials with OpenID4VCI in a Credo wallet on Node.js or React Native, bind them to the wallet's keys and store them.

This page covers the holder side of OpenID4VCI: resolving a credential offer, getting an access token, requesting the credentials and storing them. The holder API is the same on Node.js and React Native. The examples continue the SD-JWT VC flow from [Issuing credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/issuer.md). To present the credentials afterwards, see [Presenting credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/present.md).

## Set up the holder

Register `OpenId4VcModule` without options. The holder part is always available as `agent.openid4vc.holder`.

**Node.js**

```ts
import { Agent, Kms, MdocRecord, SdJwtVcRecord, W3cCredentialRecord, X509Module } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import {
  type OpenId4VciCredentialBindingResolver,
  OpenId4VcModule,
  preAuthorizedCodeGrantIdentifier,
} from '@credo-ts/openid4vc'
import { issuerCertificate } from './openid4vc-issuer.js'
import { verifierCertificate } from './openid4vc-verifier.js'

export const holder = new Agent({
  config: {
    // Allows the http://localhost URLs of this example. Never enable this in production.
    allowInsecureHttpUrls: true,
  },
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    // Certificates (or root CAs) of the issuers and verifiers you trust
    x509: new X509Module({ trustedCertificates: [issuerCertificate, verifierCertificate] }),
    openid4vc: new OpenId4VcModule(),
  },
})

await holder.initialize()
```

**React Native**

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent, X509Module } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { OpenId4VcModule } from '@credo-ts/openid4vc'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native'

// PEM certificates (or root CAs) of the issuers and verifiers the wallet trusts, bundled with the app
```
