[W3C VCs with DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/w3c.md) covers the exception for Data Integrity VCDM 2.0 credentials.

Deleting the exchange record with `agent.didcomm.credentials.deleteById` also deletes the stored credential, unless you pass `deleteAssociatedCredentials: false`.

## Start with a proposal

The holder proposes the credential it wants, in the same shape as an offer:

:::holder

```ts
await holder.didcomm.credentials.proposeCredential({
  connectionId: connectionRecord.id,
  protocolVersion: 'v2',
  credentialFormats: {
    jsonld: {
      credential: {
        '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1', 'https://purl.imsglobal.org/spec/ob/v3p0/context.json'],
        type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'OpenBadgeCredential'],
        issuer: issuerDid,
        issuanceDate: w3cDate(),
        credentialSubject: {
          id: holderDid,
          type: ['AchievementSubject'],
          achievement: {
            id: 'https://example.com/achievements/credo-docs',
            type: ['Achievement'],
            name: 'Read the Credo docs',
          },
        },
      },
      options: { proofType: 'Ed25519Signature2018', proofPurpose: 'assertionMethod' },
    },
  },
})
```

:::

The issuer accepts the proposal, which sends an offer with the proposed content. To offer something else, call `negotiateProposal` instead.

:::issuer

```ts
if (credentialExchangeRecord.state === DidCommCredentialState.ProposalReceived) {
  await issuer.didcomm.credentials.acceptProposal({ credentialExchangeRecordId: credentialExchangeRecord.id })
}
```

:::

With `ContentApproved` auto-accept on both sides, the rest of this exchange runs by itself: the offer matches the proposal, the request matches the offer, and the credential matches the request.

## Auto-accept

Set `autoAcceptCredentials` on the credentials module, or `autoAcceptCredential` on a single API call (it then applies to that exchange).

| `DidCommAutoAcceptCredential` | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `Never` (default) | Every step needs an API call: `acceptOffer`, `acceptRequest`, `acceptCredential`, and so on. |
| `ContentApproved` | After one manual approval, Credo continues as long as each message matches the previous one. An offer that doesn't answer your own proposal always needs `acceptOffer`. |
| `Always` | Credo answers every message, including offers from any connection. |

For an issuer, `ContentApproved` is a good default: creating the offer is the approval, and Credo issues when the request matches it. Proposals still wait for `acceptProposal`. For a wallet, `ContentApproved` keeps the user in control: offers wait for `acceptOffer`, and Credo sends the ack when the credential arrives. Don't use `Always` on either side: an issuer would issue whatever a holder proposes, and a wallet would accept every offer.

## States and events

Listen to `DidCommCredentialEventTypes.DidCommCredentialStateChanged`. The payload has the `credentialExchangeRecord` and its `previousState`.

| `DidCommCredentialState` | Agent | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ProposalSent` | holder | wait for the offer |
| `ProposalReceived` | issuer | `acceptProposal` or `negotiateProposal` |
| `OfferSent` | issuer | wait for the request |
| `OfferReceived` | holder | `acceptOffer`, `declineOffer` or `negotiateOffer` |
| `RequestSent` | holder | wait for the credential |
| `RequestReceived` | issuer | `acceptRequest` issues the credential |
| `CredentialIssued` | issuer | wait for the ack |
| `CredentialReceived` | holder | the credential is stored, `acceptCredential` sends the ack |
| `Done` | both | |
| `Declined` | holder | |
| `Abandoned` | both | the exchange failed, `errorMessage` says why |

Query exchanges with `agent.didcomm.credentials.findAllByQuery({ state, connectionId })`.

## Issue Credential v1

:::warning[Deprecated]

Issue Credential v1 ([Aries RFC 0036](https://github.com/decentralized-identity/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0036-issue-credential)) is deprecated and removed in Credo 0.8. Use v2 unless the other agent only supports v1.

:::

Issue Credential v1 only carries AnonCreds credentials in the `indy` format. Register it next to v2, and pass `protocolVersion: 'v1'` in the API calls:

```ts
import { DidCommCredentialV1Protocol, LegacyIndyDidCommCredentialFormatService } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm'

const credentialProtocol = new DidCommCredentialV1Protocol({
  indyCredentialFormat: new LegacyIndyDidCommCredentialFormatService(),
})
```

# Requesting proofs

> Request and verify presentations over DIDComm with the Present Proof v2 protocol, using AnonCreds or DIF Presentation Exchange.

Present Proof v2 ([Aries RFC 0454](https://github.com/decentralized-identity/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0454-present-proof-v2)) lets a verifier request a presentation from a connected holder and verify it. Like issuance, the protocol relies on format services for the request and presentation. This page shows the protocol with DIF Presentation Exchange and a W3C JSON-LD credential. You need an agent with the DIDComm module and a connection, see [DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm.md) and [Connections](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/connections.md).

## Register proof formats

The proofs module that `DidCommModule` enables by default runs Present Proof v2 without formats. Pass a `DidCommProofV2Protocol` with the format services you need, on both the verifier and the holder.

```ts
import { Agent, type KeyDidCreateOptions, w3cDate } from '@credo-ts/core'
import {
  DidCommAutoAcceptCredential,
  DidCommCredentialEventTypes,
  DidCommCredentialState,
  type DidCommCredentialStateChangedEvent,
  DidCommCredentialV2Protocol,
  DidCommDifPresentationExchangeProofFormatService,
  DidCommHttpOutboundTransport,
  DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService,
  DidCommModule,
  DidCommProofEventTypes,
  DidCommProofState,
  type DidCommProofStateChangedEvent,
  DidCommProofV2Protocol,
} from '@credo-ts/didcomm'
import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node'

function createAgent(port: number, storage: ExampleStorage) {
  return new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
      didcomm: new DidCommModule({
        endpoints: [`http://localhost:${port}`],
        transports: {
          inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port })],
          outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()],
        },
        connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true },
        credentials: {
          credentialProtocols: [
            new DidCommCredentialV2Protocol({ credentialFormats: [new DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService()] }),
          ],
        },
        proofs: {
          proofProtocols: [
            new DidCommProofV2Protocol({
              proofFormats: [new DidCommDifPresentationExchangeProofFormatService()],
            }),
          ],
        },
      }),
    },
  })
}
```

| Format | Format service | Import from | Key | Presents |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AnonCreds | `AnonCredsDidCommProofFormatService` | `@credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm` | `anoncreds` | AnonCreds credentials |
| AnonCreds with Hyperledger Indy attachments | `LegacyIndyDidCommProofFormatService` | `@credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm` | `indy` | AnonCreds credentials |
| DIF Presentation Exchange ([RFC 0510](https://github.com/decentralized-identity/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0510-dif-pres-exch-attach)) | `DidCommDifPresentationExchangeProofFormatService` | `@credo-ts/didcomm` | `presentationExchange` | W3C VCDM 1.1 credentials as JSON-LD (`ldp_vp`) or JWT (`jwt_vp`) presentations, and AnonCreds credentials issued in W3C format |

Use `anoncreds` for AnonCreds credentials and `presentationExchange` for W3C credentials. Present Proof doesn't support SD-JWT VC, mdoc or W3C VCDM 2.0 credentials, including the VCDM 2.0 credentials you can receive over DIDComm. Present SD-JWT VC, mdoc and VCDM 2.0 SD-JWT credentials with [OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc.md) instead.

The Presentation Exchange format uses version 1 presentation definitions, which need a `schema` on each input descriptor.

## How a presentation works

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Verifier
  participant Holder
  opt Holder starts
    Holder->>Verifier: propose-presentation
  end
  Verifier->>Holder: request-presentation
  Note over Holder: selects credentials
  Holder->>Verifier: presentation
  Note over Verifier: verifies the presentation
  Verifier->>Holder: ack
```

The verifier usually starts with a request. The holder can also propose what it wants to share with `proposeProof`, and the verifier answers with `acceptProposal`. Both sides track the exchange in a `DidCommProofExchangeRecord`.

## Request a proof

:::verifier

```ts
await verifier.didcomm.proofs.requestProof({
  connectionId,
  protocolVersion: 'v2',
  proofFormats: {
    presentationExchange: {
      presentationDefinition: {
        id: 'credo-docs-badge',
        input_descriptors: [
          {
            id: 'open-badge',
            schema: [{ uri: 'https://purl.imsglobal.org/spec/ob/v3p0/context.json' }],
            constraints: {
              fields: [
                {
                  path: ['$.credentialSubject.achievement.name'],
                  filter: { type: 'string', const: 'Read the Credo docs' },
                },
              ],
            },
          },
        ],
      },
    },
  },
})
```

:::

Credo looks up candidate credentials by the `schema` URI, which matches a JSON-LD context or an expanded type of the credential. The `constraints` then filter on the credential's content with JSONPath and JSON Schema. Credo adds a random challenge to the request, which the holder signs, unless you set `options.challenge` yourself.

To request a proof without a connection, create it with `createRequest` and attach the returned `message` to an out-of-band invitation, with `handshake: false` to skip creating a connection.

## Respond to a request

:::holder

```ts
holder.events.on<DidCommProofStateChangedEvent>(
  DidCommProofEventTypes.ProofStateChanged,
  async ({ payload: { proofRecord } }) => {
    if (proofRecord.state !== DidCommProofState.RequestReceived) return

    // Picks the first matching credential for every requested item
    const { proofFormats } = await holder.didcomm.proofs.selectCredentialsForRequest({
      proofExchangeRecordId: proofRecord.id,
    })

    await holder.didcomm.proofs.acceptRequest({ proofExchangeRecordId: proofRecord.id, proofFormats })
  }
)
```

:::

`selectCredentialsForRequest` picks the first matching credential for each requested item and throws if something can't be satisfied. To let the user choose, call `getCredentialsForRequest`, which lists all candidates per item, and pass the chosen credentials in `proofFormats` to `acceptRequest`. `declineRequest` rejects the request.

The holder signs a JSON-LD or JWT presentation with an `authentication` key of the DID in `credentialSubject.id`, so that DID must be one the holder created in its agent.

## Check the result

The verifier verifies the presentation as soon as it arrives. A valid presentation moves the exchange to `PresentationReceived` with `isVerified: true`. An invalid one moves it to `Abandoned`, sets `errorMessage` and sends a problem report to the holder.

:::verifier

```ts
verifier.events.on<DidCommProofStateChangedEvent>(
  DidCommProofEventTypes.ProofStateChanged,
  async ({ payload: { proofRecord } }) => {
    if (proofRecord.state === DidCommProofState.PresentationReceived) {
      // Only valid presentations reach this state, so `proofRecord.isVerified` is true
      const { presentation } = await verifier.didcomm.proofs.getFormatData(proofRecord.id)
      console.log('Verified presentation', JSON.stringify(presentation?.presentationExchange))

      // Sends the ack and completes the exchange
      await verifier.didcomm.proofs.acceptPresentation({ proofExchangeRecordId: proofRecord.id })
    }

    if (proofRecord.state === DidCommProofState.Abandoned) {
      console.log('Verification failed', proofRecord.errorMessage)
    }
  }
)
```

:::

Verification covers the signatures, the challenge, holder binding and whether the presentation satisfies the request. Which issuers you trust is up to you: restrict them in the request (for AnonCreds with `restrictions`), configure [trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md) for W3C credentials, or check the issuer in the format data.

`acceptPresentation` sends the ack and completes the exchange. With `ContentApproved` auto-accept, Credo sends the ack for you, so leave that call out.

## Auto-accept

Set `autoAcceptProofs` on the proofs module, or `autoAcceptProof` on a single API call.

| `DidCommAutoAcceptProof` | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `Never` (default) | Every step needs an API call: `acceptRequest`, `acceptPresentation`, and so on. |
| `ContentApproved` | The holder answers a request automatically only when it matches the holder's own proposal. The verifier acknowledges valid presentations automatically. |
| `Always` | The holder answers every request with automatically selected credentials, without asking the user. |

The verifier only acknowledges automatically when the request had `willConfirm` set, which is the default.

For a verifier, `ContentApproved` saves the `acceptPresentation` call. For a wallet, use `ContentApproved` or `Never`, so the user approves each request. `Always` shares credentials without asking the user.

## States and events

Listen to `DidCommProofEventTypes.ProofStateChanged`. The payload has the `proofRecord` and its `previousState`.

| `DidCommProofState` | Agent | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ProposalSent` | holder | wait for the request |
| `ProposalReceived` | verifier | `acceptProposal` or `negotiateProposal` |
| `RequestSent` | verifier | wait for the presentation |
| `RequestReceived` | holder | `acceptRequest`, `declineRequest` or `negotiateRequest` |
| `PresentationSent` | holder | wait for the ack |
| `PresentationReceived` | verifier | the presentation is valid, `acceptPresentation` sends the ack |
| `Done` | both | |
| `Declined` | holder | |
| `Abandoned` | both | the exchange failed, `errorMessage` says why |

`agent.didcomm.proofs.getFormatData(proofRecordId)` returns the proposal, request and presentation per format.

## Present Proof v1

:::warning[Deprecated]

Present Proof v1 ([Aries RFC 0037](https://github.com/decentralized-identity/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0037-present-proof)) is deprecated and removed in Credo 0.8. Use v2 unless the other agent only supports v1.

:::

Present Proof v1 only carries AnonCreds proofs in the `indy` format. Register it next to v2, and pass `protocolVersion: 'v1'` in the API calls:

```ts
import { DidCommProofV1Protocol, LegacyIndyDidCommProofFormatService } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm'

const proofProtocol = new DidCommProofV1Protocol({
  indyProofFormat: new LegacyIndyDidCommProofFormatService(),
})
```

# Mediation

> Run a DIDComm mediator with Credo and connect mobile agents to it, with message pickup, live delivery and keylist updates.

A mediator is an agent that receives messages on behalf of agents that can't be reached directly, and holds them until they are picked up. This page covers running a mediator, connecting an agent to it as a recipient, choosing a pickup strategy, and how routing keys stay in sync.

## When you need a mediator

An agent needs a mediator when other agents can't reach it. A mobile wallet always needs one when it uses DIDComm: a phone has no public address, and the app is often closed. A server agent with public `endpoints` doesn't need one.

A wallet with a mediator puts the mediator's endpoint and routing key in its invitations and DID documents. Senders wrap their messages in a forward message to the mediator, and the mediator delivers them to the wallet over a WebSocket, or queues them until the wallet picks them up.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Alice as Alice (wallet)
    participant Mediator
    participant Bob
    Alice->>Mediator: Request mediation
    Mediator->>Alice: Grant (endpoint, routing key)
    Alice->>Mediator: Keylist update (add key)
    Alice-->>Bob: Invitation with the mediator's endpoint
    Bob->>Mediator: Forward message for Alice
    Mediator->>Alice: Deliver over WebSocket, or queue for pickup
```

Credo implements [Coordinate Mediation 1.0](https://github.com/hyperledger/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0211-route-coordination) and message pickup ([Pickup 1.0](https://github.com/hyperledger/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0212-pickup) and [2.0](https://github.com/hyperledger/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0685-pickup-v2)) for both roles. Messages from a wallet to other agents don't go through its mediator.

## Run a mediator

A mediator is a Node.js agent with the `mediator` protocol turned on. It needs an HTTP endpoint for senders and a WebSocket endpoint so wallets can receive messages live.

```ts
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import {
  DidCommBasicMessageEventTypes,
  DidCommBasicMessageRole,
  type DidCommBasicMessageStateChangedEvent,
  DidCommHttpOutboundTransport,
  type DidCommKeylistUpdatedEvent,
  DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy,
  DidCommModule,
  DidCommRoutingEventTypes,
  DidCommWsOutboundTransport,
} from '@credo-ts/didcomm'
import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport, DidCommWsInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node'

const mediator = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...mediatorStorage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    didcomm: new DidCommModule({
      endpoints: ['http://localhost:4040', 'ws://localhost:4041'],
      transports: {
        inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port: 4040 }), new DidCommWsInboundTransport({ port: 4041 })],
        outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport(), new DidCommWsOutboundTransport()],
      },
      connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true },
      mediator: { autoAcceptMediationRequests: true },
      // A mediator only routes messages, so it doesn't need the other protocols
      mediationRecipient: false,
      credentials: false,
      proofs: false,
      basicMessages: false,
    }),
  },
})

await mediator.initialize()

const mediatorOutOfBandRecord = await mediator.didcomm.oob.createInvitation({
  label: 'Mediator',
  multiUseInvitation: true,
})
const mediatorInvitationUrl = mediatorOutOfBandRecord.outOfBandInvitation.toUrl({
  domain: 'http://localhost:4040/invite',
})
```

The mediator shares one multi-use invitation with all wallets. Without `autoAcceptMediationRequests`, listen for `DidCommRoutingEventTypes.MediationStateChanged` and grant requests in the `requested` state with `agent.didcomm.mediator.grantRequestedMediation(mediationRecordId)`.

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mediator.autoAcceptMediationRequests` | `false` | Grant every mediation request. |
| `mediator.messageForwardingStrategy` | `DirectDelivery` | `DirectDelivery` sends a forwarded message right away over an open session with the recipient, and queues it if that isn't possible. `QueueOnly` always queues. `QueueAndLiveModeDelivery` queues, then delivers the queue to recipients in live mode. |
| `messagePickup.maximumBatchSize` | `10` | Maximum number of messages per pickup batch. |
| `queueTransportRepository` | in memory | Where queued messages are stored. Pass a persistent implementation in production, or messages are lost on restart. |

For production, look at [DIDComm Mediator Credo](https://github.com/openwallet-foundation/didcomm-mediator-credo), a mediator built on Credo with a persistent message queue and a Docker image.

## Connect to a mediator

On the recipient, set `mediatorInvitationUrl` in the `mediationRecipient` options:

**Node.js**

```ts
const alice = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...aliceStorage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    didcomm: new DidCommModule({
      transports: {
        outbound: [new DidCommWsOutboundTransport(), new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()],
      },
      connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true },
      mediationRecipient: {
        mediatorInvitationUrl,
        mediatorPickupStrategy: DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.PickUpV2LiveMode,
      },
      mediator: false,
    }),
  },
})

// Connects to the mediator, requests mediation and starts message pickup
await alice.initialize()
```

**React Native**

```ts
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import {
  DidCommHttpOutboundTransport,
  DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy,
  DidCommModule,
  DidCommWsOutboundTransport,
} from '@credo-ts/didcomm'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native'

// The invitation URL your mediator hands out
const mediatorInvitationUrl = 'https://mediator.example.com/invite?oob=eyJ...'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    askar: new AskarModule({
      askar: NativeAskar,
      store: { id: 'wallet', key: 'wallet-key' },
    }),
    didcomm: new DidCommModule({
      // No endpoints and no inbound transports: messages reach the wallet through the mediator
      transports: {
        outbound: [new DidCommWsOutboundTransport(), new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()],
      },
      mediationRecipient: {
        mediatorInvitationUrl,
        mediatorPickupStrategy: DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.PickUpV2LiveMode,
      },
      // A wallet doesn't act as a mediator
      mediator: false,
    }),
  },
})

await agent.initialize()
```

`DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy` is exported from `@credo-ts/didcomm`. [Pickup strategies](#pickup-strategies) explains the options.

During `initialize()`, Credo connects to the mediator if it isn't connected yet, requests mediation, waits for the grant and sets the mediator as the default. Then it starts picking up messages. Startup therefore depends on the mediator being reachable. To keep startup independent, leave out `mediatorInvitationUrl` and connect later with the API:

| Method on `agent.didcomm.mediationRecipient` | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `provision(connection)` | Request mediation over a connection, wait for the grant, and set the mediator as default. |
| `initiateMessagePickup(mediator?, strategy?)` | Start picking up messages, from the default mediator unless you pass a mediation record. |
| `stopMessagePickup()` | Stop all message pickup. |
| `findDefaultMediator()` | Get the mediation record of the default mediator. |
| `setDefaultMediator(mediationRecord)` | Change the default mediator. |

Once a default mediator is set, new invitations and connections route through it without extra code:

```ts
// The invitation points to the mediator's endpoint and routing keys
const outOfBandRecord = await alice.didcomm.oob.createInvitation({ label: 'Alice' })
const invitationUrl = outOfBandRecord.outOfBandInvitation.toUrl({ domain: 'https://alice.example.com' })
```

To use another mediator for one connection, create routing with `agent.didcomm.mediationRecipient.getRouting({ mediatorId })` and pass it as `routing` to `createInvitation()` or `receiveInvitation()`.

## Pickup strategies

`mediatorPickupStrategy` decides how the recipient gets its messages:

| Strategy | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| `PickUpV2LiveMode` | Opens a WebSocket, picks up queued messages, then asks the mediator to push new messages as they arrive (Pickup 2.0 live mode). |
| `PickUpV2` | Polls with Pickup 2.0 every `mediatorPollingInterval` milliseconds. |
| `PickUpV1` | Polls with Pickup 1.0 every `mediatorPollingInterval` milliseconds. |
| `Implicit` | Opens a WebSocket and keeps it open, so the mediator can send messages over it. |
| `None` | Doesn't pick up messages automatically. |

For a mobile wallet, use `PickUpV2LiveMode`: messages arrive as soon as the mediator receives them, and Credo reopens the WebSocket when it drops. It needs a WebSocket endpoint on the mediator and `DidCommWsOutboundTransport` on the wallet. Use `PickUpV2` if the mediator has no WebSocket endpoint, and `Implicit` for mediators that don't support a pickup protocol.

Without a strategy, Credo asks the mediator which pickup protocols it supports and uses `PickUpV2`, `PickUpV1` or `Implicit`, in that order. It never chooses live mode on its own. Credo stores the choice on the mediation record, and the stored choice wins over `mediatorPickupStrategy` from then on, so set the strategy before the agent first connects to the mediator.

| Option | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mediatorPollingInterval` | `5000` | Milliseconds between polls for `PickUpV1` and `PickUpV2`. |
| `maximumMessagePickup` | `10` | Messages per batch when polling. |
| `baseMediatorReconnectionIntervalMs` | `100` | First delay before reconnecting a closed WebSocket. It doubles after each attempt. |
| `maximumMediatorReconnectionIntervalMs` | no limit | Longest delay between reconnection attempts. |

## Control message pickup

A mobile app usually stops pickup when it goes to the background and starts it again when it returns:

```ts
// For example when the app goes to the background
await alice.didcomm.mediationRecipient.stopMessagePickup()

// Back in the foreground: picks up queued messages, then resumes live delivery
await alice.didcomm.mediationRecipient.initiateMessagePickup()
```

If you'd rather decide when pickup runs, set `mediatorPickupStrategy: DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.None` and pass the strategy when you start it: `initiateMessagePickup(undefined, DidCommMediatorPickupStrategy.PickUpV2LiveMode)`.

To fetch queued messages once, for example in a background task, use the message pickup API and wait until the messages are processed:

```ts
const mediatorConnection = await alice.didcomm.mediationRecipient.findDefaultMediatorConnection()
if (mediatorConnection) {
  await alice.didcomm.messagePickup.pickupMessages({
    connectionId: mediatorConnection.id,
    protocolVersion: 'v2',
    awaitCompletion: true,
  })
}
```

## Keylist updates

The mediator only forwards messages for keys in the recipient's keylist. Credo keeps the keylist up to date: every time it creates routing through a mediator, for a new invitation, connection or DID rotation, it adds the new key and waits for the mediator to confirm. Deleting a connection with `connections.deleteById()`, or with `connections.hangup({ connectionId, deleteAfterHangup: true })`, removes its keys again. After a DID rotation, `connections.removePreviousDids({ connectionId })` removes the old keys.

Each confirmed update emits an event:

```ts
alice.events.on<DidCommKeylistUpdatedEvent>(DidCommRoutingEventTypes.RecipientKeylistUpdated, ({ payload }) => {
  for (const update of payload.keylist) {
    console.log(`Mediator keylist update: ${update.action} ${update.recipientKey}`)
  }
})
```

For keys created outside of Credo's routing, send the update yourself with `agent.didcomm.mediationRecipient.notifyKeylistUpdate(connection, verkey, action)`.

# Messaging and other protocols

> Send basic messages over a DIDComm connection, and add the action menu, question answer and DIDComm RPC protocols to a Credo agent.

Besides credentials and proofs, two connected agents can exchange plain text messages, menus, questions and remote procedure calls. Basic messages are built into `@credo-ts/didcomm`. The other three protocols come in separate packages. All examples on this page assume an Acme and a Bob agent with a [connection](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/connections.md) between them.

## Basic messages

[Basic Message](https://github.com/hyperledger/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0095-basic-message) sends a text message over a connection, like a chat. The protocol is on by default.

```ts
await acme.didcomm.basicMessages.sendMessage(acmeToBob.id, 'Your order has shipped')
```

The receiving agent stores the message and emits an event:

```ts
bob.events.on<DidCommBasicMessageStateChangedEvent>(
  DidCommBasicMessageEventTypes.DidCommBasicMessageStateChanged,
  ({ payload: { basicMessageRecord } }) => {
    // The event fires for sent and received messages
    if (basicMessageRecord.role !== DidCommBasicMessageRole.Receiver) return

    console.log(`Bob received: ${basicMessageRecord.content}`)
  }
)
```

Every message, sent or received, is stored as a `DidCommBasicMessageRecord` with `content`, `sentTime`, `role` and `connectionId`. To load the history of a connection:

```ts
const history = await bob.didcomm.basicMessages.findAllByQuery({ connectionId: bobToAcme.id })
```

`sendMessage()` takes a thread id as third argument, to link the message to another thread with `~thread.pthid`. To turn the protocol off, pass `basicMessages: false` to the `DidCommModule`.

## Optional protocol packages

| Package | Protocol | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@credo-ts/question-answer` | [Question Answer 1.0](https://github.com/hyperledger/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0113-question-answer) | Asking a question with a fixed set of answers. |
| `@credo-ts/action-menu` | [Action Menu 1.0](https://github.com/hyperledger/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0509-action-menu) | Offering a menu of actions that the other agent can choose from. |
| `@credo-ts/drpc` | [DIDComm RPC 1.0](https://github.com/hyperledger/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0804-didcomm-rpc) | Sending JSON-RPC 2.0 requests and responses. |

Install the packages you need:

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/question-answer@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/action-menu@^0.7.2 @credo-ts/drpc@^0.7.2
```

Register each one as an agent module next to the `DidCommModule`. Both agents in a conversation need the module. Its API is available under the key you register it with, for example `agent.modules.questionAnswer`.

```ts
import {
  ActionMenu,
  ActionMenuEventTypes,
  ActionMenuModule,
  ActionMenuRole,
  ActionMenuState,
  type ActionMenuStateChangedEvent,
} from '@credo-ts/action-menu'
import type { BaseEvent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { Agent } from '@credo-ts/core'
import {
  DidCommBasicMessageEventTypes,
  DidCommBasicMessageRole,
  type DidCommBasicMessageStateChangedEvent,
  DidCommHttpOutboundTransport,
  DidCommModule,
} from '@credo-ts/didcomm'
import { DrpcModule } from '@credo-ts/drpc'
import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node'
import {
  QuestionAnswerEventTypes,
  QuestionAnswerModule,
  QuestionAnswerState,
  type QuestionAnswerStateChangedEvent,
} from '@credo-ts/question-answer'

function createAgent(port: number, storage: ExampleStorage) {
  return new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
      didcomm: new DidCommModule({
        endpoints: [`http://localhost:${port}`],
        transports: {
          inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port })],
          outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()],
        },
        connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true },
      }),
      // Each package adds its API under the key you choose: agent.modules.actionMenu, ...
      actionMenu: new ActionMenuModule(),
      questionAnswer: new QuestionAnswerModule(),
      drpc: new DrpcModule(),
    },
  })
}
```

### Question answer

The questioner sends a question with the answers it accepts. The responder picks one of them.

```ts
await acme.modules.questionAnswer.sendQuestion(acmeToBob.id, {
  question: 'Do you want to receive your membership credential?',
  detail: 'We will issue it right after you answer.',
  validResponses: [{ text: 'Yes' }, { text: 'No' }],
})
```

The responder answers when the question arrives, and the questioner reads the answer from the record:

```ts
bob.events.on<QuestionAnswerStateChangedEvent>(
  QuestionAnswerEventTypes.QuestionAnswerStateChanged,
  async ({ payload: { questionAnswerRecord } }) => {
    if (questionAnswerRecord.state !== QuestionAnswerState.QuestionReceived) return

    console.log(`Acme asks: ${questionAnswerRecord.questionText}`)
    await bob.modules.questionAnswer.sendAnswer(questionAnswerRecord.id, 'Yes')
  }
)

acme.events.on<QuestionAnswerStateChangedEvent>(
  QuestionAnswerEventTypes.QuestionAnswerStateChanged,
  ({ payload: { questionAnswerRecord } }) => {
    if (questionAnswerRecord.state !== QuestionAnswerState.AnswerReceived) return

    console.log(`Bob answered: ${questionAnswerRecord.response}`)
  }
)
```

`sendAnswer()` throws if the response isn't one of the `validResponses`.

### Action menu

The responder sends a menu, the requester chooses an option, and the responder acts on the choice, for example by offering a credential. The requester can also ask for the menu with `requestMenu({ connectionId })`.

```ts
await acme.modules.actionMenu.sendMenu({
  connectionId: acmeToBob.id,
  menu: new ActionMenu({
    title: 'Acme services',
    description: 'What would you like to do?',
    options: [
      { name: 'get-membership', title: 'Get a membership credential', description: 'Issue a new credential' },
      { name: 'contact', title: 'Contact support', description: 'Start a chat with Acme' },
    ],
  }),
})
```

The requester shows the menu and performs the chosen action. The responder receives the selection in `performedAction`:

```ts
bob.events.on<ActionMenuStateChangedEvent>(
  ActionMenuEventTypes.ActionMenuStateChanged,
  async ({ payload: { actionMenuRecord } }) => {
    if (actionMenuRecord.state !== ActionMenuState.PreparingSelection || !actionMenuRecord.menu) return

    // A wallet would show the menu and let the user pick an option
    const [firstOption] = actionMenuRecord.menu.options
    await bob.modules.actionMenu.performAction({
      connectionId: actionMenuRecord.connectionId,
      performedAction: { name: firstOption.name },
    })
  }
)

acme.events.on<ActionMenuStateChangedEvent>(
  ActionMenuEventTypes.ActionMenuStateChanged,
  ({ payload: { actionMenuRecord } }) => {
    if (actionMenuRecord.role !== ActionMenuRole.Responder || actionMenuRecord.state !== ActionMenuState.Done) return

    console.log(`Bob selected: ${actionMenuRecord.performedAction?.name}`)
  }
)
```

An option can include a `form` with parameters. The requester then sends the values as `params` in the selection. `findActiveMenu({ connectionId, role })` returns the current menu of a connection, and `clearActiveMenu({ connectionId, role })` removes it. By default the module checks the state of the menu before each step. Pass `new ActionMenuModule({ strictStateChecking: false })` to skip that check.

### DIDComm RPC

DIDComm RPC carries [JSON-RPC 2.0](https://www.jsonrpc.org/specification) requests and responses over a connection. The server waits for a request and answers it:

```ts
async function handleNextRequest() {
  const incoming = await acme.modules.drpc.recvRequest()
  // Batch requests arrive as an array
  if (!incoming || Array.isArray(incoming.request)) return

  const { request, sendResponse } = incoming
  if (request.method === 'getOrderStatus') {
    await sendResponse({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: request.id, result: { status: 'shipped' } })
  } else {
    await sendResponse({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: request.id, error: { code: -32601, message: 'Method not found' } })
  }
}

// Start listening before the request can arrive
const handledRequest = handleNextRequest()
```

The client sends a request and gets a function that waits for the response:

```ts
const waitForResponse = await bob.modules.drpc.sendRequest(bobToAcme.id, {
  jsonrpc: '2.0',
  method: 'getOrderStatus',
  params: { orderId: '1234' },
  id: 1,
})

// Resolves to undefined if no response arrives within 5000 ms
const response = await waitForResponse(5000)
```

`recvRequest()` only returns the next request that arrives after you call it, from any connection. Call it again for every request you want to handle. Both `recvRequest()` and the function returned by `sendRequest()` take an optional timeout in milliseconds and resolve to `undefined` when it expires.

# AnonCreds with DIDComm

> Issue AnonCreds credentials and request proofs with predicates over DIDComm, and handle revocation.

You exchange AnonCreds credentials over DIDComm, with [Issue Credential v2](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/issue-credential.md) and [Present Proof v2](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/present-proof.md). This page issues a credential and requests a proof with a predicate, then covers revocation. The AnonCreds specification calls the holder the prover when it presents. Both agents need the `AnonCredsModule` with a registry, and the issuer needs a registered credential definition: see [AnonCreds](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/anoncreds.md).

## Register the format services

The AnonCreds format services are exported from `@credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm` since Credo 0.7.2. `@credo-ts/anoncreds` still exports them too, but those exports are deprecated and removed in 0.8. Register the services on both the credentials and the proofs protocol.

```ts
import { AnonCredsModule } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds'
import {
  AnonCredsDidCommCredentialFormatService,
  AnonCredsDidCommProofFormatService,
  LegacyIndyDidCommCredentialFormatService,
  LegacyIndyDidCommProofFormatService,
} from '@credo-ts/anoncreds/didcomm'
import { CheqdDidRegistrar, CheqdDidResolver, CheqdModule } from '@credo-ts/cheqd'
import { CheqdAnonCredsRegistry } from '@credo-ts/cheqd/anoncreds'
import { Agent, DidsModule } from '@credo-ts/core'
import {
  DidCommAutoAcceptCredential,
  DidCommAutoAcceptProof,
  DidCommCredentialEventTypes,
  DidCommCredentialState,
  type DidCommCredentialStateChangedEvent,
  DidCommCredentialV2Protocol,
  DidCommHttpOutboundTransport,
  DidCommModule,
  DidCommProofEventTypes,
  DidCommProofState,
  type DidCommProofStateChangedEvent,
  DidCommProofV2Protocol,
} from '@credo-ts/didcomm'
import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAnoncreds } from '@hyperledger/anoncreds-nodejs'

function createAgent(port: number, storage: ExampleStorage) {
  return new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
      // The registry and its DID module, see the AnonCreds page
      cheqd: new CheqdModule({ networks: [{ network: 'testnet', cosmosPayerSeed: '<cosmos payer seed>' }] }),
      dids: new DidsModule({ registrars: [new CheqdDidRegistrar()], resolvers: [new CheqdDidResolver()] }),
      anoncreds: new AnonCredsModule({ anoncreds: NativeAnoncreds, registries: [new CheqdAnonCredsRegistry()] }),
      didcomm: new DidCommModule({
        endpoints: [`http://localhost:${port}`],
        transports: {
          inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port })],
          outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()],
        },
        connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true },
        credentials: {
          autoAcceptCredentials: DidCommAutoAcceptCredential.ContentApproved,
          credentialProtocols: [
            new DidCommCredentialV2Protocol({
              credentialFormats: [
                new AnonCredsDidCommCredentialFormatService(),
                new LegacyIndyDidCommCredentialFormatService(),
              ],
            }),
          ],
        },
        proofs: {
          autoAcceptProofs: DidCommAutoAcceptProof.ContentApproved,
          proofProtocols: [
            new DidCommProofV2Protocol({
              proofFormats: [new AnonCredsDidCommProofFormatService(), new LegacyIndyDidCommProofFormatService()],
            }),
          ],
        },
      }),
    },
  })
}
```

There are two formats for the same credentials. `anoncreds` uses the AnonCreds attachments of [RFC 0771](https://github.com/decentralized-identity/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0771-anoncreds-attachments). `indy` uses the older Hyperledger Indy attachments of [RFC 0592](https://github.com/decentralized-identity/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0592-indy-attachments), which some agents still require. Their API options are the same, under the `anoncreds` or `indy` key. The deprecated Issue Credential v1 and Present Proof v1 protocols only support the `indy` format, see [Issuing credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/issue-credential.md#issue-credential-v1).

## Issue a credential

:::issuer

```ts
await issuer.didcomm.credentials.offerCredential({
  connectionId,
  protocolVersion: 'v2',
  credentialFormats: {
    anoncreds: {
      credentialDefinitionId,
      // Values are strings, also for numbers you want to use in predicates
      attributes: [
        { name: 'name', value: 'Jane Doe' },
        { name: 'role', value: 'Developer' },
        { name: 'age', value: '32' },
      ],
    },
  },
})
```

:::

The attribute names must match the schema of the credential definition exactly: no missing and no extra attributes. AnonCreds values are strings. Predicates work on attributes whose value is an integer string.

:::holder

```ts
holder.events.on<DidCommCredentialStateChangedEvent>(
  DidCommCredentialEventTypes.DidCommCredentialStateChanged,
  async ({ payload: { credentialExchangeRecord } }) => {
    if (credentialExchangeRecord.state !== DidCommCredentialState.OfferReceived) return

    // The attribute names and values to show to the user
    console.log(credentialExchangeRecord.credentialAttributes)

    // Uses the default link secret, and creates it if there is none yet
    await holder.didcomm.credentials.acceptOffer({ credentialExchangeRecordId: credentialExchangeRecord.id })
  }
)
```

:::

The holder binds the credential to its link secret. Credo creates a default link secret on the first credential request if there is none. To use another one, create it with `agent.modules.anoncreds.createLinkSecret` and pass `credentialFormats: { anoncreds: { linkSecretId } }` to `acceptOffer`. The holder stores the credential as a W3C credential record. [AnonCreds](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/anoncreds.md) shows how to query it.

## Request a proof

:::verifier

```ts
await issuer.didcomm.proofs.requestProof({
  connectionId,
  protocolVersion: 'v2',
  proofFormats: {
    anoncreds: {
      name: 'Employee check',
      version: '1.0',
      requested_attributes: {
        name: { name: 'name', restrictions: [{ cred_def_id: credentialDefinitionId }] },
        role: { name: 'role', restrictions: [{ cred_def_id: credentialDefinitionId }] },
      },
      requested_predicates: {
        // Proves age >= 18 without revealing the age
        adult: { name: 'age', p_type: '>=', p_value: 18, restrictions: [{ cred_def_id: credentialDefinitionId }] },
      },
    },
  },
})
```

:::

The keys of `requested_attributes` and `requested_predicates` (`name`, `role`, `adult`) are referents: names you choose to find the values in the presentation. Use `names: ['name', 'role']` instead of `name` to require attributes from the same credential. A predicate (`>=`, `>`, `<=` or `<` with an integer `p_value`) proves a comparison without revealing the value. Credo generates the `nonce` of the request when you leave it out.

`restrictions` decide which credentials qualify, for example by `cred_def_id`, `issuer_id` or `schema_id`. Without restrictions, the holder can use any credential with that attribute, including one it issued itself, so restrict every item to the issuers you trust.

:::holder

```ts
holder.events.on<DidCommProofStateChangedEvent>(
  DidCommProofEventTypes.ProofStateChanged,
  async ({ payload: { proofRecord } }) => {
    if (proofRecord.state !== DidCommProofState.RequestReceived) return

    // Lists all matching credentials per attribute and predicate, to let the user choose
    const { proofFormats: options } = await holder.didcomm.proofs.getCredentialsForRequest({
      proofExchangeRecordId: proofRecord.id,
    })
    console.log(options.anoncreds?.attributes)

    // Or let Credo pick the first match for each
    const { proofFormats } = await holder.didcomm.proofs.selectCredentialsForRequest({
      proofExchangeRecordId: proofRecord.id,
    })
    await holder.didcomm.proofs.acceptRequest({ proofExchangeRecordId: proofRecord.id, proofFormats })
  }
)
```

:::

All credentials in one presentation must be bound to the same link secret.

:::verifier

```ts
issuer.events.on<DidCommProofStateChangedEvent>(
  DidCommProofEventTypes.ProofStateChanged,
  async ({ payload: { proofRecord } }) => {
    if (proofRecord.state !== DidCommProofState.PresentationReceived) return

    // Only valid presentations reach this state, so `proofRecord.isVerified` is true
    const { presentation } = await issuer.didcomm.proofs.getFormatData(proofRecord.id)
    const revealedAttributes = presentation?.anoncreds?.requested_proof.revealed_attrs ?? {}
    for (const [referent, { raw }] of Object.entries(revealedAttributes)) {
      console.log(referent, raw)
    }
  }
)
```

:::

The presentation contains the revealed attribute values under their referents. Predicates appear only as proven, without the value.

## Revocation

Revocation needs a revocable credential definition with a revocation registry and status list. [AnonCreds](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/anoncreds.md) shows how to create them and how to revoke.

When you issue a revocable credential, pass the revocation registry and an index in it. Credo doesn't track which indexes you used: each credential needs its own, and you need the index later to revoke the credential.

:::issuer

```ts
await issuer.didcomm.credentials.offerCredential({
  connectionId,
  protocolVersion: 'v2',
  credentialFormats: {
    anoncreds: {
      credentialDefinitionId: revocableCredentialDefinitionId,
      attributes: [
        { name: 'name', value: 'Jane Doe' },
        { name: 'role', value: 'Developer' },
        { name: 'age', value: '32' },
      ],
      revocationRegistryDefinitionId,
      // Track which indexes you used, each credential needs its own
      revocationRegistryIndex: 1,
    },
  },
})
```

:::

After you revoke a credential, you can tell the holder with a revocation notification. The holder agent emits a `DidCommCredentialEventTypes.DidCommRevocationNotificationReceived` event and stores the notification on the exchange record (`revocationNotification`).

:::issuer

```ts
// After revoking index 1 with updateRevocationStatusList, optionally notify the holder
await issuer.didcomm.credentials.sendRevocationNotification({
  connectionId,
  revocationFormat: 'anoncreds',
  revocationId: `${revocationRegistryDefinitionId}::1`,
})
```

:::

A verifier that wants proof that a credential isn't revoked sets `non_revoked`, on the whole request or per attribute or predicate. Set `to`, the time in seconds. If you also set `from`, it must equal `to`.

:::verifier

```ts
await issuer.didcomm.proofs.requestProof({
  connectionId,
  protocolVersion: 'v2',
  proofFormats: {
    anoncreds: {
      name: 'Employee check',
      version: '1.0',
      // Require a proof that the credential was not revoked at this time (seconds)
      non_revoked: { to: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) },
      requested_attributes: {
        name: { name: 'name', restrictions: [{ cred_def_id: revocableCredentialDefinitionId }] },
      },
    },
  },
})
```

:::

The holder fetches the status list for that time from the registry. `selectCredentialsForRequest` skips revoked credentials, and throws when no valid credential is left.

## AnonCreds in W3C format

The [Data Integrity format](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/w3c.md) can also issue AnonCreds credentials as W3C VCDM 1.1 credentials: offer with `anonCredsLinkSecretBinding: { credentialDefinitionId }` and `bindingRequired: true`, and register the `AnonCredsModule` on both agents. The offered credential may only contain `@context`, `type`, `issuer`, `issuanceDate` or `validFrom`, and `credentialSubject`, and `type` must be `['VerifiableCredential']`. Present these credentials with DIF Presentation Exchange.

# W3C VCs with DIDComm

> Issue W3C Verifiable Credentials over DIDComm as JSON-LD, Data Integrity or VCDM 2.0 SD-JWT credentials, and present them with DIF Presentation Exchange.

Credo issues W3C Verifiable Credentials over DIDComm with three credential formats, and presents VCDM 1.1 credentials with DIF Presentation Exchange. This page covers the options and limits of each format. The protocol flow itself is on [Issuing credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/issue-credential.md) and [Requesting proofs](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/present-proof.md), and the credential model on [W3C Verifiable Credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/w3c-vc.md).

## Formats

| Format key | Spec | Credential | Holder binding | Stored as | Present over DIDComm |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `jsonld` | [RFC 0593](https://github.com/decentralized-identity/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0593-json-ld-cred-attach) | VCDM 1.1 with an Ed25519 Linked Data signature | DID in `credentialSubject.id` | `W3cCredentialRecord` | yes, as `ldp_vp` |
| `dataIntegrity` | [RFC 0809](https://github.com/decentralized-identity/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0809-w3c-data-integrity-credential-attachment) | VCDM 1.1 with a Linked Data signature, or VCDM 2.0 with a Data Integrity proof | signed nonce, AnonCreds link secret, or DID in `credentialSubject.id` | VCDM 1.1: `W3cCredentialRecord`, VCDM 2.0: `W3cV2CredentialRecord` | VCDM 1.1 only |
| `w3cV2SdJwt` | [RFC 0881](https://github.com/decentralized-identity/aries-rfcs/tree/main/features/0881-w3c-vc-sd-jwt-credential-attachment) | VCDM 2.0 secured with SD-JWT (`vc+sd-jwt`) | signed nonce, as `cnf` | `W3cV2CredentialRecord` | no |

`vc+sd-jwt` here is a W3C VCDM 2.0 credential secured with SD-JWT, not an IETF [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/sd-jwt-vc.md) (`dc+sd-jwt`). There is no DIDComm format for SD-JWT VC, mdoc or VCDM 1.1 JWT credentials.

Use `jsonld` when holders present the credential over DIDComm. Use `w3cV2SdJwt` for VCDM 2.0 credentials with selective disclosure, which holders present with OpenID4VP. Use `dataIntegrity` for [AnonCreds credentials in W3C format](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/anoncreds.md#anoncreds-in-w3c-format), or for agents that only support RFC 0809.

## Set up

Register the formats you need on both agents:

```ts
import { Agent, DidKey, type KeyDidCreateOptions, w3cDate } from '@credo-ts/core'
import {
  DidCommAutoAcceptCredential,
  DidCommCredentialEventTypes,
  DidCommCredentialState,
  type DidCommCredentialStateChangedEvent,
  DidCommCredentialV2Protocol,
  DidCommDataIntegrityCredentialFormatService,
  DidCommHttpOutboundTransport,
  DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService,
  DidCommModule,
  DidCommW3cV2SdJwtCredentialFormatService,
} from '@credo-ts/didcomm'
import { agentDependencies, DidCommHttpInboundTransport } from '@credo-ts/node'

function createAgent(port: number, storage: ExampleStorage) {
  return new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
      didcomm: new DidCommModule({
        endpoints: [`http://localhost:${port}`],
        transports: {
          inbound: [new DidCommHttpInboundTransport({ port })],
          outbound: [new DidCommHttpOutboundTransport()],
        },
        connections: { autoAcceptConnections: true },
        credentials: {
          autoAcceptCredentials: DidCommAutoAcceptCredential.ContentApproved,
          credentialProtocols: [
            new DidCommCredentialV2Protocol({
              credentialFormats: [
                new DidCommJsonLdCredentialFormatService(),
                new DidCommDataIntegrityCredentialFormatService(),
                new DidCommW3cV2SdJwtCredentialFormatService(),
              ],
            }),
          ],
        },
      }),
    },
  })
}
```

The issuer signs with a key of a DID it created in its own agent, for example a `did:key`:

:::issuer

```ts
const { didState } = await issuer.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({
  method: 'key',
  options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } },
})
if (didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the issuer DID failed')
const issuerDid = didState.did
```

:::

## JSON-LD credentials

:::issuer

```ts
await issuer.didcomm.credentials.offerCredential({
  connectionId,
  protocolVersion: 'v2',
  credentialFormats: {
    jsonld: {
      credential: {
        '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1', 'https://purl.imsglobal.org/spec/ob/v3p0/context.json'],
        type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'OpenBadgeCredential'],
        issuer: issuerDid,
        issuanceDate: w3cDate(),
        credentialSubject: {
          id: holderDid,
          type: ['AchievementSubject'],
          achievement: {
            id: 'https://example.com/achievements/credo-docs',
            type: ['Achievement'],
            name: 'Read the Credo docs',
          },
        },
      },
      // did:key Ed25519 keys are Ed25519VerificationKey2018 verification methods
      options: { proofType: 'Ed25519Signature2018', proofPurpose: 'assertionMethod' },
    },
  },
})
```

:::

The holder accepts the offer without format options, and stores the credential as a `W3cCredentialRecord`.

Credo signs with `Ed25519Signature2018` or `Ed25519Signature2020`, so the issuer needs an Ed25519 key. Each suite only accepts its own verification method type: a `did:key` has `Ed25519VerificationKey2018` methods, so use `Ed25519Signature2018`, with `proofPurpose: 'assertionMethod'`. Credo signs with the first verification method of the issuer DID that fits the proof type. Pass `jsonld: { verificationMethod }` to `acceptRequest` to choose another.

Every `@context` must resolve. Credo bundles common contexts, such as the VC data model, the security suites, Open Badges 3.0 and schema.org, and fetches others over the network. [W3C Verifiable Credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/w3c-vc.md) shows how to add your own.

- Don't add `credentialStatus`. Credo can't check W3C credential status, so the holder fails to verify such a credential.
- The holder proves control of the DID in `credentialSubject.id` when it presents the credential. To learn the holder's DID, let the holder [start with a proposal](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/issue-credential.md#start-with-a-proposal) that contains it.

## Present VCDM 1.1 credentials

Present JSON-LD credentials, and VCDM 1.1 Data Integrity credentials, with the DIF Presentation Exchange format, as shown on [Requesting proofs](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/present-proof.md). The holder signs an `ldp_vp` presentation with an `authentication` key of the DID in `credentialSubject.id`. VCDM 1.1 JWT credentials you received another way, such as with OpenID4VC, can be presented as `jwt_vp`.

## VCDM 2.0 SD-JWT credentials

The RFC 0881 format issues a VCDM 2.0 credential secured with SD-JWT, with selectively disclosable claims. It needs `@credo-ts/didcomm` 0.7.2 or later.

:::issuer

```ts
await issuer.didcomm.credentials.offerCredential({
  connectionId,
  protocolVersion: 'v2',
  credentialFormats: {
    w3cV2SdJwt: {
      credential: {
        '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/ns/credentials/v2'],
        type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'EmployeeCredential'],
        issuer: issuerDid,
        validFrom: w3cDate(),
        credentialSubject: { name: 'Jane Doe', role: 'Developer' },
      },
      disclosureFrame: { credentialSubject: { _sd: ['name', 'role'] } },
      // The holder proves control of a DID, which becomes the credential subject and `cnf`
      bindingRequired: true,
      didCommSignedAttachmentBinding: {},
    },
  },
})
```

:::

`credential` is a VCDM 2.0 credential without proof. You can leave out `issuer` and pass it to `acceptRequest` instead. `disclosureFrame` lists the claims the holder can disclose selectively. `@context`, `type`, `credentialStatus`, `credentialSchema` and `relatedResource` can't be selectively disclosable at the top level.

With `bindingRequired` and `didCommSignedAttachmentBinding`, the holder must sign a nonce with a key of one of its DIDs. Restrict the accepted keys with `didMethodsSupported` and `algsSupported`. Without binding, anyone who has the credential can present it, so require binding unless you want a bearer credential.

Auto-accept can't answer an offer that requires binding. The holder calls `acceptOffer` and picks the key:

:::holder

```ts
await holder.didcomm.credentials.acceptOffer({
  credentialExchangeRecordId: credentialExchangeRecord.id,
  credentialFormats: {
    // Signs the issuer's nonce with this key, the issuer binds the credential to it
    w3cV2SdJwt: { didCommSignedAttachment: { kid: holderKid } },
  },
})
```

:::

The issuer sets the holder's DID as `credentialSubject.id` and the key as `cnf`, signs the credential and sends it. With `ContentApproved` this happens automatically. Otherwise call `acceptRequest`, where you can also set `alg`, `issuerVerificationMethod`, `disclosureFrame` or `credentialSubjectId`. The holder verifies the credential, checks that it matches the offer and stores it as a `W3cV2CredentialRecord`.

The exchange always starts with an offer: proposals and holder-initiated requests aren't supported. Holders can't present these credentials over DIDComm. They present them with [OpenID4VP](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/w3c.md).

## Data Integrity credentials

The RFC 0809 format issues VCDM 1.1 and 2.0 credentials. The first `@context` entry decides the data model.

:::issuer

```ts
await issuer.didcomm.credentials.offerCredential({
  connectionId,
  protocolVersion: 'v2',
  credentialFormats: {
    dataIntegrity: {
      credential: {
        '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/ns/credentials/v2'],
        type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'EmployeeCredential'],
        issuer: issuerDid,
        validFrom: w3cDate(),
        credentialSubject: { id: holderDid, name: 'Jane Doe', role: 'Developer' },
      },
      bindingRequired: false,
    },
  },
})
```

:::

A VCDM 1.1 credential gets a Linked Data signature, as with the JSON-LD format. A VCDM 2.0 credential gets a Data Integrity proof with `eddsa-jcs-2022`, the only cryptosuite Credo registers, so the issuer needs an Ed25519 key. The exchange always starts with an offer.

Binding with `didCommSignedAttachmentBinding` works as in the RFC 0881 format, but the issuer doesn't derive `credentialSubject.id` from it. Put the holder's DID in the offer, or pass `credentialSubjectId` to `acceptRequest`; without a subject id, auto-accept doesn't issue the credential. The `anonCredsLinkSecretBinding` option issues AnonCreds credentials in W3C format, see [AnonCreds with DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/anoncreds.md#anoncreds-in-w3c-format).

`@credo-ts/anoncreds` also exports this service as `DataIntegrityDidCommCredentialFormatService`. That alias is deprecated and removed in 0.8: import `DidCommDataIntegrityCredentialFormatService` from `@credo-ts/didcomm`.

For VCDM 2.0 credentials:

- Credo doesn't check the holder's binding proof. Put the holder's DID in `credentialSubject.id` instead.
- The holder stores the credential as a `W3cV2CredentialRecord`, but the exchange record lists it with `credentialRecordType: 'w3c'`. Look it up with `agent.w3cV2Credentials.getById`.
- The credential can't be presented over DIDComm or OpenID4VC.

# Credential formats

> The credential formats Credo supports, how they compare, and which one to use.

A credential format defines what a credential looks like, how the issuer signs it and how the holder presents it. Formats are separate from exchange protocols: you can sign, store, present and verify a credential with the agent APIs alone, and most formats work over more than one protocol. The pages in this section cover each format on its own. For the flows, see [Protocols](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols.md).

## Compare the formats

| | [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/sd-jwt-vc.md) | [mdoc](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/mdoc.md) | [W3C VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/w3c-vc.md) | [AnonCreds](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/anoncreds.md) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Standard | IETF | ISO/IEC 18013-5 | W3C | Hyperledger AnonCreds |
| Selective disclosure | Per claim | Per data element | Only data model 2.0 secured as SD-JWT | Per attribute, plus predicates such as "age at least 18" |
| Unlinkable presentations | With batch issuance | With batch issuance | With batch issuance | Yes |
| Holder binding | Key (`cnf`), as JWK or DID | Device key | DID of the subject, or key (`cnf`) in data model 2.0 | Link secret |
| Issuer signs with | DID or X.509 certificate | X.509 certificate | DID | Keys of a credential definition on a registry |
| Revocation in Credo | [Token Status List](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/status-lists.md) | [Token Status List](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/status-lists.md) | None | Revocation registry |
| Exchange in Credo | OpenID4VC, Digital Credentials API | OpenID4VC, Digital Credentials API, ISO 18013-5 proximity | OpenID4VC, DIDComm, depending on the variant | DIDComm |
| Used in | EUDI Wallet (PID and attestations) | Mobile driving licence, EUDI Wallet (PID) | Open Badges, EBSI | Aries and Indy based ecosystems |

For SD-JWT VC, mdoc and W3C VCs, every presentation of a credential carries the same issuer signature, so verifiers that compare notes can link presentations of it. Batch issuance avoids that: the holder gets several copies, each bound to its own key, and presents each copy once. AnonCreds presentations are zero-knowledge proofs and don't need this.

For the protocol versions and the full matrix, see [Supported standards](https://credo.js.org/guides/supported-standards.md).

## Which one should I use?

Follow your ecosystem first. Without a required format:

| You're building | Use |
| --- | --- |
| An issuer, wallet or verifier for the EUDI Wallet | SD-JWT VC and mdoc. The EUDI Wallet uses both, including for the PID. |
| A mobile driving licence, or in-person presentation over NFC or Bluetooth | mdoc. It's the only format Credo presents with ISO 18013-5. |
| A new OpenID4VC deployment | SD-JWT VC. It has selective disclosure, plain JSON claims, and works with both DIDs and X.509 certificates. |
| Something for an ecosystem built on W3C VCs, such as EBSI or Open Badges | W3C VC. [Choose a variant](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/w3c-vc.md#choose-a-variant) explains which one. |
| A DIDComm deployment that needs predicates, or unlinkable presentations without batch issuance | AnonCreds. |

## Choices for every format

### Holder binding

Bind credentials to a key of the holder, so that a copy of a credential is useless to someone else. For SD-JWT VC and W3C data model 2.0, bind to a JWK by default: the holder needs no DID, and the key can stay in the secure hardware of a phone. Bind to a DID when holders and verifiers already use DIDs. mdocs are always bound to a device key, AnonCreds credentials to the link secret, and W3C data model 1.1 credentials to the DID in `credentialSubject.id`.

### Key type

For SD-JWT VC and mdoc, use P-256 keys (ES256) for both issuer and holder. HAIP requires every party to support ES256, and it's the curve that the secure hardware of phones supports. W3C JSON-LD and Data Integrity credentials need Ed25519 keys, because all signature suites that Credo has for them use Ed25519.

### Revocation

Use a status list or revocation registry only if you must be able to revoke credentials before they expire. Short-lived credentials that you reissue don't need one. See [Status lists](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/status-lists.md) and [AnonCreds revocation](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/anoncreds.md#revocation).

## Agent APIs

| Format | Agent API | Record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SD-JWT VC | `agent.sdJwtVc` | `SdJwtVcRecord` |
| mdoc | `agent.mdoc` | `MdocRecord` |
| W3C VC 1.1 | `agent.w3cCredentials` | `W3cCredentialRecord` |
| W3C VC 2.0 | `agent.w3cV2Credentials` | `W3cV2CredentialRecord` |
| AnonCreds | `agent.modules.anoncreds` (the key you register it under) | `W3cCredentialRecord` |

All formats except AnonCreds are part of `@credo-ts/core`, and their modules are registered on every agent. AnonCreds needs `@credo-ts/anoncreds` and a registry such as a ledger.

- [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/sd-jwt-vc.md): Sign, store, present and verify IETF SD-JWT VCs with agent.sdJwtVc, independent of the exchange protocol.
- [mdoc](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/mdoc.md): Sign, store, present and verify ISO 18013-5 mdocs, such as the mobile driving licence, with agent.mdoc.
- [W3C Verifiable Credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/w3c-vc.md): Sign, store, present and verify W3C Verifiable Credentials (data model 1.1 and 2.0) as JWT, SD-JWT, JSON-LD or Data Integrity.
- [AnonCreds](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/anoncreds.md): Set up AnonCreds in Credo with a registry, register schemas, credential definitions and revocation registries, and manage link secrets and stored credentials.
- [Status lists](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/status-lists.md): Revoke and suspend SD-JWT VCs and mdocs with IETF Token Status Lists, using agent.tokenStatusList.

# SD-JWT VC

> Sign, store, present and verify IETF SD-JWT VCs with agent.sdJwtVc, independent of the exchange protocol.

An SD-JWT VC ([IETF SD-JWT VC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc/)) is a JWT signed by the issuer, in which the holder can disclose claims one by one. It's usually bound to a key the holder controls. This page covers `agent.sdJwtVc`: signing, storing, presenting and verifying SD-JWT VCs yourself. To issue and present them over OpenID4VC, see [SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/sd-jwt-vc.md). The protocol calls these same APIs for you.

## Set up

Everything on this page is in `@credo-ts/core`. `SdJwtVcModule` is a default module, so every agent has `agent.sdJwtVc`. The agent also needs [storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage.md) and key management. The examples use three agents: an issuer, a holder and a verifier.

```ts
import { Agent, DidKey, type KeyDidCreateOptions, SdJwtVcModule, SdJwtVcRecord } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { PublicJwk } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'

function createAgent(storage: ExampleStorage, sdJwtVc?: SdJwtVcModule) {
  return new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
      // SdJwtVcModule is a default module. Register it yourself only to configure it.
      ...(sdJwtVc ? { sdJwtVc } : {}),
    },
  })
}
```

## Sign a credential

The issuer signs with a key of a DID it created (or imported with its keys), and binds the credential to the holder's public key:

:::issuer

```ts
// The issuer signs with a key of a DID it created
const { didState } = await issuer.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({
  method: 'key',
  options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } },
})
if (didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the issuer DID failed')
const issuerDid = didState.did
const issuerDidUrl = `${issuerDid}#${DidKey.fromDid(issuerDid).publicJwk.fingerprint}`

// The holder key. In a real flow the wallet sends the public key, for example in an OpenID4VCI proof.
const holderKey = await holder.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })
const holderJwk = PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(holderKey.publicJwk)

const credential = await issuer.sdJwtVc.sign({
  payload: {
    vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity',
    given_name: 'Jane',
    family_name: 'Doe',
    birthdate: '1990-01-01',
    address: { street_address: 'Main Street 1', locality: 'Utrecht', country: 'NL' },
    nationalities: ['NL', 'DE'],
  },
  issuer: { method: 'did', didUrl: issuerDidUrl },
  holder: { method: 'jwk', jwk: holderJwk },
  disclosureFrame: {
    _sd: ['given_name', 'family_name', 'birthdate'],
    _sd_decoy: 2,
    address: { _sd: ['street_address', 'locality'] },
    nationalities: { _sd: [0, 1] },
  },
  hashingAlgorithm: 'sha-256',
})

// The compact SD-JWT VC: issuer-signed JWT followed by the disclosures
console.log(credential.compact)
```

:::

- `payload` holds the claims and needs a `vct`, the credential type. Credo sets `iss`, `cnf` and `iat` (pass `iat: null` to leave `iat` out). Add `exp`, `nbf` or `status` yourself.
- `issuer` is `{ method: 'did', didUrl }` with a DID URL that points to a key, or `{ method: 'x5c', x5c }` with a certificate chain (see below).
- `holder` is `{ method: 'jwk', jwk }`, which sets `cnf.jwk`, or `{ method: 'did', didUrl }`, which sets `cnf.kid`.
- `disclosureFrame` lists the claims the holder can disclose one by one (see below).

`hashingAlgorithm` sets the digest algorithm of the disclosures: `sha-256` (default), `sha-384` or `sha-512`. `headerType` sets the `typ` header. Keep the default `dc+sd-jwt`, and use `vc+sd-jwt` only for verifiers that don't support `dc+sd-jwt` yet.

### Choose the holder binding

Bind to a JWK by default. The holder doesn't need a DID, and the key can stay in the secure hardware of a phone. Bind to a DID when holders and verifiers already work with DIDs. Without `holder` the credential is a bearer credential: anyone with a copy can present it, and a verifier can't require key binding.

### Design the disclosure frame

Each `_sd` lists the claims of one object that the holder can disclose separately: property names, or positions for array elements. Claims that aren't listed are always disclosed, and `iss`, `nbf`, `exp`, `cnf`, `vct` and `status` can't be listed.

- List every claim about the person, so the holder shares only what a verifier asks for. Leave claims visible that every verifier needs and that say nothing about the person.
- For a nested object, give it its own `_sd`, as for `address` above, so the holder can disclose the locality without the street. Also list the object in the parent `_sd` if even its presence says something about the person.
- Set `_sd_decoy` to add fake digests, so verifiers can't tell how many claims are hidden.

### Sign with an X.509 certificate

Sign with X.509 when your verifiers expect certificates, as HAIP and the EUDI Wallet do. Otherwise a DID is simpler. Put the certificate chain in `x5c`, leaf certificate first. Credo signs with the leaf certificate's key, so that key must be in the agent's KMS. A certificate you create with `agent.x509.createCertificate` from a KMS key is ready to use. For certificate chains and trust anchors, see [X.509 certificates](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/x509.md).

:::issuer

```ts
const issuerKey = await issuer.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })
const issuerCertificate = await issuer.x509.createCertificate({
  authorityKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(issuerKey.publicJwk),
  issuer: { commonName: 'Example Issuer', countryName: 'NL' },
  extensions: { subjectAlternativeName: { name: [{ type: 'dns', value: 'issuer.example.com' }] } },
})

const x509Credential = await issuer.sdJwtVc.sign({
  payload: { vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity', given_name: 'Jane' },
  // `issuer` is optional. When set, it must match a SAN of the leaf certificate.
  issuer: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate], issuer: 'https://issuer.example.com' },
  holder: { method: 'jwk', jwk: holderJwk },
  disclosureFrame: { _sd: ['given_name'] },
})
```

:::

## Store and query

The holder verifies a received credential, then stores it as an `SdJwtVcRecord`:

:::holder

```ts
const verification = await holder.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: credential.compact })
if (verification.isValid === false) throw verification.error

const record = await holder.sdJwtVc.store({
  record: new SdJwtVcRecord({
    // The KMS key id lets Credo sign the key binding JWT when presenting
    credentialInstances: [{ compactSdJwtVc: credential.compact, kmsKeyId: holderKey.keyId }],
  }),
})

const [identityRecord] = await holder.sdJwtVc.findAllByQuery({ vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity' })
console.log(identityRecord.firstCredential.prettyClaims)
```

:::

`kmsKeyId` is the KMS key the credential is bound to. Credo signs the key binding JWT with it when presenting. A DID-bound credential doesn't need it, because Credo finds the key through the DID. `credentialInstances` can hold several copies of the same credential, each bound to its own key, as issued with batch issuance.

Records are tagged with `vct`, `alg` and `sdAlg` for queries. `agent.sdJwtVc` also has `getById`, `getAll`, `update` and `deleteById`, and `fromCompact` decodes a credential without verifying it. With [OpenID4VCI](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/sd-jwt-vc.md), the holder flow returns the `SdJwtVcRecord` with `kmsKeyId` set, and you only store it.

## Present

The holder chooses which claims to disclose with a presentation frame, and adds a key binding JWT for the verifier:

:::holder

```ts
// Received from the verifier
const audience = 'https://verifier.example.com'
const nonce = 'f8b4a1d2-7c1e-4b0a-9d3e-2a6c5e8f1b90'

const presentation = await holder.sdJwtVc.present({
  // firstCredential carries the kmsKeyId of the record
  sdJwtVc: record.firstCredential,
  presentationFrame: { given_name: true, address: { locality: true } },
  verifierMetadata: { audience, nonce, issuedAt: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) },
})
```

:::

- `presentationFrame` sets `true` for each selectively disclosable claim to disclose, nested like the payload. Claims that aren't selectively disclosable are always included.
- `verifierMetadata` creates the key binding JWT with the verifier's `audience` and `nonce`, and `additionalPayload` adds claims to it. Key binding fails for a credential without `cnf`. Leave `verifierMetadata` out to present without key binding.

Pass `record.firstCredential` rather than the compact string, so Credo knows which key to sign with. For records with several instances, `useInstanceFromCredentialRecord` from `@credo-ts/core` picks an unused one.

## Verify

:::verifier

```ts
const result = await verifier.sdJwtVc.verify({
  compactSdJwtVc: presentation,
  keyBinding: { audience, nonce },
  requiredClaimKeys: ['given_name', 'address.locality'],
  fetchTypeMetadata: true,
  trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'did', issuance: issuerDid }],
})

if (result.isValid === false) throw result.error
// { vct, iss, cnf, iat, given_name, address: { locality, country }, nationalities: [] }
console.log(result.sdJwtVc.prettyClaims)
console.log(result.sdJwtVc.typeMetadata?.name)
```

:::

`verify` returns `{ isValid: true, sdJwtVc }` or `{ isValid: false, error }`, and `sdJwtVc.prettyClaims` holds the disclosed claims. Verification checks the issuer signature, the digests of the disclosures, `iat`, `nbf` and `exp` (with the agent's `validitySkewSeconds`), the `typ` header and the status. Options:

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `keyBinding` | Requires a key binding JWT signed by the `cnf` key, with this `audience` and `nonce`. |
| `requiredClaimKeys` | Claims that must be disclosed, as dot paths such as `address.locality`. |
| `trustedIssuers` | The issuers to accept for this call. |
| `fetchTypeMetadata` | Resolves the type metadata of the `vct` into `sdJwtVc.typeMetadata`. A failed fetch doesn't fail verification. |
| `disableStatusValidation` | Skips the status check. |
| `now` | The time to verify against. |

Trust depends on how the credential is signed:

- DID: any issuer DID is accepted unless `trustedIssuers` or the agent's `getTrustedIssuersForVerification` callback returns a list. With a list, the issuer DID must be on it.
- X.509: verification fails unless a trust anchor is configured, per call or on the agent.

:::verifier

```ts
const x509Result = await verifier.sdJwtVc.verify({
  compactSdJwtVc: x509Credential.compact,
  trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: [issuerCertificate.toString('pem')] }],
})
if (x509Result.isValid === false) throw x509Result.error
```

:::

To configure trust once for all verifications, see [Trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md).

If the credential has a `status` claim, `verify` fetches the status list and fails when the credential is revoked or suspended. See [Status lists](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/status-lists.md).

### Errors

`error` is the error of the first check that failed. Read its message to see why:

```ts
const expired = await issuer.sdJwtVc.sign({
  payload: { vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity', exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) - 3600 },
  issuer: { method: 'did', didUrl: issuerDidUrl },
})

const expiredResult = await verifier.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: expired.compact })
if (expiredResult.isValid === false) {
  console.log(expiredResult.error.message)
}
```

## Type metadata and module options

SD-JWT VC type metadata describes a `vct`: display names, claim labels and rendering. By default Credo only resolves `vct` values that are HTTPS URLs, by fetching them. To serve type metadata yourself, or resolve other `vct` values, register `SdJwtVcModule` with a `customTypeMetadataResolver`:

```ts
const identityTypeMetadata = {
  vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity',
  name: 'Identity credential',
  display: [{ locale: 'en-US', name: 'Identity credential' }],
  claims: [{ path: ['given_name'], display: [{ locale: 'en-US', label: 'Given name' }] }],
}

const sdJwtVcModule = new SdJwtVcModule({
  // Called for the `vct` of a credential and for every `extends` value in its type metadata
  customTypeMetadataResolver: async (vct, _integrity, { defaultResolver }) => {
    if (vct === identityTypeMetadata.vct) return identityTypeMetadata
    return defaultResolver({})
  },
})
```

`customTypeMetadataResolver` is called for the `vct`, and for each `extends` value in the type metadata. Return the type metadata document, `undefined` for none, or call `defaultResolver` for the HTTPS fetch. If the credential has a `vct#integrity` claim, your resolver has to check it; `IntegrityVerifier` from `@credo-ts/core` does that. The default resolver checks integrity itself.

Pass the module under the `sdJwtVc` key, which replaces the default module. `agent.sdJwtVc.fetchTypeMetadata(sdJwtVc)` resolves type metadata outside of verification.

- [SD-JWT VC with OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/sd-jwt-vc.md)
- [Status lists](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/status-lists.md)
- [Trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md)

# mdoc

> Sign, store, present and verify ISO 18013-5 mdocs, such as the mobile driving licence, with agent.mdoc.

An mdoc is the credential format of [ISO/IEC 18013-5](https://www.iso.org/standard/69084.html), used for the mobile driving licence (mDL) and the EU PID. The issuer signs a salted digest of each data element with an X.509 certificate, and binds the mdoc to a device key of the holder. To present, the holder signs a device response that contains only the requested elements. This page covers `agent.mdoc` and `MdocDeviceResponse`.
