To issue and present mdocs over OpenID4VC, see [mdoc with OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/mdoc.md). To present them in person or in the browser with the ISO protocols, see [Proximity (ISO 18013-5)](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/mdoc/proximity.md) and [Digital Credentials API (ISO 18013-7)](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/dc-api.md).

## Set up

Everything on this page is in `@credo-ts/core`. `MdocModule` is a default module without options, so every agent has `agent.mdoc`. The agent also needs [storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage.md) and key management. The examples use three agents: an issuer, a holder and a verifier.

```ts
import {
  Agent,
  DateOnly,
  Mdoc,
  MdocDeviceResponse,
  MdocRecord,
  X509ExtendedKeyUsage,
  X509KeyUsage,
} from '@credo-ts/core'
import { PublicJwk } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'

function createAgent(storage: ExampleStorage) {
  return new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    },
  })
}
```

## Create an issuer certificate

mdocs are always signed with an X.509 certificate, never with a DID. This example creates a self-signed document signer certificate from a key in the issuer's KMS:

:::issuer

```ts
const issuerKey = await issuer.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })

// A self-signed document signer certificate. Production issuers use a certificate issued by their IACA.
const issuerCertificate = await issuer.x509.createCertificate({
  authorityKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(issuerKey.publicJwk),
  // Verification fails when the subject has no country (C)
  issuer: { commonName: 'Example mDL Issuer', countryName: 'NL' },
  validity: { notBefore: new Date(), notAfter: new Date(Date.now() + 365 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) },
  extensions: {
    keyUsage: { usages: [X509KeyUsage.DigitalSignature] },
    extendedKeyUsage: { usages: [X509ExtendedKeyUsage.MdlDs] },
  },
})
```

:::

The certificate subject must include a country (`C`). Verification fails without it, and also when the mdoc has an `issuing_country` element that doesn't match. In production, the document signer certificate is issued by your IACA root certificate, and verifiers trust the root. See [X.509 certificates](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/x509.md).

## Sign an mdoc

:::issuer

```ts
// The device key of the wallet. In a real flow the wallet sends the public key, for example in an OpenID4VCI proof.
const deviceKey = await holder.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })

const mdoc = await issuer.mdoc.sign({
  docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL',
  namespaces: {
    'org.iso.18013.5.1': {
      family_name: 'Doe',
      given_name: 'Jane',
      birth_date: new DateOnly('1990-01-01'),
      issuing_country: 'NL',
      age_over_18: true,
    },
  },
  // `signed` and `validFrom` default to the time of signing
  validityInfo: { validUntil: new Date(Date.now() + 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) },
  issuerCertificate,
  holderKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(deviceKey.publicJwk),
})

// base64url encoded IssuerSigned structure, as returned over OpenID4VCI
const issued = mdoc.base64Url
```

:::

- `docType` is the document type, such as `org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL`, and `namespaces` maps each namespace to its data elements. Use `DateOnly` from `@credo-ts/core` for elements that are a date without a time, such as `birth_date`.
- `validityInfo.validUntil` is required. `signed` and `validFrom` default to the time of signing. If you set `validFrom`, also set `signed` to a time no later than it, because signing fails when `validFrom` is before `signed`.
- `issuerCertificate` is the signing certificate, or a chain with the signing certificate first. Its key must be in the issuer's KMS. `holderKey` is the public device key the mdoc is bound to.

`keyAuthorizations` lists the namespaces or elements the holder may sign itself (device-signed elements). By default there are none. `statusInfo` points to a status list entry, see [Status lists](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/status-lists.md).

The signature algorithm follows from the certificate key: ES256, ES384, ES512 or EdDSA. Use P-256 keys (ES256) for the certificate and the device key unless your ecosystem asks for something else: HAIP requires every party to support ES256, and the secure hardware of phones supports P-256. Element digests always use SHA-256.

## Store and query

The holder parses the received mdoc, verifies it, and stores it as an `MdocRecord`:

:::holder

```ts
const receivedMdoc = Mdoc.fromBase64Url(issued)
// The KMS key id is not part of the mdoc. Set it so Credo can sign device responses.
receivedMdoc.deviceKeyId = deviceKey.keyId

const verification = await holder.mdoc.verify(receivedMdoc, {
  trustedCertificates: [issuerCertificate.toString('pem')],
})
if (verification.isValid === false) throw new Error(verification.error)

const record = await holder.mdoc.store({ record: MdocRecord.fromMdoc(receivedMdoc) })

const [mdl] = await holder.mdoc.findAllByQuery({ docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL' })
console.log(mdl.firstCredential.issuerSignedNamespaces)
```

:::

- `deviceKeyId` is the KMS key id of the device key. It isn't part of the mdoc, so set it before you store the mdoc. `MdocRecord.fromMdoc` copies it to the record.
- `verify` returns `{ isValid: true }` or `{ isValid: false, error }`, with `error` as a message. Without `trustedCertificates` it uses the agent's [trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md) configuration, and throws when no trusted certificates are configured at all.
- Records are tagged with `docType` and `alg`. `agent.mdoc` also has `getById`, `getAll`, `update` and `deleteById`. A record can hold several instances of the same mdoc, each bound to its own key, for batch issuance.

With [OpenID4VCI](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/mdoc.md), the holder flow verifies the mdoc and returns the `MdocRecord` for you. You only store it.

## Present

A presentation is a device response: the mdoc with only the requested elements, signed with the device key. Over OpenID4VP, Credo builds it for you. To build one yourself, use `MdocDeviceResponse.createDeviceResponse`:

:::holder

```ts
// Values the verifier sends in its OpenID4VP request
const sessionTranscriptOptions = {
  type: 'openId4Vp',
  clientId: 'x509_san_dns:verifier.example.com',
  responseUri: 'https://verifier.example.com/response',
  verifierGeneratedNonce: 'b5c2f9e1-3a7d-4c8b-9e0f-1d2a3b4c5d6e',
} as const

const deviceResponse = await MdocDeviceResponse.createDeviceResponse(holder.context, {
  mdocs: [record.firstCredential],
  documentRequests: [
    {
      docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL',
      // Element identifier mapped to intent to retain
      nameSpaces: { 'org.iso.18013.5.1': { family_name: false, age_over_18: false } },
    },
  ],
  sessionTranscriptOptions,
})

const encodedDeviceResponse = deviceResponse.encoded
```

:::

- `documentRequests` lists the elements to disclose per namespace. Every element of an mdoc is selectively disclosable, so the response contains these elements and nothing else. The boolean is the verifier's intent to retain the element.
- `sessionTranscriptOptions` binds the response to one exchange. The `openId4Vp` and `openId4VpDcApi` types take the values from an OpenID4VP request. For other transports, such as [ISO 18013-5 proximity](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/mdoc/proximity.md), compute the session transcript yourself and pass `{ type: 'sessionTranscriptBytes', sessionTranscriptBytes }`.
- `deviceNameSpaces` adds device-signed elements. They're only included when requested and authorized by `keyAuthorizations`.

Only device signatures are supported. Device MAC authentication fails.

## Verify a device response

:::verifier

```ts
const receivedResponse = MdocDeviceResponse.fromBase64Url(encodedDeviceResponse)

// Throws when the response is invalid. Pass the trusted certificates explicitly:
// this method does not use the agent trust configuration.
await receivedResponse.verify(verifier.context, {
  trustedCertificates: [issuerCertificate.toString('pem')],
  sessionTranscriptOptions,
})

// { 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL': { 'org.iso.18013.5.1': { family_name: 'Doe', age_over_18: true } } }
console.log(receivedResponse.issuerClaims)
```

:::

`verify` resolves when the response is valid and throws an `MdocError` when it isn't. It checks the issuer signature and certificate chain, the element digests, the device signature over the session transcript, the validity period (with the agent's `validitySkewSeconds`) and the status. `issuerClaims` and `deviceClaims` hold the disclosed elements per document type and namespace.

:::warning[Pass the trusted certificates]
`MdocDeviceResponse.verify` doesn't use the agent's trusted issuers configuration or the trusted certificates of the X.509 module. Without `trustedCertificates`, every response fails verification. The OpenID4VP verifier and the DC API flow resolve trust for you.
:::

`trustedCertificates` takes certificates as PEM or base64 strings. To trust a separate certificate for signing status lists, pass `[{ issuance: [...], status: [...] }]` instead.

## Next steps

- [mdoc with OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/mdoc.md)
- [Proximity (ISO 18013-5)](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/mdoc/proximity.md)
- [Digital Credentials API (ISO 18013-7)](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/dc-api.md)
- [Status lists](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/status-lists.md)
- [X.509 certificates](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/x509.md)

# W3C Verifiable Credentials

> Sign, store, present and verify W3C Verifiable Credentials (data model 1.1 and 2.0) as JWT, SD-JWT, JSON-LD or Data Integrity.

The [W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model](https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/) defines a JSON structure for credentials and presentations. It doesn't fix how they're signed: the same credential can be secured as a JWT, an SD-JWT, or with an embedded proof. Credo supports data model 1.1 on `agent.w3cCredentials` and data model 2.0 on `agent.w3cV2Credentials`. This page covers signing, storing, presenting and verifying with both. For exchange, see [W3C VCs with OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/w3c.md) and [W3C VCs with DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/w3c.md).

## Data models and securing mechanisms

| Data model | Secured as | Claim format | Selective disclosure | Holder binding | Exchange |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.1 | JWT | `jwt_vc` (`jwt_vc_json` in OpenID4VC) | No | DID in `credentialSubject.id` | OpenID4VC, DIDComm presentation only |
| 1.1 | JSON-LD with an Ed25519 Linked Data proof | `ldp_vc` | No | DID in `credentialSubject.id` | DIDComm (OpenID4VC has known problems) |
| 2.0 | JWT | `vc+jwt` | No | `cnf` claim | None, sign and verify only |
| 2.0 | SD-JWT | `vc+sd-jwt` | Yes | `cnf` claim | OpenID4VC, DIDComm issuance |
| 2.0 | Data Integrity (`eddsa-jcs-2022`) | `di_vc` | No | DID in `credentialSubject.id` | DIDComm issuance |

The issuer always signs with a key of a DID it created (or imported with its keys). X.509 issuers aren't supported. W3C 2.0 `vc+sd-jwt` is a different format from [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/sd-jwt-vc.md) (`dc+sd-jwt`), even though both use SD-JWT. For the protocol details, see [W3C VCs with OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/w3c.md) and [W3C VCs with DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/w3c.md).

### Choose a variant

Use the variant your ecosystem or verifiers ask for. Without such a requirement:

- Over OpenID4VC, use data model 1.1 as JWT (`jwt_vc_json`). Use 2.0 as SD-JWT (`vc+sd-jwt`) when you need selective disclosure.
- Over DIDComm, use 1.1 as JSON-LD (`ldp_vc`), the only 1.1 variant that DIDComm can issue, or 2.0 as SD-JWT for selective disclosure.
- Avoid 2.0 as plain JWT and with Data Integrity. Credo can't exchange `vc+jwt` over any protocol, can't present `di_vc` over any protocol, and doesn't check the issuer trust and validity period of `di_vc` credentials.

If you don't need W3C VCs, [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/sd-jwt-vc.md) is simpler and has selective disclosure.

## Set up

Everything on this page is in `@credo-ts/core`, and both modules are default modules. The agent also needs [storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage.md) and key management. The examples use an issuer, a holder and a verifier, each with an Ed25519 `did:key`:

```ts
import {
  Agent,
  ClaimFormat,
  DidKey,
  defaultDocumentLoader,
  JsonTransformer,
  type KeyDidCreateOptions,
  purposes,
  utils,
  W3cCredential,
  W3cCredentialRecord,
  W3cCredentialsModule,
  W3cJsonLdVerifiablePresentation,
  w3cDate,
} from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'

const membershipContext = {
  '@context': {
    MembershipCredential: 'https://example.com/vocab#MembershipCredential',
    name: 'https://schema.org/name',
    memberSince: { '@id': 'https://example.com/vocab#memberSince', '@type': 'http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#date' },
  },
}

function createAgent(storage: ExampleStorage) {
  return new Agent({
    dependencies: agentDependencies,
    modules: {
      ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
      // Serve your own JSON-LD contexts instead of fetching them from the network
      w3cCredentials: new W3cCredentialsModule({
        documentLoader: (agentContext) =>
          defaultDocumentLoader(agentContext, { 'https://example.com/contexts/membership/v1': membershipContext }),
      }),
    },
  })
}

async function createDidKey(agent: Agent) {
  const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({
    method: 'key',
    options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } },
  })
  if (didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the DID failed')
  return { did: didState.did, didUrl: `${didState.did}#${DidKey.fromDid(didState.did).publicJwk.fingerprint}` }
}
```

### JSON-LD contexts

Every property of a JSON-LD credential must be defined in one of its `@context`s, and signing and verifying load those contexts through a document loader. The default loader has copies of the common contexts (credentials v1 and v2, the security suites, DIDs, ODRL, schema.org, Open Badges 3.0), resolves DIDs, and fetches every other URL from the network. Pass your own contexts to `defaultDocumentLoader` as shown above, or set your own `documentLoader` to control what is fetched. Register `W3cCredentialsModule` under the `w3cCredentials` key to replace the default module. Data model 2.0 uses the same document loader.

## Data model 1.1

### Sign a credential

```ts
const issuerDid = await createDidKey(issuer)
const holderDid = await createDidKey(holder)

const credential = W3cCredential.fromJson({
  '@context': ['https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1', 'https://example.com/contexts/membership/v1'],
  type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'MembershipCredential'],
  issuer: issuerDid.did,
  issuanceDate: w3cDate(Date.now()),
  // The subject id binds the credential to the holder DID
  credentialSubject: { id: holderDid.did, name: 'Jane Doe', memberSince: '2024-01-01' },
})

const jwtVc = await issuer.w3cCredentials.signCredential<ClaimFormat.JwtVc>({
  format: ClaimFormat.JwtVc,
  credential,
  alg: 'EdDSA',
  verificationMethod: issuerDid.didUrl,
})
console.log(jwtVc.serializedJwt)

const ldpVc = await issuer.w3cCredentials.signCredential<ClaimFormat.LdpVc>({
  format: ClaimFormat.LdpVc,
  credential,
  // did:key Ed25519 keys are Ed25519VerificationKey2018 verification methods
  proofType: 'Ed25519Signature2018',
  verificationMethod: issuerDid.didUrl,
})
console.log(ldpVc.toJson())
```

- `verificationMethod` is the DID URL of an `assertionMethod` key of the issuer DID.
- For `jwt_vc`, `alg` must fit the key. A JWT VC can have only one `credentialSubject`.
- For `ldp_vc`, `proofType` is `Ed25519Signature2018` for `Ed25519VerificationKey2018` verification methods (such as `did:key`) or `Ed25519Signature2020` for `Ed25519VerificationKey2020`. These are the only Linked Data suites. There is no BBS+ suite, so 1.1 credentials have no selective disclosure.

:::caution
Build JSON-LD credentials with `W3cCredential.fromJson`, as above. A `new W3cCredential({ ... })` without `expirationDate` fails to sign as `ldp_vc` with `"expirationDate" must be a valid date: undefined`.
:::

### Store and query

:::holder

```ts
const jwtResult = await holder.w3cCredentials.verifyCredential({ credential: jwtVc.serializedJwt })
const ldpResult = await holder.w3cCredentials.verifyCredential({ credential: ldpVc })
if (!jwtResult.isValid || !ldpResult.isValid) throw new Error('Received an invalid credential')

await holder.w3cCredentials.store({ record: W3cCredentialRecord.fromCredential(jwtVc) })
await holder.w3cCredentials.store({ record: W3cCredentialRecord.fromCredential(ldpVc) })

// Returns credentials, not records
const memberships = await holder.w3cCredentials.findAllByQuery({
  types: ['MembershipCredential'],
  claimFormat: ClaimFormat.LdpVc,
})
console.log(memberships.length)
```

:::

`findAllByQuery` returns the credentials, not the records. Records are tagged with `claimFormat`, `types`, `issuerId`, `subjectIds`, `schemaIds` and `contexts`. `getById` and `getAll` return records, and `deleteById` removes one. There is no `update`. Store JSON-LD credentials with `agent.w3cCredentials.store`: it adds the expanded types that OpenID4VP queries on.

### Present

The holder wraps credentials in a presentation and signs it with an `authentication` key of its DID, the DID in `credentialSubject.id`:

:::holder

```ts
// Received from the verifier
const challenge = 'c0ffee12-3456-4789-abcd-ef0123456789'
const domain = 'https://verifier.example.com'

const jwtPresentation = await holder.w3cCredentials.createPresentation({
  credentials: [jwtVc],
  holder: holderDid.did,
})
const jwtVp = await holder.w3cCredentials.signPresentation<ClaimFormat.JwtVp>({
  format: ClaimFormat.JwtVp,
  presentation: jwtPresentation,
  alg: 'EdDSA',
  verificationMethod: holderDid.didUrl,
  challenge,
  domain,
})

const ldpPresentation = await holder.w3cCredentials.createPresentation({
  // Signing a JSON-LD presentation without an id fails
  id: `urn:uuid:${utils.uuid()}`,
  credentials: [ldpVc],
  holder: holderDid.did,
})
const ldpVp = await holder.w3cCredentials.signPresentation<ClaimFormat.LdpVp>({
  format: ClaimFormat.LdpVp,
  presentation: ldpPresentation,
  proofType: 'Ed25519Signature2018',
  proofPurpose: new purposes.AuthenticationProofPurpose({ challenge, domain }),
  verificationMethod: holderDid.didUrl,
  challenge,
  domain,
})
```

:::

- `challenge` and `domain` come from the verifier. In a JWT VP they're the `nonce` and `aud` claims.
- A JWT VP can only contain JWT VCs, and a JSON-LD VP only JSON-LD VCs.
- A JSON-LD presentation needs a `proofPurpose`, and an `id`: signing fails without one.

### Verify

:::verifier

```ts
const jwtVpResult = await verifier.w3cCredentials.verifyPresentation({
  presentation: jwtVp.serializedJwt,
  challenge,
  domain,
  trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'did', issuance: issuerDid.did }],
})

// A JSON-LD presentation must be passed as an instance, not as JSON
const ldpVpResult = await verifier.w3cCredentials.verifyPresentation({
  presentation: JsonTransformer.fromJSON(ldpVp.toJson(), W3cJsonLdVerifiablePresentation),
  challenge,
  domain,
  trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'did', issuance: issuerDid.did }],
})

if (!jwtVpResult.isValid) console.error(jwtVpResult.error, jwtVpResult.validations)
console.log(jwtVpResult.isValid, ldpVpResult.isValid)
```

:::

`verifyCredential` and `verifyPresentation` return `{ isValid, validations, error }`, where `validations` shows which check failed. For a presentation, Credo checks the holder signature, `challenge` and `domain`, every credential in it, and that the holder is the subject of each credential. A JSON-LD credential or presentation must be passed as an instance, such as from `JsonTransformer.fromJSON`. The date checks of JSON-LD credentials don't use the agent's `validitySkewSeconds`.

Without `trustedIssuers` and without a [trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md) callback on the agent, any issuer DID is accepted.

## Data model 2.0

The 2.0 examples use the same agents and DIDs, and these imports:

```ts
import {
  Agent,
  ClaimFormat,
  DidKey,
  type KeyDidCreateOptions,
  W3cV2Credential,
  W3cV2CredentialRecord,
  W3cV2EnvelopedVerifiableCredential,
  W3cV2Presentation,
  W3cV2SdJwtCredentialService,
  w3cDate,
} from '@credo-ts/core'
```

### Sign a credential

:::issuer

```ts
const credential = new W3cV2Credential({
  type: ['VerifiableCredential', 'MembershipCredential'],
  issuer: issuerDid.did,
  validFrom: w3cDate(Date.now()),
  credentialSubject: { id: holderDid.did, name: 'Jane Doe', memberSince: '2024-01-01' },
})

// vc+jwt
const jwtVc = await issuer.w3cV2Credentials.signCredential<ClaimFormat.JwtW3cVc>({
  format: ClaimFormat.JwtW3cVc,
  credential,
  alg: 'EdDSA',
  verificationMethod: issuerDid.didUrl,
})

// vc+sd-jwt: `cnf` binds the credential to the holder key
const sdJwtVc = await issuer.w3cV2Credentials.signCredential<ClaimFormat.SdJwtW3cVc>({
  format: ClaimFormat.SdJwtW3cVc,
  credential,
  alg: 'EdDSA',
  verificationMethod: issuerDid.didUrl,
  holder: { method: 'did', didUrl: holderDid.didUrl },
  disclosureFrame: { credentialSubject: { _sd: ['name', 'memberSince'] } },
})

// di_vc with a Data Integrity proof
const diVc = await issuer.w3cV2Credentials.signCredential<ClaimFormat.DiVc>({
  format: ClaimFormat.DiVc,
  credential,
  cryptosuite: 'eddsa-jcs-2022',
  verificationMethod: issuerDid.didUrl,
})

// `encoded` is a compact string for vc+jwt and vc+sd-jwt, and JSON for di_vc
console.log(sdJwtVc.encoded, diVc.encoded)
```

:::

- `verificationMethod` is the DID URL of an `assertionMethod` key of the issuer DID, and `alg` must fit the key.
- `holder` adds a `cnf` claim with a DID URL or a JWK, for `vc+jwt` and `vc+sd-jwt`. Choose as for [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/sd-jwt-vc.md#choose-the-holder-binding). A `di_vc` credential is bound through `credentialSubject.id`.
- `disclosureFrame` works as for [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/sd-jwt-vc.md). `@context`, `type`, `credentialStatus`, `credentialSchema` and `relatedResource` can't be selectively disclosable at the top level.
- `cryptosuite` for `di_vc` is `eddsa-jcs-2022`, the only cryptosuite, which needs an Ed25519 key.

### Store and query

:::holder

```ts
const sdJwtResult = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.verifyCredential({ credential: sdJwtVc.encoded })
const diResult = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.verifyCredential({ credential: diVc })
if (!sdJwtResult.isValid || !diResult.isValid) throw new Error('Received an invalid credential')

const record = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.store({ record: W3cV2CredentialRecord.fromCredential(sdJwtVc) })

// Returns credentials, not records
const memberships = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.findAllByQuery({
  claimFormat: ClaimFormat.SdJwtW3cVc,
  types: ['MembershipCredential'],
})
console.log(memberships.length)
```

:::

As in 1.1, `findAllByQuery` returns credentials and there is no `update`. A record can hold several instances of the same credential for batch issuance.

### Present

There is no key binding JWT for 2.0. The holder proves possession by signing a presentation that contains the credential:

:::holder

```ts
// Received from the verifier
const challenge = '9d0e4c6a-2b1f-4e8d-a7c3-5f6b8e9d0a1c'
const domain = 'https://verifier.example.com'

// Selective disclosure is only available on the service
const sdJwtService = holder.dependencyManager.resolve(W3cV2SdJwtCredentialService)
const disclosed = await sdJwtService.present(holder.context, {
  credential: record.encoded,
  presentationFrame: { credentialSubject: { name: true } },
})

const sdJwtVp = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.signPresentation<ClaimFormat.SdJwtW3cVp>({
  format: ClaimFormat.SdJwtW3cVp,
  presentation: new W3cV2Presentation({
    holder: holderDid.did,
    verifiableCredential: [W3cV2EnvelopedVerifiableCredential.fromVerifiableCredential(disclosed)],
  }),
  challenge,
  domain,
})

const diVp = await holder.w3cV2Credentials.signPresentation<ClaimFormat.DiVp>({
  format: ClaimFormat.DiVp,
  presentation: new W3cV2Presentation({ holder: holderDid.did, verifiableCredential: [diVc] }),
  cryptosuite: 'eddsa-jcs-2022',
  verificationMethod: holderDid.didUrl,
  challenge,
  domain,
})
```

:::

- Selective disclosure for `vc+sd-jwt` is only on `W3cV2SdJwtCredentialService`. Wrap the result with `W3cV2EnvelopedVerifiableCredential` to put it in a presentation.
- For `vp+jwt` and `vp+sd-jwt`, Credo signs with the `authentication` key of the `holder` DID. The DID must be created in this agent, with exactly one `authentication` key in its KMS. Without `holder`, Credo signs with the key in the credentials' `cnf`.
- For `di_vp`, pass the `verificationMethod` and `cryptosuite`.

### Verify

:::verifier

```ts
const sdJwtVpResult = await verifier.w3cV2Credentials.verifyPresentation({
  presentation: sdJwtVp.encoded,
  challenge,
  domain,
})
const diVpResult = await verifier.w3cV2Credentials.verifyPresentation({ presentation: diVp, challenge, domain })

if (!sdJwtVpResult.isValid) console.error(sdJwtVpResult.presentation.validations, sdJwtVpResult.credentialEntries)
console.log(sdJwtVpResult.isValid, diVpResult.isValid)
```

:::

The result has `presentation.validations` for the presentation itself and `credentialEntries` with a result per credential. `verifyCredential` verifies a single credential, and takes `trustedIssuers`:

:::verifier

```ts
const jwtVcResult = await verifier.w3cV2Credentials.verifyCredential({
  credential: jwtVc.encoded,
  trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'did', issuance: issuerDid.did }],
})
console.log(jwtVcResult.isValid)
```

:::

:::warning[Trust in 2.0]
- `trustedIssuers` on `verifyPresentation` isn't applied to the credentials in the presentation. Configure a [trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md) callback on the agent instead.
- For `di_vc` credentials, Credo checks neither trusted issuers nor `validFrom` and `validUntil`. Check them yourself.
:::

## Status and revocation

Credo doesn't verify `credentialStatus` for W3C credentials. There is no support for Bitstring Status List or Status List 2021.

- Data model 1.1: verifying a credential with a `credentialStatus`, or a presentation that contains one, fails by default. Pass `verifyCredentialStatus: false` and check the status yourself.
- Data model 2.0: `credentialStatus` is ignored, unless you pass `verifyCredentialStatus: true`, which makes verification fail.

For revocation with SD-JWT VC and mdoc, see [Status lists](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/status-lists.md).

## Next steps

- [W3C VCs with OpenID4VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/w3c.md)
- [W3C VCs with DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/w3c.md)
- [Trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md)

# AnonCreds

> Set up AnonCreds in Credo with a registry, register schemas, credential definitions and revocation registries, and manage link secrets and stored credentials.

[AnonCreds](https://hyperledger.github.io/anoncreds-spec/) credentials are signed with CL signatures, which let a holder present zero-knowledge proofs: reveal only some attributes and prove a predicate such as "age is at least 18" without the value. Verifiers can't link presentations through the signature. Holders bind credentials to a link secret instead of a key. Issuers publish schemas, credential definitions and revocation data on an AnonCreds registry, usually a ledger. This page covers setup and the issuer and holder APIs. Credo exchanges AnonCreds credentials only over DIDComm: see [AnonCreds with DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/anoncreds.md).

## Install

**Node.js**

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/anoncreds@^0.7.2 @hyperledger/anoncreds-nodejs@^0.4.1
```

**React Native**

```bash
npm install @credo-ts/anoncreds@^0.7.2 @hyperledger/anoncreds-react-native@^0.4.1
```

Also install the package of your registry (see below).

## Configure

Register the `AnonCredsModule` with the native AnonCreds library and at least one registry.

**Node.js**

```ts
import { AnonCredsModule } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds'
import { CheqdDidRegistrar, CheqdDidResolver, CheqdModule } from '@credo-ts/cheqd'
import { CheqdAnonCredsRegistry } from '@credo-ts/cheqd/anoncreds'
import { Agent, DidsModule } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAnoncreds } from '@hyperledger/anoncreds-nodejs'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    cheqd: new CheqdModule({
      networks: [{ network: 'testnet', cosmosPayerSeed: '<cosmos payer seed or mnemonic>' }],
    }),
    dids: new DidsModule({
      registrars: [new CheqdDidRegistrar()],
      resolvers: [new CheqdDidResolver()],
    }),
    anoncreds: new AnonCredsModule({
      anoncreds: NativeAnoncreds,
      registries: [new CheqdAnonCredsRegistry()],
    }),
  },
})

await agent.initialize()
```

**React Native**

```ts
import { AnonCredsModule } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds'
import { AskarModule } from '@credo-ts/askar'
import { CheqdDidResolver, CheqdModule } from '@credo-ts/cheqd'
import { CheqdAnonCredsRegistry } from '@credo-ts/cheqd/anoncreds'
import { Agent, DidsModule } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/react-native'
import { NativeAnoncreds } from '@hyperledger/anoncreds-react-native'
import { NativeAskar } from '@openwallet-foundation/askar-react-native'

const agent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    // Derive the store key from secure storage or user input, see the Askar page
    askar: new AskarModule({ askar: NativeAskar, store: { id: 'wallet', key: '<store key>' } }),
    // A holder only resolves objects, so it needs no payer seed
    cheqd: new CheqdModule({ networks: [{ network: 'testnet' }] }),
    dids: new DidsModule({ resolvers: [new CheqdDidResolver()] }),
    anoncreds: new AnonCredsModule({
      anoncreds: NativeAnoncreds,
      registries: [new CheqdAnonCredsRegistry()],
    }),
  },
})

await agent.initialize()
```

Pass the `NativeAnoncreds` class (supported since Credo 0.7.2): Credo resolves the native binding when it needs it, so import order doesn't matter. The module's API is available as `agent.modules.anoncreds` under the key you register it with. With [Drizzle storage](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/storage/drizzle.md#bundles), also register `anoncredsBundle`, as AnonCreds stores its own records.

Each registry handles the identifiers of one DID method, and Credo uses the first registry that matches an identifier. A registry also needs the module of its network, which provides the DID resolver:

| Registry | Import from | Identifiers | Network setup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `IndyVdrAnonCredsRegistry` | `@credo-ts/indy-vdr` | `did:indy`, and unqualified Indy identifiers for resolving | [Indy VDR](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/indy-vdr.md) |
| `CheqdAnonCredsRegistry` | `@credo-ts/cheqd/anoncreds` | `did:cheqd` | [cheqd](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/cheqd.md) |
| `HederaAnonCredsRegistry` | `@credo-ts/hedera/anoncreds` | `did:hedera` | [Hedera](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/hedera.md) |
| `WebVhAnonCredsRegistry` | `@credo-ts/webvh/anoncreds` | `did:webvh` | [did:webvh](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/webvh.md) |

Import the cheqd and Hedera registries from their `/anoncreds` subpaths, available since Credo 0.7.2. The package roots still export them, but those exports are deprecated and removed in 0.8. To register objects on Indy, the issuer needs a `did:indy`.

## Register a schema

A schema lists the attribute names of a credential type. An issuer can also use a schema that someone else registered.

:::issuer

```ts
const { schemaState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.registerSchema({
  schema: {
    issuerId,
    name: 'Employee',
    version: '1.0',
    attrNames: ['name', 'role', 'age'],
  },
  // Registry specific, cheqd needs none
  options: {},
})

if (schemaState.state !== 'finished') {
  throw new Error(
    `Registering the schema failed: ${schemaState.state === 'failed' ? schemaState.reason : schemaState.state}`
  )
}
```

:::

- `issuerId` is a DID on the registry that the issuer created or imported in its agent.
- `options` depend on the registry. Indy VDR needs `endorserMode` and `endorserDid`, and you can type them with `registerSchema<IndyVdrRegisterSchemaOptions>`. cheqd needs none.
- The register methods don't throw when registration fails. Check `state`: `finished`, `failed` (with `reason`), `wait`, or `action` (for example when an external Indy endorser has to sign).

## Register a credential definition

A credential definition binds a schema to an issuer and holds the issuer's public keys. You issue against a credential definition.

:::issuer

```ts
const { credentialDefinitionState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.registerCredentialDefinition({
  credentialDefinition: {
    issuerId,
    schemaId: schemaState.schemaId,
    tag: 'default',
  },
  options: { supportRevocation: false },
})

if (credentialDefinitionState.state !== 'finished') {
  throw new Error(`Registering the credential definition failed: ${credentialDefinitionState.state}`)
}
const credentialDefinitionId = credentialDefinitionState.credentialDefinitionId
```

:::

Credo keeps the private keys in the issuer's storage. Without them you can no longer issue with this credential definition. Use `tag` to create several credential definitions for one schema. Set `supportRevocation: true` if you want to revoke credentials later: you can't add revocation afterwards.

## Revocation

Revocation is optional and adds work on both sides. The issuer hosts a tails file and writes to the registry for every status list update, and holders download the tails file to prove non-revocation. Enable it when a credential can stop being valid while the holder still has it, such as an employee or membership credential. Leave it off for credentials that stay true, such as a diploma.

A revocable credential definition needs a revocation registry and a status list. The revocation registry has a tails file that holders download to prove non-revocation, so the issuer must publish it. The default `BasicTailsFileService` only downloads tails files. Give issuers a tails file service that uploads:

```ts
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'
import { AnonCredsModule, type AnonCredsRevocationRegistryDefinition, BasicTailsFileService } from '@credo-ts/anoncreds'
import { CheqdDidRegistrar, CheqdDidResolver, CheqdModule } from '@credo-ts/cheqd'
import { CheqdAnonCredsRegistry } from '@credo-ts/cheqd/anoncreds'
import { Agent, type AgentContext, DidsModule } from '@credo-ts/core'
import { anoncredsBundle } from '@credo-ts/drizzle-storage/anoncreds'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { NativeAnoncreds } from '@hyperledger/anoncreds-nodejs'
import { exampleStorage } from './example-storage.js'

class TailsServerFileService extends BasicTailsFileService {
  public async uploadTailsFile(
    _agentContext: AgentContext,
    { revocationRegistryDefinition }: { revocationRegistryDefinition: AnonCredsRevocationRegistryDefinition }
  ) {
    // Before the upload, `tailsLocation` is the path of the tails file Credo generated
    const tailsFile = await readFile(revocationRegistryDefinition.value.tailsLocation)
    const tailsFileUrl = `https://tails.example.com/${revocationRegistryDefinition.value.tailsHash}`

    const response = await fetch(tailsFileUrl, { method: 'PUT', body: tailsFile })
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Uploading the tails file failed with status ${response.status}`)

    return { tailsFileUrl }
  }
}
```

```ts
anoncreds: new AnonCredsModule({
  anoncreds: NativeAnoncreds,
  registries: [new CheqdAnonCredsRegistry()],
  tailsFileService: new TailsServerFileService(),
}),
```

Then create the revocation registry and its first status list:

:::issuer

```ts
const { credentialDefinitionState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.registerCredentialDefinition({
  credentialDefinition: { issuerId, schemaId, tag: 'revocable' },
  options: { supportRevocation: true },
})
if (credentialDefinitionState.state !== 'finished') {
  throw new Error(`Registering the credential definition failed: ${credentialDefinitionState.state}`)
}

const { revocationRegistryDefinitionState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.registerRevocationRegistryDefinition({
  revocationRegistryDefinition: {
    issuerId,
    credentialDefinitionId: credentialDefinitionState.credentialDefinitionId,
    tag: 'default',
    maximumCredentialNumber: 1000,
  },
  options: {},
})
if (revocationRegistryDefinitionState.state !== 'finished') {
  throw new Error(`Registering the revocation registry failed: ${revocationRegistryDefinitionState.state}`)
}
const revocationRegistryDefinitionId = revocationRegistryDefinitionState.revocationRegistryDefinitionId

// The initial list, in which no credential is revoked
const { revocationStatusListState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.registerRevocationStatusList({
  revocationStatusList: { issuerId, revocationRegistryDefinitionId },
  options: {},
})
if (revocationStatusListState.state !== 'finished') {
  throw new Error(`Registering the revocation status list failed: ${revocationStatusListState.state}`)
}
```

:::

Credo marks the registry as active, and you can issue up to `maximumCredentialNumber` credentials with it. Each credential gets an index in the registry, which you choose when you issue and must track yourself. To revoke, publish a new status list with the revoked indexes:

:::issuer

```ts
// Revoke the credentials issued with revocationRegistryIndex 1 and 2
const { revocationStatusListState: updatedState } = await agent.modules.anoncreds.updateRevocationStatusList({
  revocationStatusList: { revocationRegistryDefinitionId, revokedCredentialIndexes: [1, 2] },
  options: {},
})
if (updatedState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error(`Revoking failed: ${updatedState.state}`)
```

:::

:::warning[Indy VDR in 0.7.2]
In Credo 0.7.2, issuing revocable credentials with the Indy VDR registry can fail, because the issuer can't resolve the status list of its own revocation registry.
:::

[AnonCreds with DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/anoncreds.md#revocation) shows how to issue revocable credentials, notify holders and request proof of non-revocation.

## Link secrets and stored credentials

A link secret is the holder's secret that all its AnonCreds credentials are bound to. By default (`autoCreateLinkSecret: true`) Credo creates one on the first credential request. The first link secret becomes the default. You can also create one yourself, and `getLinkSecretIds` lists them:

:::holder

```ts
// Optional: without a link secret, one is created on the first credential request
const linkSecretId = await agent.modules.anoncreds.createLinkSecret({ setAsDefault: true })

const credentials = await agent.modules.anoncreds.getCredentials({ credentialDefinitionId })
for (const credential of credentials) {
  console.log(credential.credentialId, credential.attributes, credential.linkSecretId === linkSecretId)
}
```

:::

The holder stores AnonCreds credentials as W3C VCDM 1.1 credentials (`W3cCredentialRecord`) with a `DataIntegrityProof` using the `anoncreds-2023` cryptosuite. `getCredentials` filters them by credential definition, schema or issuer and returns the attributes and identifiers, and `getCredential(id)` returns one. `agent.w3cCredentials` lists the same records, but its `verifyCredential` rejects AnonCreds proofs.

## Verifying

A verifier checks AnonCreds presentations during the [Present Proof](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/didcomm/present-proof.md) exchange. It resolves the schemas, credential definitions and status lists from the registries. Which issuers you accept is part of the proof request, through `restrictions`. The agent's [trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md) configuration doesn't apply to AnonCreds.

# Status lists

> Revoke and suspend SD-JWT VCs and mdocs with IETF Token Status Lists, using agent.tokenStatusList.

A [Token Status List](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-status-list/) is a signed, compressed list with one status entry per credential, which the issuer publishes at a URL. Each credential points to its entry with the URL and an index, and the verifier fetches the list to check the entry. Credo uses status lists for [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/sd-jwt-vc.md) (as a JWT) and [mdoc](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/mdoc.md) (as a CWT). This page covers creating and updating lists with `agent.tokenStatusList`, referencing them from credentials, and how verification checks them.

## When you need one

Use a status list when you must be able to revoke or suspend credentials before they expire. Credentials that are short-lived and reissued often don't need one: their expiry does the job, and you have no list to host. Use 1 bit per entry if you only revoke, and 2 bits if you also suspend.

Credo supports Token Status Lists for SD-JWT VC and mdoc only. It doesn't support the W3C Bitstring Status List, so W3C credentials have no revocation in Credo (see [W3C Verifiable Credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/w3c-vc.md#status-and-revocation)). AnonCreds uses its own revocation registries, published on the ledger, and the holder proves non-revocation in the presentation (see [AnonCreds](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/anoncreds.md#revocation)).

## What your app does

`agent.tokenStatusList` creates, updates and fetches status list tokens, and verification checks them. Everything around that is up to your app:

- Host each token at its URL, with content type `application/statuslist+jwt` or `application/statuslist+cwt`.
- Store the current token, and publish a new one after each change and before the current one expires.
- Allocate an index for each credential and remember which credential has which index. Pick unused indexes at random: indexes handed out in order reveal when a credential was issued.

The examples run an issuer, a holder and a verifier in one process, with a small HTTP server that stands in for your hosting:

```ts
// Your app hosts the status list tokens. This is a minimal stand-in for that endpoint.
const hostedStatusLists = new Map<string, { contentType: string; body: string | Uint8Array }>()
const server = createServer((request, response) => {
  const hosted = hostedStatusLists.get(request.url ?? '')
  if (!hosted) return response.writeHead(404).end()
  response.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': hosted.contentType }).end(hosted.body)
})
await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.listen(4070, resolve))
```

## Create a status list

:::issuer

```ts
const statusListUri = 'http://localhost:4070/status-lists/1'

const { statusList: statusListJwt } = await issuer.tokenStatusList.createTokenStatusList<'jwt'>({
  format: 'jwt',
  signer: { method: 'did', didUrl: issuerDidUrl },
  alg: 'EdDSA',
  // A new list has every entry set to 0 (valid)
  statusList: { statusListLength: 100_000, bitsPerStatus: 1 },
  statusListUri,
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000),
  // Seconds a verifier may cache the list
  timeToLive: 60 * 60,
})

hostedStatusLists.set('/status-lists/1', { contentType: 'application/statuslist+jwt', body: statusListJwt })
```

:::

- `format` is `jwt` for SD-JWT VC and `cwt` for mdoc.
- `statusList` sets the number of entries and the bits per entry (1, 2, 4 or 8). The statuses are 0 (valid), 1 (invalid) and 2 (suspended), so suspension needs at least 2 bits. Every entry starts at 0.
- `statusListUri` is the URL where you host the token. It becomes the `sub` claim, and verification fails when it doesn't match the URL in the credential.
- `signer` is `{ method: 'did', didUrl }` or `{ method: 'x5c', x5c }`, with a key in the agent's KMS. CWT lists need `x5c`.

`expiresAt` and `timeToLive` set `exp` and `ttl`, where `ttl` tells verifiers how long they may cache the list. The result has the encoded token in `statusList` and the parsed token in `parsed`. Pass the format as type parameter, such as `createTokenStatusList<'jwt'>`, to get the matching result type.

## Reference the list from a credential

For an SD-JWT VC, add a `status` claim to the payload:

:::issuer

```ts
// Your app allocates the index and remembers which credential uses it
const statusListIndex = 4821

const credential = await issuer.sdJwtVc.sign({
  payload: {
    vct: 'https://credentials.example.com/identity',
    given_name: 'Jane',
    status: { status_list: { idx: statusListIndex, uri: statusListUri } },
  },
  issuer: { method: 'did', didUrl: issuerDidUrl },
  holder: { method: 'jwk', jwk: holderJwk },
  disclosureFrame: { _sd: ['given_name'] },
})
```

:::

The `status` claim can't be selectively disclosable. For an mdoc, pass `statusInfo: { index, uri }` to `agent.mdoc.sign` (see [mdoc](#mdoc) below).

## Revoke or suspend

Set the new status in the current token, and host the result:

:::issuer

```ts
// Load the current token (from your own storage, or fetch it), then set the new status
const { statusList: currentToken } = await issuer.tokenStatusList.fetchTokenStatusList<'jwt'>({
  uri: statusListUri,
  acceptedFormats: ['jwt'],
})

const { statusList: updatedStatusListJwt } = await issuer.tokenStatusList.updateTokenStatusList<'jwt'>({
  format: 'jwt',
  token: currentToken,
  // 0 = valid, 1 = invalid (revoked), 2 = suspended. Needs `bitsPerStatus: 2` or more for 2.
  status: { index: statusListIndex, status: 1 },
  signer: { method: 'did', didUrl: issuerDidUrl },
  alg: 'EdDSA',
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000),
})

hostedStatusLists.set('/status-lists/1', { contentType: 'application/statuslist+jwt', body: updatedStatusListJwt })
```

:::

`status` takes one `{ index, status }` or an array, so you can change many entries in one update. The update keeps the URL, sets a new `iat`, and keeps `exp` and `ttl` unless you pass new values, so pass `expiresAt` again when the list should stay valid longer. `fetchTokenStatusList` downloads and parses a token, but doesn't verify its signature: load the current token from your own storage if you can.

## Verify

`agent.sdJwtVc.verify` fetches the status list of a credential with a `status` claim, verifies its signature and reads the entry:

:::verifier

```ts
const validResult = await verifier.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: credential.compact })
console.log(validResult.isValid) // true
```

:::

After the update the same credential fails:

:::verifier

```ts
const revokedResult = await verifier.sdJwtVc.verify({ compactSdJwtVc: credential.compact })
if (revokedResult.isValid === false) {
  // 'Status is not valid'
  console.log(revokedResult.error.message)
}
```

:::

Any status other than 0 fails verification, including suspended, and `disableStatusValidation: true` skips the check. Credo fetches the list on every verification, with the agent's `fetch`.

Which key may sign the status list depends on the [trusted issuer](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md) that matched the credential:

- No trusted issuers configured (DID issuers only): the list must be signed with the credential issuer's key.
- A trusted DID: the list's `iss` must be that DID.
- A trusted X.509 issuer: the list's certificate chain must chain to the `status` certificates of the trusted issuer. Without `status`, it must chain to the `issuance` certificates and be the same chain that signed the credential.

### mdoc

mdoc status lists are CWTs signed with an X.509 certificate, and need an expiration time. Verification of an mdoc, and of a device response, checks the status the same way: any status other than valid fails.

```ts
// mdoc status lists are CWTs, signed with the issuer certificate
const issuerKey = await issuer.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })
const issuerCertificate = await issuer.x509.createCertificate({
  authorityKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(issuerKey.publicJwk),
  issuer: { commonName: 'Example mDL Issuer', countryName: 'NL' },
})

const mdocStatusListUri = 'http://localhost:4070/status-lists/mdoc-1'
const { statusList: statusListCwt } = await issuer.tokenStatusList.createTokenStatusList<'cwt'>({
  format: 'cwt',
  signer: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate] },
  alg: 'ES256',
  statusList: { statusListLength: 100_000, bitsPerStatus: 1 },
  statusListUri: mdocStatusListUri,
  // Required for mdoc
  expiresAt: new Date(Date.now() + 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000),
})
hostedStatusLists.set('/status-lists/mdoc-1', { contentType: 'application/statuslist+cwt', body: statusListCwt })

const mdoc = await issuer.mdoc.sign({
  docType: 'org.iso.18013.5.1.mDL',
  namespaces: { 'org.iso.18013.5.1': { family_name: 'Doe', issuing_country: 'NL' } },
  validityInfo: { validUntil: new Date(Date.now() + 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) },
  issuerCertificate,
  holderKey: holderJwk,
  statusInfo: { index: statusListIndex, uri: mdocStatusListUri },
})

const { statusList: updatedStatusListCwt } = await issuer.tokenStatusList.updateTokenStatusList<'cwt'>({
  format: 'cwt',
  token: statusListCwt,
  status: { index: statusListIndex, status: 1 },
  signer: { method: 'x5c', x5c: [issuerCertificate] },
  alg: 'ES256',
})
hostedStatusLists.set('/status-lists/mdoc-1', { contentType: 'application/statuslist+cwt', body: updatedStatusListCwt })

const mdocResult = await verifier.mdoc.verify(Mdoc.fromBase64Url(mdoc.base64Url), {
  trustedCertificates: [issuerCertificate.toString('pem')],
})
console.log(mdocResult.isValid) // false
```

As with SD-JWT VC, the status list must be signed by the same certificate chain as the mdoc, unless you trust a separate status list certificate with `trustedCertificates: [{ issuance: [...], status: [...] }]`.

# DIDs

> Choose between X.509 certificates and DIDs, pick a DID method, and create, resolve and import DIDs with agent.dids.

Credo uses DIDs to sign and verify credentials, as AnonCreds issuer identifiers, and for DIDComm connections. `agent.dids` creates, resolves and imports DIDs, and keeps track of the ones your agent controls. For what DIDs are, see [DIDs and DIDComm](https://credo.js.org/guides/concepts/did-and-didcomm.md).

## X.509 certificates or DIDs

An issuer signs with a key that's bound to an [X.509 certificate](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/x509.md) or to a DID. The credential format and the ecosystem usually decide which one:

| You issue | Identify the issuer with |
| --- | --- |
| mdoc | An X.509 certificate. mdoc doesn't support DIDs. |
| SD-JWT VC for HAIP or EUDI wallets | An X.509 certificate chain (`x5c`) that leads to a root the verifier trusts. |
| SD-JWT VC in other ecosystems | An X.509 certificate or a DID. |
| W3C VC | A DID. W3C credentials can't be signed with a certificate. |
| AnonCreds | A DID on the network of the [AnonCreds registry](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/anoncreds.md). |

As a rule of thumb: use X.509 certificates for OpenID4VC, and DIDs for DIDComm and AnonCreds. OpenID4VP verifiers make the same choice for their client identifier, see [Verifying credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/verifier.md). How a verifier decides whether to accept the signer is on [Trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md).

## Choose a DID method

| You need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| A holder DID, or a DID for tests | `did:key` (default) or `did:jwk`. The DID contains the public key, so there's nothing to publish. |
| DIDComm connections | `did:peer`. DIDComm creates these for each connection. |
| A public issuer DID without a ledger | `did:web` (default) to host a DID document under your domain. `did:webvh` adds a verifiable history of the document, and can hold AnonCreds objects. |
| An AnonCreds issuer on a ledger | The method of the network your ecosystem uses: `did:indy` (Indy networks such as Sovrin), `did:cheqd` or `did:hedera`. |

## Supported DID methods

| Method | Create | Update | Deactivate | Resolve | Package |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `did:key` | Yes | No | No | Yes | `@credo-ts/core` |
| `did:jwk` | Yes | No | No | Yes | `@credo-ts/core` |
| `did:peer` | Yes | No | No | Yes | `@credo-ts/core` |
| `did:web` | Import only | No | No | Yes | `@credo-ts/core` |
| `did:webvh` | Yes | Yes | No | Yes | [`@credo-ts/webvh`](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/webvh.md) |
| `did:cheqd` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | [`@credo-ts/cheqd`](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/cheqd.md) |
| `did:indy` | Yes | No | No | Yes | [`@credo-ts/indy-vdr`](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/indy-vdr.md) |
| `did:sov` | No | No | No | Yes | [`@credo-ts/indy-vdr`](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/indy-vdr.md) |
| `did:hedera` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | [`@credo-ts/hedera`](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/hedera.md) |

## Create a DID

`agent.dids.create` creates the DID and its keys, registers it when the method needs that, and stores a `DidRecord`. The record links the verification methods to the keys in the [KMS](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md), so the agent can sign with the DID later.

```ts
const { didState } = await agent.dids.create<KeyDidCreateOptions>({
  method: 'key',
  options: { createKey: { type: { kty: 'OKP', crv: 'Ed25519' } } },
})

// Registrars report failures in the result instead of throwing
if (didState.state !== 'finished') {
  throw new Error(`Creating the did failed: ${didState.state === 'failed' ? didState.reason : didState.state}`)
}

// A did:key has one verification method, identified by the key fingerprint
const didKey = DidKey.fromDid(didState.did)
const verificationMethodId = `${didKey.did}#${didKey.publicJwk.fingerprint}`
```

The generic parameter (`KeyDidCreateOptions`, `JwkDidCreateOptions`, `CheqdDidCreateOptions`, and so on) types the options for the method. Registrars return failures instead of throwing, so always check `didState.state`:

- `finished`: `didState.did` and `didState.didDocument` are set.
- `failed`: `didState.reason` says why.
- `action` or `wait`: the method needs another step, for example an endorsement of an Indy transaction.

To use a key that's already in the KMS, pass its `keyId` instead of `createKey`:

```ts
const { keyId } = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })

const jwkResult = await agent.dids.create<JwkDidCreateOptions>({
  method: 'jwk',
  options: { keyId },
})
if (jwkResult.didState.state !== 'finished') throw new Error('Creating the did:jwk failed')

// The verification method of a did:jwk is always `#0`
const jwkVerificationMethodId = `${jwkResult.didState.did}#0`
```

## Resolve a DID

```ts
const resolution = await agent.dids.resolve(didState.did)
if (!resolution.didDocument) {
  throw new Error(`Resolving failed: ${resolution.didResolutionMetadata.error}`)
}

// resolveDidDocument returns the document, or throws when resolution fails
const didDocument = await agent.dids.resolveDidDocument(didState.did)
const verificationMethod = didDocument.dereferenceKey(verificationMethodId, ['assertionMethod'])
```

`resolve` returns the full resolution result, with `didResolutionMetadata.error` when resolution fails. `resolveDidDocument` returns only the document and throws on failure.

Credo caches resolved documents for 5 minutes for methods whose resolver allows it (`did:web`, `did:webvh`, `did:cheqd`, `did:indy`, `did:sov` and `did:hedera`). Pass `{ useCache: false }` to `resolve` to skip the cache, or `cacheDurationInSeconds` to change the duration. For DIDs that you created or imported, these resolvers (except `did:sov`) return the document from your `DidRecord` instead of fetching it.

## Import a DID

Import a DID that you created outside Credo, such as a `did:web` (there's no `did:web` registrar) or an existing ledger DID. `keys` links verification methods in the document to keys in the KMS. Without it the agent can resolve the DID, but not sign with it.

```ts
const did = 'did:web:issuer.example.com'
const webKey = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })

const webVerificationMethod = getMultikey({
  did,
  verificationMethodId: `${did}#key-1`,
  publicJwk: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(webKey.publicJwk),
})

const webDidDocument = new DidDocumentBuilder(did)
  .addContext('https://w3id.org/security/multikey/v1')
  .addVerificationMethod(webVerificationMethod)
  .addAuthentication(webVerificationMethod.id)
  .addAssertionMethod(webVerificationMethod.id)
  .build()

await agent.dids.import({
  did,
  didDocument: webDidDocument,
  // Links the verification method to the KMS key, so the agent can sign with this did
  keys: [{ didDocumentRelativeKeyId: '#key-1', kmsKeyId: webKey.keyId }],
})

// Host this JSON at https://issuer.example.com/.well-known/did.json
const didJson = webDidDocument.toJSON()
```

`PublicJwk` comes from `@credo-ts/core/kms`. Without `didDocument`, Credo resolves the DID to get the document. Importing a DID that already exists throws, unless you pass `overwrite: true`.

To list the DIDs your agent created or imported, use `getCreatedDids`, optionally filtered by `method` or `did`:

```ts
const createdWebDids = await agent.dids.getCreatedDids({ method: 'web' })
```

## Configure DID methods

`DidsModule` is registered by default under the key `dids`, with these registrars and resolvers:

- Registrars: `did:key`, `did:peer` and `did:jwk`.
- Resolvers: `did:web`, `did:key`, `did:peer` and `did:jwk`.

To add a method, register `DidsModule` yourself. The packages for ledger and web methods don't add their registrar and resolver to `DidsModule`, so you always list them:

```ts
import {
  Agent,
  DidsModule,
  JwkDidRegistrar,
  JwkDidResolver,
  KeyDidRegistrar,
  KeyDidResolver,
  PeerDidRegistrar,
  PeerDidResolver,
  WebDidResolver,
} from '@credo-ts/core'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
import { WebVhDidRegistrar, WebVhDidResolver, WebVhModule } from '@credo-ts/webvh'

const didModules = {
  webvh: new WebVhModule(),
  dids: new DidsModule({
    // These lists replace the defaults, so include the built-in methods you still need
    registrars: [new KeyDidRegistrar(), new PeerDidRegistrar(), new JwkDidRegistrar(), new WebVhDidRegistrar()],
    resolvers: [
      new KeyDidResolver(),
      new PeerDidResolver(),
      new JwkDidResolver(),
      new WebDidResolver(),
      new WebVhDidResolver(),
    ],
  }),
}
```

:::warning[Your lists replace the defaults]
Passing `registrars` or `resolvers` replaces the default list. Credo adds the `did:key` and `did:peer` registrar and resolver back, because DIDComm needs them, but not `did:web` and `did:jwk`. Include `WebDidResolver`, `JwkDidResolver` and `JwkDidRegistrar` yourself if you still need them.
:::

`publicDidMethods` lists the methods whose documents are the same for every agent context. With [multi-tenancy](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/multi-tenancy.md), their documents are cached once for all tenants instead of per tenant. The default is `['web', 'indy', 'sov', 'cheqd', 'hedera', 'webvh']`.

## Next steps

- [X.509 certificates](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/x509.md): Create self-signed and CA-issued X.509 certificates and certificate signing requests with agent.x509, parse certificates, validate chains and check revocation.
- [Trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md): How Credo decides whether to trust the issuer of a credential or the signer of a request, what it does by default, and how to configure trust with getTrustedIssuersForVerification and trusted X.509 certificates.
- [cheqd](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/cheqd.md): Create, update and deactivate did:cheqd DIDs, publish DID-linked resources, and use cheqd as an AnonCreds registry with @credo-ts/cheqd.
- [Indy VDR](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/indy-vdr.md): Connect to Hyperledger Indy networks with @credo-ts/indy-vdr to resolve did:indy and did:sov, register did:indy DIDs with an endorser, and use Indy as an AnonCreds registry.
- [Hedera](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/hedera.md): Create, update, deactivate and resolve did:hedera DIDs, and use Hedera as an AnonCreds registry with @credo-ts/hedera.
- [did:webvh](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/webvh.md): Create, update and resolve did:webvh DIDs with @credo-ts/webvh, host the DID log, and use did:webvh as an AnonCreds registry.

# X.509 certificates

> Create self-signed and CA-issued X.509 certificates and certificate signing requests with agent.x509, parse certificates, validate chains and check revocation.

mdoc issuers, SD-JWT VC issuers and OpenID4VP verifiers often sign with a key that's bound to an X.509 certificate instead of a DID. `agent.x509` creates certificates and certificate signing requests (CSRs), validates certificate chains and creates certificate revocation lists (CRLs). How a verifier decides which certificates to trust is on [Trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md).

In the examples, one agent plays the certificate authority (CA) and a second agent is a verifier. They use these imports:

```ts
import {
  Agent,
  CredoWebCrypto,
  X509Certificate,
  X509CertificateRevocationListEntryReason,
  X509ExtendedKeyUsage,
  X509KeyUsage,
  X509Module,
  X509RevocationCheckMode,
  X509ValidationError,
} from '@credo-ts/core'
import { PublicJwk } from '@credo-ts/core/kms'
import { agentDependencies } from '@credo-ts/node'
```

## Create a CA certificate

A CA signs the certificates of issuers or verifiers, and whoever checks those certificates trusts the root certificate of the CA. For mdoc issuers, this root is the issuing authority CA (IACA). Create a key in the [KMS](https://credo.js.org/guides/agent-setup/key-management.md) and a self-signed certificate for it:

```ts
const rootKey = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })
const rootPublicJwk = PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(rootKey.publicJwk)

// Without a subjectPublicKey the certificate is self-signed
const rootCertificate = await agent.x509.createCertificate({
  authorityKey: rootPublicJwk,
  issuer: { commonName: 'Example Root CA', countryName: 'NL' },
  validity: { notBefore: new Date(), notAfter: new Date(Date.now() + 5 * oneYear) },
  extensions: {
    subjectKeyIdentifier: { include: true },
    keyUsage: { usages: [X509KeyUsage.KeyCertSign, X509KeyUsage.CrlSign], markAsCritical: true },
    basicConstraints: { ca: true, pathLenConstraint: 0, markAsCritical: true },
  },
})

const rootCertificatePem = rootCertificate.toString('pem')
```

Without `subjectPublicKey`, the `authorityKey` signs its own certificate and `issuer` is also the subject. Passing `subject` for a self-signed certificate throws. `pathLenConstraint: 0` lets this CA sign end-entity certificates, but no intermediate CAs.

`issuer` and `subject` take `commonName`, `countryName`, `stateOrProvinceName` and `organizationalUnit`. For other name attributes, pass a distinguished name string such as `'CN=Example Root CA, O=Example, C=NL'`.

## Issue a certificate

Sign a certificate for another key with the CA key. This one is an issuer certificate:

```ts
const issuerKey = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })

const issuerCertificate = await agent.x509.createCertificate({
  authorityKey: rootPublicJwk,
  subjectPublicKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(issuerKey.publicJwk),
  issuer: rootCertificate.subject,
  subject: { commonName: 'Example Issuer', countryName: 'NL' },
  validity: { notBefore: new Date(), notAfter: new Date(Date.now() + oneYear) },
  extensions: {
    authorityKeyIdentifier: { include: true },
    subjectKeyIdentifier: { include: true },
    keyUsage: { usages: [X509KeyUsage.DigitalSignature], markAsCritical: true },
    // Document signer usage, required for mdoc issuer certificates
    extendedKeyUsage: { usages: [X509ExtendedKeyUsage.MdlDs], markAsCritical: true },
    // An SD-JWT VC `iss` must match a SAN URI, or its host a SAN DNS name
    subjectAlternativeName: { name: [{ type: 'dns', value: 'issuer.example.com' }] },
  },
})

// The certificate keeps the KMS key id of the subject key, so Credo can sign with it
console.log(issuerCertificate.keyId === issuerKey.keyId)
```

Credo signs with `authorityKey`, so it must be a key in the agent's KMS. The certificate gets the key id of `subjectPublicKey`, which lets the agent that holds that key sign with the certificate.

The extensions and subject alternative names (SANs) depend on what the certificate is for:

| Certificate | What it needs |
| --- | --- |
| CA, or mdoc IACA | `basicConstraints` with `ca: true`, and a key usage with `KeyCertSign`, plus `CrlSign` if the CA signs CRLs. Credo rejects a CA certificate without `basicConstraints`, or with a key usage that lacks these. |
| mdoc issuer (document signer) | A country (`countryName`) in the subject, `DigitalSignature` key usage, and the `MdlDs` extended key usage. Credo checks the country but not the extended key usage, which ISO 18013-5 requires. See [mdoc](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/mdoc.md). |
| SD-JWT VC issuer | When the credential has an `iss`, a SAN URI equal to it, or a SAN DNS name equal to its host. Without `iss`, no SAN is needed. See [SD-JWT VC](https://credo.js.org/guides/credential-formats/sd-jwt-vc.md). |
| OpenID4VP verifier (access certificate) | With the `x509_san_dns` client id prefix (the default), the host of the verifier's `baseUrl` as a SAN DNS name. With `x509_hash`, no SAN is needed. See [Verifying credentials](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/openid4vc/verifier.md). |
| mdoc reader (DC API reader authentication) | No specific extensions: the wallet checks that the chain leads to a reader certificate it trusts. See [Digital Credentials API](https://credo.js.org/guides/protocols/dc-api/verifier.md#sign-the-requests). |

## Configure the X.509 module

`X509Module` is registered by default under the key `x509`. Register it yourself to pass options:

```ts
const verifierAgent = new Agent({
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
    x509: new X509Module({
      trustedCertificates: [rootCertificatePem],
      revocationCheck: { mode: X509RevocationCheckMode.SoftFail },
    }),
  },
})
```

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `trustedCertificates` | PEM or base64 DER strings, or `X509Certificate` instances. Credo uses them as trust anchors when nothing else decides trust, see [Trusted issuers](https://credo.js.org/guides/dids-and-trust/trust.md). |
| `getTrustedCertificatesForVerification` | Deprecated. Use the agent's `getTrustedIssuersForVerification` callback instead. |
| `revocationCheck` | Enables CRL checking during chain validation. See [Revocation](#revocation). |

To change the trusted certificates at runtime, use `agent.x509.config.addTrustedCertificate(certificate)` or `agent.x509.config.setTrustedCertificates(certificates)`.

## Certificate signing requests

When the key holder and the CA are different parties, the key holder sends a CSR. Here the verifier requests an access certificate:

```ts
// Verifier: create a key and a certificate signing request (CSR) for it
const verifierKey = await verifierAgent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })

const csr = await verifierAgent.x509.createCertificateSigningRequest({
  subjectPublicKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(verifierKey.publicJwk),
  subject: { commonName: 'Example Verifier', countryName: 'NL' },
  extensions: {
    // With the x509_san_dns client id prefix, the verifier's host must be a SAN DNS name
    subjectAlternativeName: { name: [{ type: 'dns', value: 'verifier.example.com' }] },
  },
})
const encodedCsr = csr.toString('pem')

// CA: parse the CSR and check its signature, which proves possession of the key
const receivedCsr = agent.x509.parseCertificateSigningRequest({ encodedCertificateSigningRequest: encodedCsr })
await receivedCsr.verify(new CredoWebCrypto(agent.context))

const accessCertificate = await agent.x509.createCertificate({
  authorityKey: rootPublicJwk,
  subjectPublicKey: receivedCsr.publicJwk,
  issuer: rootCertificate.subject,
  subject: receivedCsr.subject,
  validity: { notBefore: new Date(), notAfter: new Date(Date.now() + oneYear) },
  extensions: {
    authorityKeyIdentifier: { include: true },
    keyUsage: { usages: [X509KeyUsage.DigitalSignature], markAsCritical: true },
    subjectAlternativeName: { name: receivedCsr.sanDnsNames.map((value) => ({ type: 'dns', value })) },
  },
})
const accessCertificatePem = accessCertificate.toString('pem')
```

`parseCertificateSigningRequest` doesn't check the CSR signature. Call `verify` to make sure the requester holds the private key. The CA decides which extensions go into the certificate: copy only the values from the CSR that you've checked.

## Parse a certificate

`X509Certificate.fromEncodedCertificate` parses a PEM or base64 DER certificate. A parsed certificate has no key id, so set `keyId` to the KMS key id before you sign with it:

```ts
// Verifier: parse the certificate returned by the CA and link it to the KMS key
const verifierCertificate = X509Certificate.fromEncodedCertificate(accessCertificatePem)
verifierCertificate.keyId = verifierKey.keyId

console.log(verifierCertificate.subject, verifierCertificate.sanDnsNames)
```

Getters include `subject`, `issuer`, `sanDnsNames`, `sanUriNames`, `keyUsage`, `extendedKeyUsage`, `isCertificateAuthority`, `crlDistributionPoints` and `publicJwk`. Encode a certificate with `toString('pem')` or `toString('base64')`, and compare two with `equal`.

## Validate a certificate chain

```ts
const validatedChain = await verifierAgent.x509.validateCertificateChain({
  // Leaf first, as in an x5c header. The root may be left out when it is a trusted certificate.
  certificateChain: [issuerCertificate.toString('base64')],
  trustedCertificates: [rootCertificatePem],
})

// The chain starts at the trust anchor and ends with the leaf
console.log(
  validatedChain[0].equal(rootCertificate),
  validatedChain[validatedChain.length - 1].equal(issuerCertificate)
)
```

Pass the chain leaf first, as in an `x5c` header. The chain may leave out the root if it's in `trustedCertificates`. On success Credo returns the chain from the trust anchor to the leaf. On failure it throws an `X509ValidationError`, whose `validationResult.validations` shows which check failed.

Credo checks the signatures and validity periods, basic constraints, the `keyCertSign` key usage of CA certificates, path length constraints, critical extensions, and revocation when enabled. It doesn't check OCSP, name constraints or certificate policies, and it doesn't enforce extended key usage.

:::caution
Without `trustedCertificates`, Credo validates the chain but doesn't check that it ends at a certificate you trust. The module's `trustedCertificates` aren't used here.
:::

`allowNonRootTrustedCertificate` defaults to `true`: a trusted intermediate or leaf certificate acts as the trust anchor, and Credo doesn't verify its signature. ISO 18013-5 needs this, because mdoc issuers don't include the root in the chain. Set it to `false` to require that trusted certificates are verified up to a self-signed root. The default may change in a future version.

## Revocation

Credo checks revocation with CRLs, from the URLs in a certificate's `crlDistributionPoints`. Revocation checking is off unless you set `revocationCheck` on the module:

| Mode | Behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `X509RevocationCheckMode.SoftFail` | Default when `revocationCheck` is set. Rejects revoked certificates and invalid CRLs, and skips the check when the CRL can't be downloaded. |
| `X509RevocationCheckMode.Require` | Also fails when the CRL can't be downloaded. |
| `X509RevocationCheckMode.Disabled` | No revocation checks. |

Certificates without a CRL distribution point pass the check. Credo checks every certificate in the chain except the root (`checkFullChain`), and caches a CRL for an hour (`crlCacheExpirySeconds`), but never past its `nextUpdate`.

:::warning[Large CRLs]
Credo 0.7 parses CRLs with the default node limit of the ASN.1 parser (`asn1js`), which rejects CRLs with more than about 2,000 entries. Validation of a certificate whose CRL is that large fails, also in `SoftFail` mode.
:::

To revoke certificates, create a CRL signed by the CA key and publish it at the distribution point URL:

```ts
const revokedKey = await agent.kms.createKey({ type: { kty: 'EC', crv: 'P-256' } })
const revokedCertificate = await agent.x509.createCertificate({
  authorityKey: rootPublicJwk,
  subjectPublicKey: PublicJwk.fromPublicJwk(revokedKey.publicJwk),
  issuer: rootCertificate.subject,
  subject: { commonName: 'Revoked Issuer', countryName: 'NL' },
  validity: { notBefore: new Date(), notAfter: new Date(Date.now() + oneYear) },
  extensions: {
    authorityKeyIdentifier: { include: true },
    keyUsage: { usages: [X509KeyUsage.DigitalSignature], markAsCritical: true },
    crlDistributionPoints: { urls: [crlUrl] },
  },
})

const crl = await agent.x509.createCertificateRevocationList({
  authorityKey: rootPublicJwk,
  issuer: rootCertificate.subject,
  validity: { nextUpdate: new Date(Date.now() + 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000) },
  entries: [{ certificate: revokedCertificate, reason: X509CertificateRevocationListEntryReason.KeyCompromise }],
  extensions: { crlNumber: { value: 1 }, authorityKeyIdentifier: { include: true } },
})

// Serve the DER encoded CRL at the URL in the certificate's crlDistributionPoints
const crlBytes = crl.rawCertificateRevocationList
```

Validating the revoked certificate now fails on the revocation check:

```ts
try {
  await verifierAgent.x509.validateCertificateChain({
    certificateChain: [revokedCertificate.toString('base64')],
    trustedCertificates: [rootCertificatePem],
  })
} catch (error) {
  if (!(error instanceof X509ValidationError)) throw error
  // The validations show which check failed, here revocationStatus
  console.log('Rejected:', error.message, error.validationResult.validations.revocationStatus?.isValid)
}
```

# Trusted issuers

> How Credo decides whether to trust the issuer of a credential or the signer of a request, what it does by default, and how to configure trust with getTrustedIssuersForVerification and trusted X.509 certificates.

A valid signature shows that a credential is intact and who signed it. Whether you accept that signer is a separate decision: when Credo verifies a credential or a signed request, it looks up the issuers you trust for that verification and checks the signer against them.

## How Credo finds trusted issuers

Credo checks these sources in order, and the first one that returns trusted issuers decides:

1. Trusted issuers or certificates passed to the verify call, such as `trustedIssuers` on `agent.sdJwtVc.verify`.
2. The agent's `getTrustedIssuersForVerification` callback.
3. The X.509 module's `getTrustedCertificatesForVerification` callback (deprecated, X.509 only).
4. The X.509 module's `trustedCertificates` (X.509 only).

What happens when no source returns trusted issuers depends on how the object is signed:

| Signer | No trusted issuers found (default) | Trusted issuers found |
| --- | --- | --- |
| X.509 certificate chain | Verification fails. | The chain must lead to one of the trusted certificates. |
| DID | Any DID is accepted. | The DID (without fragment) must be in the list. |

So an agent without trust configuration accepts credentials signed with any DID, and rejects all X.509-signed credentials. Return an empty list (`{ trustedIssuers: [] }`) to reject every signer, including DIDs. OpenID4VC objects signed with a bare `jwk` header, without a DID or certificate, aren't checked against trusted issuers.

This applies to SD-JWT VCs, mdocs, W3C credentials signed as JWT, SD-JWT or with JSON-LD proofs, and to the signed objects in OpenID4VC. AnonCreds and Data Integrity credentials don't use it.

## Which should I use?

In production, set `getTrustedIssuersForVerification` and return a list for every signer type you accept: the root certificates for X.509 signers, for example from a trust list, and the DIDs you accept for DID signers. For signer types you don't accept, return `{ trustedIssuers: [] }`. Returning `undefined` for a DID signer accepts any DID.

The X.509 module's `trustedCertificates` are enough when the agent trusts one fixed set of root certificates for everything, for example in tests. Pass `trustedIssuers` to a verify call for a one-off check.

## The `getTrustedIssuersForVerification` callback

Set the callback in the agent config. Credo calls it for each verification with the `signer` and the `verification` context:

```ts
const trustedRootCertificates = [rootCertificatePem]
const trustedIssuerDids = ['did:web:issuer.example.com']

const agent = new Agent({
  config: {
    getTrustedIssuersForVerification: async (_agentContext, { signer, verification }) => {
      // Fall through to the X.509 module configuration for anything other than credentials
      if (verification.type !== 'credential') return undefined

      if (signer.method === 'x509') {
        return { trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: trustedRootCertificates }] }
      }

      return { trustedIssuers: trustedIssuerDids.map((did) => ({ method: 'did', issuance: did })) }
    },
  },
  dependencies: agentDependencies,
  modules: {
    ...storage, // Storage and key management, see Agent setup
  },
})
```

`signer` is either `{ method: 'x509', certificateChain }` with the parsed certificates, leaf first, or `{ method: 'did', didUrl }`. Return one of:

- `{ trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'x509', issuance: [...] }] }`: the PEM or base64 DER certificates that X.509 chains must lead to.
- `{ trustedIssuers: [{ method: 'did', issuance: 'did:...' }, ...] }`: the DIDs you trust.
- `{ trustedIssuers: [] }` to reject the signer.
- `undefined` to fall through to the X.509 module configuration, or, for a DID signer, to accept it.

All returned entries must use the same `method` as the signer, otherwise verification throws.

`verification.type` tells you what Credo is verifying:

| Type | When | Package |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `credential` | Verifying a credential, including credentials the holder receives over OpenID4VCI. | `@credo-ts/core` |
| `mdocReaderAuth` | The holder checks the reader certificate of an mdoc request over the Digital Credentials API. | `@credo-ts/core` |
| `openId4VpCredential` | A verifier checks a credential in an OpenID4VP response. Includes the `openId4VcVerificationSessionRecord`. | `@credo-ts/openid4vc` |
| `oauth2SecuredAuthorizationRequest` | The holder checks a signed OpenID4VP authorization request. | `@credo-ts/openid4vc` |
| `openId4VciCredentialIssuerMetadata` | The holder checks signed credential issuer metadata. | `@credo-ts/openid4vc` |
